knowledge_statements.statement_title: Subgradient KKT Characterization for Problem (5.1)
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Necessary and sufficient optimality conditions under a relative-interior Slater-type condition.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Assume there exists \bar x\in\operatorname{ri}(\operatorname{dom}f^1)\cap\operatorname{ri}(\operatorname{dom}\mathcal Q) such that g_i^1(\bar x)<0 for i=1,\ldots,\bar m_1 and g_i^1(\bar x)=0 for i=\bar m_1+1,\ldots,m_1. Then x^* is optimal for (5.1) if and only if x^*\in K_1 and there are multipliers \lambda_i^*\geq0 for i\leq\bar m_1 and unrestricted multipliers \lambda_i^* for i>\bar m_1 such that \lambda_i^*g_i^1(x^*)=0 for i\leq\bar m_1 and 0\in\partial f^1(x^*)+\partial\mathcal Q(x^*)+\sum_{i=1}^{m_1}\lambda_i^*\partial g_i^1(x^*).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: If a relative-interior point strictly satisfies all inequalities and satisfies all equalities, then a point solves problem (5.1) exactly when it is first-stage feasible and admits multipliers satisfying the sign restrictions, complementary slackness, and subgradient stationarity.
assumptions_latex: \exists\bar x\in\operatorname{ri}(\operatorname{dom}f^1)\cap\operatorname{ri}(\operatorname{dom}\mathcal Q).
g_i^1(\bar x)<0\quad(i=1,\ldots,\bar m_1).
g_i^1(\bar x)=0\quad(i=\bar m_1+1,\ldots,m_1).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: x^*\text{ solves (5.1)}\iff\left\{\begin{array}{l}x^*\in K_1,\\ \exists\lambda^*:\ \lambda_i^*\geq0\ (i\leq\bar m_1),\ \lambda_i^*g_i^1(x^*)=0\ (i\leq\bar m_1),\\ 0\in\partial f^1(x^*)+\partial\mathcal Q(x^*)+\sum_{i=1}^{m_1}\lambda_i^*\partial g_i^1(x^*)\end{array}\right.

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Almost-Sure Slater Condition for Recourse
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Scenario-wise strict feasibility for every first-stage decision with finite expected recourse.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: \forall x\text{ such that }\mathcal Q(x)<\infty,\quad \text{for almost every }\omega\in\Omega,\ \exists y(\omega):\ g_i^2(x,y(\omega),\omega)<0\ \ (i=1,\ldots,\bar m_2),\quad g_i^2(x,y(\omega),\omega)=0\ \ (i=\bar m_2+1,\ldots,m_2).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: For every first-stage decision having finite expected recourse, almost every scenario admits a second-stage decision that strictly satisfies all inequality constraints and exactly satisfies all equality constraints.
assumptions_latex: \mathcal Q(x)<\infty
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \text{For almost every }\omega\in\Omega,\ \exists y(\omega)\text{ satisfying the recourse inequalities strictly and the equalities exactly.}

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Two-Stage Stochastic Nonlinear Program with Recourse
knowledge_statements.scope_note: General two-stage nonlinear recourse model and its first-stage, scenario-feasibility, and expected-value domains.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: \inf_{x\in K_1}\{f^1(x)+\mathcal Q(x)\},\qquad \mathcal Q(x)=\mathbb E_\omega[Q(x,\omega)],\qquad Q(x,\omega)=\inf_{y\in Y(x,\omega)}f^2(x,y,\omega),\quad K_1=\{x:g_i^1(x)\leq0\ (i\leq\bar m_1),\ g_i^1(x)=0\ (i>\bar m_1)\},\quad Y(x,\omega)=\{y:g_i^2(x,y,\omega)\leq0\ (i\leq\bar m_2),\ g_i^2(x,y,\omega)=0\ (i>\bar m_2)\},\quad K_2(\omega)=\{x:Y(x,\omega)\neq\varnothing\},\qquad K_2=\{x:\mathcal Q(x)<\infty\}.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A two-stage stochastic nonlinear program minimizes first-stage cost plus expected optimal second-stage cost subject to first-stage constraints. For each scenario, the recourse value is the infimum over feasible second-stage decisions. K1 is the first-stage feasible set, K2(omega) contains decisions admitting feasible recourse in that scenario, and K2 is the finite effective domain of expected recourse.
assumptions_latex: f^1\text{ and all }g_i^1\text{ are continuous}
\forall\omega,\ f^2(\cdot,\cdot,\omega)\text{ and all }g_i^2(\cdot,\cdot,\omega)\text{ are continuous}
\forall(x,y),\ f^2(x,y,\cdot)\text{ and all }g_i^2(x,y,\cdot)\text{ are measurable}
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: Q(x,\cdot)\text{ is measurable and }\mathcal Q(x)=\mathbb E_\omega[Q(x,\omega)]\text{ is well-defined under the stated conditions.}

children.title: Stage Structure
children.top_down_role: Information-based partitions of the recourse model.

knowledge_statements.title: Stage Structure
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Information-based stage definition for a finite multistage recourse model.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \((\Omega,\mathcal F,(\mathcal F_t)_{t=0}^{T},\mathbb P)\) be a filtered probability space. Stage \(t\in\{0,\ldots,T\}\) groups the decisions made with information \(\mathcal F_t\). A stage decision \(x_t:\Omega\to\mathsf X_t\) is admissible only if it is \(\mathcal F_t\)-measurable and satisfies \(x_t(\omega)\in\mathcal X_t(x_{0:t-1}(\omega),\omega)\) almost surely. For \(t<T\), it is selected before information newly revealed between \(\mathcal F_t\) and \(\mathcal F_{t+1}\) becomes available. Calendar intervals may be grouped into one stage when they share the same decision-relevant information.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A stage groups decisions made with the same available information. Each stage decision must be measurable with respect to that information and feasible given prior decisions; calendar intervals may share a stage when their decision-relevant information is the same.
assumptions_latex: The uncertainty process is defined on a filtered probability space \((\Omega,\mathcal F,(\mathcal F_t)_{t=0}^T,\mathbb P)\).
For every stage \(t\), \(\mathsf X_t\) is a measurable decision space and \(\mathcal X_t\) is its feasible-decision correspondence.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: A stage is characterized by its available-information sigma-field, and every admissible stage decision is measurable with respect to that sigma-field and satisfies its feasibility constraint almost surely.

notation.meaning: measurable decision space at stage t

knowledge_statements.statement_title: History-adapted multistage assembly recursion
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Finite-horizon inventory and production model with nonanticipative ordering and conditional continuation values.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Let \(D_{[t]}=(D_1,\ldots,D_t)\). The order \(x_{t-1}\), chosen before observing \(D_t\), may depend only on \(D_{[t-1]}\), whereas \(z_t\) and \(y_t\) may depend on \(D_{[t]}\). At the terminal stage,
\[
Q_T(x_{T-1},y_{T-1},d_T)=\min_{z_T,y_T}\left\{(l-q)^\top z_T-s^\top y_T:y_T=y_{T-1}+x_{T-1}-A^\top z_T,\ 0\le z_T\le d_T,\ y_T\ge0\right\}.
\]
For \(t<T\),
\[
Q_t(x_{t-1},y_{t-1},d_{[t]})=\min_{z_t,y_t,x_t}\left\{(l-q)^\top z_t+h^\top y_t+c^\top x_t+\mathcal Q_{t+1}(x_t,y_t,d_{[t]})\right\}
\]
subject to \(y_t=y_{t-1}+x_{t-1}-A^\top z_t\), \(0\le z_t\le d_t\), and \(y_t\ge0\), where
\[
\mathcal Q_{t+1}(x_t,y_t,d_{[t]})=\mathbb E\left[Q_{t+1}(x_t,y_t,D_{[t+1]})\mid D_{[t]}=d_{[t]}\right].
\]
For fixed initial inventory \(y_0\), suppressed in the source notation, the initial order solves
\[
\min_{x_0\ge0}\left\{c^\top x_0+\mathbb E[Q_1(x_0,D_1)]\right\}.
\]
When \(T=1\), this reduces to the corresponding two-stage model.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: An order placed before a period's demand can use only earlier demand history, while production and end-of-period inventory may also use the current demand. Conditional expected continuation values connect adjacent stages and define a backward recursion. The initial order minimizes its cost plus the expected first-stage value, and the one-period case reduces to the two-stage model.
assumptions_latex: T\in\mathbb{N},\quad D_t\in\mathbb{R}_+^n,\quad A\in\mathbb{R}_+^{n\times m}
x_t,y_t\in\mathbb{R}_+^m,\quad z_t\in\mathbb{R}_+^n
x_{t-1}\text{ is }\sigma(D_{[t-1]})\text{-measurable}
z_t,y_t,x_t\text{ are }\sigma(D_{[t]})\text{-measurable}
y_0\text{ is fixed, costs and prices are time-independent, and the displayed conditional expectations are well-defined}
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \text{The history-adapted multistage model has the stated conditional-expectation backward recursion, with the two-stage model recovered when }T=1.

children.title: Period Structure
children.top_down_role: Physical-time partitions used by the model.

knowledge_statements.title: Period Structure
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Calendar-time period structure distinguished from information-based stages and decision epochs.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(\tau_0<\cdots<\tau_K\) be calendar boundaries. The periods \(I_k=[\tau_k,\tau_{k+1})\), for \(k\in\{0,ldots,K-1\}\), form an ordered partition of the modeled horizon \([\tau_0,\tau_K)\). Model components such as states, costs, exogenous events, decisions, and transitions may be assigned to a period or to specified points within it. Period boundaries represent physical or accounting time and need not be decision epochs or information-stage boundaries; a period may contain several decision epochs, and several periods may lie within one information stage.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Periods partition modeled calendar time. States, costs, observations, decisions, and transitions may be assigned within them, but period boundaries need not coincide with decision epochs or information stages.
assumptions_latex: The modeled calendar horizon is \([\tau_0,\tau_K)\), where \(K\in\mathbb N\) and \(\tau_0<\cdots<\tau_K\).
Events assigned within each period have a specified chronological order.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: Periods partition physical or accounting time, whereas stages partition decision-relevant information and decision epochs locate individual decisions; these temporal units need not coincide.

children.title: Decision Epoch Placement
children.top_down_role: Locations where decisions enter the temporal organization.

knowledge_statements.title: Decision Epoch Placement
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Nonanticipative and causally consistent placement of decisions on an ordered event timeline.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(D=\{d_0<\cdots<d_m\}\) be decision epochs on an event timeline, and let \(\mathcal F_d\) denote the information available when the decision at \(d\) is selected. A placement is nonanticipative when \(x_d\) is \(\mathcal F_d\)-measurable for every \(d\in D\). Hence an observation revealed before or at \(d\) may affect \(x_d\), whereas an observation revealed after \(d\) may not. The placement is causally consistent when every decision controlling a transition or other modeled event is executed before that event begins.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A decision epoch is nonanticipative when its decision uses only information available at that epoch, and it is causally consistent when the decision precedes every transition or event it controls.
assumptions_latex: \(D=\{d_0<\cdots<d_m\}\) is a finite ordered set of designated decision epochs.
For each \(d\in D\), \(\mathcal F_d\) is the sigma-field available when \(x_d\) is selected.
Every controlled transition or event has a specified position on the same timeline.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: A valid placement makes every \(x_d\) measurable with respect to \(\mathcal F_d\) and places each controlling decision before the event it controls.

notation.meaning: information available when the decision at epoch d is selected

children.title: Temporal Unit Crosswalks
children.top_down_role: Mappings among stages, periods, epochs.

knowledge_statements.title: Temporal Unit Crosswalks
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Crosswalk for aggregating consecutive calendar periods into nonempty information stages.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(P=\{0,\ldots,K-1\}\) be an ordered period set and \(G=\{0,\ldots,T\}\) an ordered stage set. A period-to-stage crosswalk is a surjection \(\phi:P\to G\) such that \(k<\ell\) implies \(\phi(k)\leq\phi(\ell)\). Consequently, each fiber \(\phi^{-1}(t)\) is a nonempty consecutive block of periods. If \(c_k\) is an additive quantity for period \(k\), its stage aggregate is \(C_t=\sum_{k\in\phi^{-1}(t)}c_k\). Dynamic or linking constraints at internal period boundaries remain part of the model. The one-to-one case has \(K=T+1\) and \(\phi(k)=k\) for every \(k\in P\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A period-to-stage crosswalk is an order-preserving assignment that maps every stage to a nonempty consecutive block of periods. Additive period data may be summed by stage without removing internal dynamic constraints.
assumptions_latex: \(P=\{0,\ldots,K-1\}\) and \(G=\{0,\ldots,T\}\) are finite ordered sets.
Every period belongs to exactly one stage, every stage contains at least one period, and stage order is consistent with period order.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The crosswalk is a monotone surjection from \(P\) to \(G\), and its fibers are nonempty consecutive period blocks.

notation.meaning: additive quantity assigned to period k
stage aggregate of the additive period quantities

children.title: Decision Timing
children.top_down_role: Placement of choices within a stage.

knowledge_statements.title: Decision Timing
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Predecision timing and nonanticipativity in a discrete-stage model.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: At stage \(t\), suppose the event order is \(S_t\to x_t\to W_{t+1}\). The decision \(x_t\) is nonanticipative when it is \(\mathcal F_t\)-measurable, where \(\mathcal F_t\) is the information available before \(W_{t+1}\) is observed. It is feasible when \(x_t\in\mathcal X_t(S_t)\) almost surely. Thus \(x_t\) may depend on information contained in \(\mathcal F_t\) but may not depend on the subsequently revealed value of \(W_{t+1}\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A predecision action is selected feasibly using only the information available before the next exogenous input is observed.
assumptions_latex: \(S_t\) is measurable with respect to the predecision sigma-field \(\mathcal F_t\).
\(W_{t+1}\) is not observed when \(x_t\) is selected.
The feasible-action correspondence \(\mathcal X_t\) is measurable and nonempty almost surely.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The stage decision is nonanticipative and feasible when \(x_t\) is \(\mathcal F_t\)-measurable and \(x_t\in\mathcal X_t(S_t)\) almost surely.

notation.meaning: exogenous input revealed after the stage-t decision
information available when the stage-t decision is selected

children.title: Observation Timing
children.top_down_role: Placement of information revelation within a stage.

assumptions_latex: Exogenous information arrives at specified points of the within-stage timeline.
The filtration records all observations available by each point.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: Observation timing determines the sigma-field against which each decision must be measurable.

notation.meaning: new information revealed for stage t

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Filtration update induced by a discrete observation event.

source_refs.locator: 3 Introduction to Markov Decision Processes p. 57

knowledge_statements.statement_latex: If \(W_t\) is revealed at the stage-\(t\) observation event, the postobservation information is \(\mathcal F_t=\mathcal F_{t^-}\vee\sigma(W_t)\). A decision executed before that event must be \(\mathcal F_{t^-}\)-measurable; a decision executed afterward may be \(\mathcal F_t\)-measurable. Observation timing therefore defines which realized components of uncertainty may enter each decision rule. Information generated after a decision cannot be included in its conditioning sigma-field without violating nonanticipativity.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: An observation enlarges the information sigma-field; only decisions made afterward may depend on its realized value.
knowledge_statements.title: Observation Timing

children.title: State-Transition Timing
children.top_down_role: Placement of physical or informational state changes.

knowledge_statements.title: State-Transition Timing
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Postdecision-state representation of a controlled discrete-time transition.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Under the chronology \(S_t\to x_t\to S_t^x\to W_{t+1}\to S_{t+1}\), let \(M_t\) be the postdecision-state map and \(F_{t+1}\) the transition map. The transition factors as \(S_t^x=M_t(S_t,x_t)\) and \(S_{t+1}=F_{t+1}(S_t^x,W_{t+1})\). The postdecision state is measurable after \(x_t\) is selected and before \(W_{t+1}\) is observed; the next predecision state becomes available after \(W_{t+1}\) is observed and the transition is applied.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The action first determines a postdecision state. After the next exogenous input is observed, the transition maps that postdecision state to the next predecision state.
assumptions_latex: The current state \(S_t\) and action \(x_t\) are available before the controlled transition.
The exogenous input \(W_{t+1}\) is revealed after the postdecision state is formed.
The maps \(M_t\) and \(F_{t+1}\) are measurable on their stated domains.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The transition produces \(S_t^x\) from \((S_t,x_t)\) before observing \(W_{t+1}\), and then produces \(S_{t+1}\) from \((S_t^x,W_{t+1})\).

notation.meaning: mapping from postdecision state and new information to the next state

children.title: Within-Stage Chronology Variants
children.top_down_role: Alternative admissible sequences for stage events.

assumptions_latex: Each variant specifies a total order compatible with causal dependence.
Every decision is measurable with respect to information revealed before it.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: Different within-stage chronologies are valid when their indexing and measurability conventions consistently encode event order.
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Two standard index-consistent orderings of observation, decision, and transition.

source_refs.locator: 4.6 The Post-Decision State Variable p. 129

knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Two common consistent chronologies are the decision-then-information convention \(S_t\to x_t\to W_{t+1}\to S_{t+1}\) and the information-then-decision convention \(S_{t-1}\to W_t\to S_t\to x_t\). In the first, \(x_t\) cannot depend on \(W_{t+1}\); in the second, \(x_t\) may depend on \(W_t\). These are index-shifted representations when they describe the same physical events and use corresponding transition and cost assignments. They are not equivalent if relabeling changes which observation precedes a decision.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Decision-first and observation-first conventions can represent the same process under consistent reindexing, but differ when they grant a decision different information.
knowledge_statements.title: Within-Stage Chronology Variants

children.title: Planning Horizon Regime Family
children.top_down_role: Horizon structures used with recourse.

children.title: Finite Horizons
children.top_down_role: Recourse structures with a fixed terminal stage.

knowledge_statements.title: Finite Horizons
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Expected-cost finite-horizon formulation with decisions before an explicit terminal state.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: A finite-horizon recourse model has decision stages \(t=0,\ldots,T-1\) and a terminal state at \(T\), where \(T\in\mathbb N\) is fixed. An admissible policy \(\pi=(\pi_0,\ldots,\pi_{T-1})\) generates feasible nonanticipative decisions \(x_t=\pi_t(S_t)\). Its expected-cost objective may be written as \(J_T(\pi)=\mathbb E[\sum_{t=0}^{T-1}c_t(S_t,x_t)+g_T(S_T)]\), and the problem is \(\inf_{\pi\in\Pi_T}J_T(\pi)\), where \(\Pi_T\) is the specified class of feasible nonanticipative policies.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A finite-horizon model optimizes a feasible nonanticipative policy over finitely many decision stages and includes any specified contribution at the terminal state.
assumptions_latex: The terminal index \(T\in\mathbb N\) is fixed and finite.
Stage costs, dynamics, and constraints are specified for \(t=0,\ldots,T-1\), and the terminal contribution is specified at state \(S_T\).
The policy class \(\Pi_T\) contains the feasible nonanticipative policies under consideration.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: A finite-horizon recourse model optimizes a feasible nonanticipative policy over decision stages \(0,\ldots,T-1\) with an explicit terminal contribution at \(S_T\).

source_refs.locator: 3.2 Finite Horizon Problems p. 65

source_witnesses.locator: 3.2 Finite Horizon Problems p. 65

children.title: Rolling Horizons
children.top_down_role: Repeatedly shifted finite planning windows.

assumptions_latex: A finite look-ahead length \(H\geq1\) is fixed.
At each epoch, the current state and updated uncertainty model are available.
Each truncated problem admits a selected feasible solution.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The rolling-horizon policy repeatedly solves an updated finite-horizon problem but implements only its first decision.

notation.meaning: terminal approximation at the look-ahead boundary

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Receding-horizon implementation of repeatedly updated finite recourse models.

source_refs.locator: 3.2 Finite Horizon Problems p. 65

knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Initialize \(k=0\) and observe \(S_k\). At epoch \(k\), solve the updated \(H\)-step problem \(\inf_{\pi}\mathbb E_k[\sum_{t=k}^{k+H-1}c_t(S_t,x_t)+\widehat V_{k+H}(S_{k+H})]\) subject to the model dynamics, feasibility constraints, and nonanticipativity over the window. Select an optimizer \(\pi^{(k)}\), implement only \(x_k=\pi_k^{(k)}(S_k)\), observe the resulting information and next state, set \(k\leftarrow k+1\), and repeat until the operational stopping epoch. The output is the implemented decision sequence, not the unimplemented tails of earlier solutions.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Rolling horizon repeatedly solves an updated finite look-ahead model, implements its first decision, advances one epoch, and discards the remaining planned tail.
knowledge_statements.title: Rolling Horizons

source_witnesses.locator: 3.2 Finite Horizon Problems p. 65

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The algorithm is mathematically plausible and fits the container, but the only locator is a general finite-horizon section and is explicitly identified as indirect. A source specifically supporting receding- or rolling-horizon reoptimization and first-decision implementation is required.

children.title: Indefinite Horizons
children.top_down_role: Structures without a predetermined terminal stage.

assumptions_latex: Decisions occur at stages \(t\in\mathbb N_0\).
The objective has a stated convergence convention, such as discounting or average cost.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: An indefinite-horizon model has no fixed terminal stage and requires an objective convention that makes infinite operation mathematically meaningful.
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Infinite operational horizon with discounted- or average-cost semantics.

source_refs.locator: 3 Introduction to Markov Decision Processes p. 57

knowledge_statements.statement_latex: An indefinite-horizon recourse model has decision stages \(t\in\mathbb N_0\) and no prescribed terminal stage. A discounted formulation with \(0<\beta<1\) is \(\inf_{\pi\in\Pi_\infty}\mathbb E_\pi[\sum_{t=0}^{\infty}\beta^t c(S_t,x_t)]\), provided the series is well defined. An average-cost formulation instead uses \(\inf_{\pi\in\Pi_\infty}\limsup_{T\to\infty}(T+1)^{-1}\mathbb E_\pi[\sum_{t=0}^{T}c(S_t,x_t)]\). These criteria define distinct models and must not be interchanged without additional assumptions.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: An indefinite-horizon model has no terminal stage and must specify a valid infinite-operation criterion, commonly discounted total cost or long-run average cost.
knowledge_statements.title: Indefinite Horizons

source_witnesses.locator: 3 Introduction to Markov Decision Processes p. 57

children.title: Terminal-Boundary Effects
children.top_down_role: Structural consequences created by horizon termination or truncation.

assumptions_latex: A finite truncation ends before some action consequences are realized.
The omitted continuation value is not represented by the terminal cost.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: Zero terminal value can reverse the optimal boundary action when benefits occur beyond the truncation point.
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Concrete truncation failure caused by omitting continuation value.

source_refs.locator: 3.2 Finite Horizon Problems p. 65

knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Consider a deterministic terminal-stage action \(a\in\{0,1\}\) that incurs cost \(ca\) at stage \(T\) and yields benefit \(ba\) at stage \(T+1\), where \(0<c<b\). A truncation at \(T\) with terminal value \(g_T\equiv0\) minimizes \(ca\) and therefore selects \(a=0\). The continued model minimizes \((c-b)a\) and selects \(a=1\). Thus omitting a continuation value can change the optimal boundary decision; including the exact terminal value \(g_T(a)=-ba\) restores the continued-model choice.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A finite truncation may reject a profitable boundary action when its cost occurs inside the horizon but its benefit occurs afterward.
knowledge_statements.title: Terminal-Boundary Effects

source_witnesses.locator: 3.2 Finite Horizon Problems p. 65

children.title: Information Patterns

children.title: Perfect Observation of Revealed Uncertainty
children.top_down_role: Fully observed history after each revelation.

knowledge_statements.title: Perfect Observation of Revealed Uncertainty
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Finite-horizon, fully observed stochastic-process formulation using the uncompleted natural filtration.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For each stage \(t\in\{0,\ldots,T\}\), let \(\mathcal F_t^\xi:=\sigma(\xi_1,\ldots,\xi_t)\), with \(\mathcal F_0^\xi\) representing the initial information. Perfect observation of revealed uncertainty means that the decision maker's stage-\(t\) information is \(\mathcal G_t=\mathcal F_t^\xi\). A policy \(x=(x_0,\ldots,x_T)\) respects this information pattern when every map \(x_t:\Omega\to X_t\) is \(\mathcal G_t\)-measurable.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: At each stage, the decision maker observes the entire uncertainty history revealed so far, and each decision may depend on that history but not on later uncertainty.
assumptions_latex: A finite horizon \(t=0,\ldots,T\) is fixed.
The uncertainty process \(\xi=(\xi_1,\ldots,\xi_T)\) is defined on \((\Omega,\mathcal F,\mathbb P)\).
Each action space \(X_t\) is a measurable space.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: Every admissible decision \(x_t\) is measurable with respect to \(\mathcal F_t^\xi\), the information generated by uncertainty revealed through stage \(t\).

notation.meaning: Natural information generated by revealed uncertainty through stage t

children.title: Observation Restriction Regimes
children.top_down_role: Coarsened, censored, or lagged information.

children.title: Partial Observation
children.top_down_role: Information structures with coarsened, censored, or incomplete signals.

knowledge_statements.title: Partial Observation
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Filtration-based partial observation represented by measurable coarsenings of revealed uncertainty.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(Y_s\) be an \(\mathcal F_s^\xi\)-measurable signal for every \(s\), and define \(\mathcal G_t:=\sigma(Y_1,ldots,Y_t)\vee\mathcal G_0\), where \(\mathcal G_0\subseteq\mathcal F_0^\xi\) is the commonly known initial information. Partial observation means that \(\mathcal G_t\subseteq\mathcal F_t^\xi\) for every \(t\) and \(\mathcal G_t\subsetneq\mathcal F_t^\xi\) for at least one stage. An admissible decision \(x_t:\Omega\to X_t\) must be \(\mathcal G_t\)-measurable.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Under partial observation, decisions use signals that reveal only a coarsening of the uncertainty history, so some histories distinguishable under full observation remain indistinguishable.
assumptions_latex: A finite horizon \(t=0,\ldots,T\) is fixed.
The natural information is \(\mathcal F_t^\xi=\sigma(\xi_1,\ldots,\xi_t)\vee\mathcal F_0^\xi\).
Each signal \(Y_s\) is \(\mathcal F_s^\xi\)-measurable.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: Partial observation is characterized by \(\mathcal G_t\subseteq\mathcal F_t^\xi\) for every \(t\), with strict inclusion at some stage, and admissibility requires \(x_t\) to be \(\mathcal G_t\)-measurable.

notation.meaning: Information generated by observations available at stage t

children.title: Delayed Observation
children.top_down_role: Information structures with lagged signal availability.

assumptions_latex: A deterministic delay \(d\in\{1,\ldots,T\}\) is fixed.
The convention \(\mathcal F_s^\xi=\mathcal F_0^\xi\) is used for \(s<0\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: A delayed policy satisfies \(x_t\in L^0(\Omega,\mathcal F_{(t-d)\vee0}^\xi;X_t)\).

notation.meaning: Number of stages by which observation is delayed
Information available to the decision maker at stage t

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Fixed deterministic observation lag in discrete time.

source_refs.locator: 1.4 Problem Classes p. 11

knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For a fixed delay \(d\), delayed observation is the information pattern \(\mathcal G_t:=\mathcal F_{(t-d)\vee0}^\xi\) at every stage \(t\). Hence uncertainty revealed during stages \((t-d)+1,\ldots,t\) is unavailable when \(x_t\) is chosen. A policy is admissible precisely when each \(x_t:\Omega\to X_t\) is \(\mathcal G_t\)-measurable. More generally, stage-dependent delays \(d_t\) are represented by \(\mathcal G_t=\mathcal F_{(t-d_t)\vee0}^\xi\), provided \((\mathcal G_t)\) is nondecreasing.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: With observation delay d, the stage-t decision can use uncertainty only through stage t-d; more recent revelations remain unavailable.
knowledge_statements.title: Delayed Observation

source_witnesses.locator: 1.4 Problem Classes p. 11

children.title: Combined Observation Restrictions
children.top_down_role: Settings where signal loss coexists with revelation lag.

knowledge_statements.title: Combined Observation Restrictions
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Simultaneous signal coarsening and stage-dependent observation delay.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For each \(t\), set \(k_t:=(t-d_t)\vee0\) and define \(\mathcal G_t:=\sigma(Y_0,ldots,Y_{k_t})\), where every signal \(Y_s\) is \(\mathcal F_s^\xi\)-measurable. Then \(\mathcal G_t\subseteq\mathcal F_{k_t}^\xi\subseteq\mathcal F_t^\xi\). Provided \((\mathcal G_t)_{t=0}^T\) is nondecreasing, it is an information filtration combining signal coarsening with reporting delay. Admissibility requires each \(x_t:\Omega\to X_t\) to be \(\mathcal G_t\)-measurable.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Combined restrictions expose only coarsened signals and expose them after a delay. Decisions may depend only on the delayed signals available at their stage.
assumptions_latex: A finite horizon \(t=0,\ldots,T\) and nonnegative integer delays \(d_t\) are specified.
For every \(s\in\{0,\ldots,T\}\), the signal \(Y_s\) is \(\mathcal F_s^\xi\)-measurable.
The sigma-fields \(\mathcal G_t:=\sigma(Y_0,ldots,Y_{(t-d_t)\vee0})\) form a nondecreasing family.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: Admissibility requires \(x_t\) to be measurable with respect to the filtration generated by the delayed, coarsened signals.

notation.meaning: Partially informative signal associated with stage s
Information available under the combined restrictions
Latest signal index available at stage t

children.title: Observation-Restriction Boundaries
children.top_down_role: Limits imposed on admissible recourse by restricted information.

knowledge_statements.title: Observation-Restriction Boundaries
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Finite-scenario boundary caused by an information class whose scenarios require distinct unique actions.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(\Omega\) be finite and let \(\sim_t\) denote indistinguishability under the information available at stage \(t\). Suppose \(\omega^a\sim_t\omega^b\), while the corresponding stagewise optimization problems have distinct unique optimal actions \(a\) and \(b\). Every admissible stage-\(t\) decision is constant on each \(\sim_t\)-equivalence class, so no admissible decision can attain both scenario-wise optima at \(\omega^a\) and \(\omega^b\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: In a finite scenario model, an observation restriction prevents simultaneous scenario-wise optimality when two indistinguishable scenarios require different unique actions.
assumptions_latex: The scenario set \(\Omega\) is finite.
At stage \(t\), the relation \(\sim_t\) partitions scenarios according to their observable histories.
Two scenarios \(\omega^a\sim_t\omega^b\) have distinct unique stagewise optimal actions \(a\ne b\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: No decision constant on the shared information class of \(\omega^a\) and \(\omega^b\) can attain the scenario-wise optimum on both scenarios.

notation.meaning: Two scenarios indistinguishable at stage t

children.title: Decision-Dependent Information
children.top_down_role: Observation structures affected by earlier decisions.

assumptions_latex: Each stage-\(t\) action \(x_t\) is selected before later uncertainty is revealed.
Observation rules may depend on the past action history \(x_{0:t-1}\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The admissibility condition is recursively \(x_t\in L^0(\Omega,\mathcal G_t^x;X_t)\), where \(\mathcal G_t^x\) depends on earlier actions.

notation.meaning: Information available at stage t under policy x

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Endogenous observation filtration generated by earlier controls.

source_refs.locator: 2.3 Information Acquisition Problems p. 47

knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Decision-dependent information is an observation structure in which \(Y_s^x=h_s(\xi_{1:s},x_{0:s-1},\varepsilon_s)\) and hence \(\mathcal G_t^x:=\sigma(Y_1^x,\ldots,Y_t^x)\) depends on earlier decisions. A policy is admissible when, recursively for every \(t\), \(x_t\) is \(\mathcal G_t^x\)-measurable. The recursion requires observations at stage \(t\) to be determined only by uncertainty and actions already realized before \(x_t\) is selected; otherwise the information rule would be circular rather than implementable.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Earlier decisions can determine which signals arrive later. Admissible policies must respect the resulting policy-dependent information history without circular dependence.
knowledge_statements.title: Decision-Dependent Information

children.title: Nonanticipative Adaptation Principle
children.top_down_role: Policy restrictions imposed by observable histories.

children.title: History-Adapted Policy Spaces
children.top_down_role: Policies indexed by observable histories.

assumptions_latex: For each stage \(t\), observable histories take values in a measurable space \((H_t,\mathcal H_t)\).
The action set \(X_t\) is a measurable space.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The history-adapted policy space is \(\Pi:=\prod_{t=0}^T\{\pi_t:H_t\to X_t:\pi_t\text{ is measurable}\}\).
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Measurable deterministic policies indexed by observable histories.

source_refs.locator: 3 Introduction to Markov Decision Processes p. 57

knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(h_t:\Omega\to H_t\) map each outcome to the history observable when stage \(t\) is reached. A history-adapted policy is a tuple \(\pi=(\pi_0,\ldots,\pi_T)\) of measurable maps \(\pi_t:H_t\to X_t\), inducing decisions \(x_t(\omega)=\pi_t(h_t(\omega))\). Its policy space is \(\Pi:=\prod_{t=0}^T\mathcal M(H_t,X_t)\), possibly intersected with pointwise feasibility constraints. Every induced \(x_t\) is measurable with respect to \(\sigma(h_t)\), and conversely every \(\sigma(h_t)\)-measurable deterministic decision admits such a history representation under standard measurable-factorization conditions.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A history-adapted policy assigns each observable history a measurable action, so decisions depend only on information available at their stage.
knowledge_statements.title: History-Adapted Policy Spaces

source_witnesses.locator: 3 Introduction to Markov Decision Processes p. 57

children.title: Shared-History Equivalence Classes
children.top_down_role: Information-equivalent scenarios and nodes.

assumptions_latex: The observable-history map at stage \(t\) is \(h_t:\Omega\to H_t\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: Nonanticipativity is equivalent to constancy of \(x_t\) on every equivalence class of \(\sim_t\).

notation.meaning: Equivalence of outcomes having the same observable stage-t history
Equivalence class of outcome omega at stage t

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Scenario equivalence induced by equality of observable histories.

source_refs.locator: 1.1.1 Recourse problems p. 5

knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Define \(\omega\sim_t\omega'\) if and only if \(h_t(\omega)=h_t(\omega')\). This is an equivalence relation whose classes \([\omega]_t:=\{\omega':\omega'\sim_t\omega\}\) collect scenarios or scenario-tree nodes indistinguishable at stage \(t\). A stage decision is nonanticipative exactly when \(x_t(\omega)=x_t(\omega')\) whenever \(\omega\sim_t\omega'\). If information accumulates with time, then \(\omega\sim_{t+1}\omega'\) implies \(\omega\sim_t\omega'\), so successive information partitions refine rather than coarsen earlier partitions.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Scenarios sharing the same observable history form an equivalence class. Nonanticipative decisions must be constant within each such class.
knowledge_statements.title: Shared-History Equivalence Classes

source_witnesses.locator: 1.1.1 Recourse problems p. 5

children.title: Information Relaxation Family
children.top_down_role: Enlarged information structures used as comparison models.

children.title: Anticipative Relaxations
children.top_down_role: Comparison models permitting access to future uncertainty.

assumptions_latex: The original minimization problem restricts \(x_t\) to be \(\mathcal G_t\)-measurable.
An enlarged family \((\mathcal H_t)\) satisfies \(\mathcal G_t\subseteq\mathcal H_t\subseteq\mathcal F\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: Replacing \(\mathcal G_t\)-measurability by \(\mathcal H_t\)-measurability defines an anticipative relaxation.
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Information relaxation for finite-horizon minimization problems.

source_refs.locator: 2.9.3 Expected Value of Perfect Information p. 154

knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Given admissible decisions satisfying \(x_t\in L^0(\Omega,\mathcal G_t;X_t)\), an anticipative relaxation replaces these constraints by \(x_t\in L^0(\Omega,\mathcal H_t;X_t)\), where \(\mathcal G_t\subseteq\mathcal H_t\). The extreme perfect-information relaxation takes \(\mathcal H_t=\sigma(\xi_1,\ldots,\xi_T)\) for every \(t\), permitting decisions to use the entire uncertainty trajectory. All original pointwise feasibility and integrability constraints are retained; only the information restriction is weakened. Thus every original policy remains feasible in the relaxed policy space.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: An anticipative relaxation lets a decision use more information than is truly available, up to the full future uncertainty path.
knowledge_statements.title: Anticipative Relaxations

source_witnesses.locator: 2.9.3 Expected Value of Perfect Information p. 154

children.title: Information-Enlargement Relaxations
children.top_down_role: Comparison models based on richer observable histories.

assumptions_latex: Two information filtrations satisfy \(\mathcal G_t\subseteq\mathcal H_t\) for every \(t\).
All non-information feasibility and integrability constraints are identical.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The corresponding policy spaces satisfy \(\Pi(\mathcal G)\subseteq\Pi(\mathcal H)\).

notation.meaning: Policies adapted to enlarged filtration H

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Nested policy spaces induced by nested information filtrations.

source_refs.locator: 2.9 The Value of Using a Stochastic Model p. 151

knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For a filtration \(\mathcal A=(\mathcal A_t)_{t=0}^T\), define \(\Pi(\mathcal A):=\{x:x_t\text{ is }\mathcal A_t\text{-measurable for every }t\}\cap\mathcal C\), where \(\mathcal C\) contains the common feasibility and integrability constraints. If \(\mathcal G_t\subseteq\mathcal H_t\) for all \(t\), then every \(\mathcal G_t\)-measurable component is \(\mathcal H_t\)-measurable, and consequently \(\Pi(\mathcal G)\subseteq\Pi(\mathcal H)\). Equality holds when the additional information does not enlarge the set of feasible measurable decisions, including when all relevant decisions already factor through \(\mathcal G_t\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Enlarging information enlarges, or leaves unchanged, the admissible policy space when all other constraints remain fixed.
knowledge_statements.title: Information-Enlargement Relaxations

source_witnesses.locator: 2.9 The Value of Using a Stochastic Model p. 151

children.title: Relaxation Value Comparisons
children.top_down_role: Value relationships induced by enlarged policy spaces.

knowledge_statements.title: Relaxation Value Comparisons
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Monotonicity of optimal values under nested information relaxations.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(\Pi_0\subseteq\Pi_1\subseteq\Pi_2\) be nonempty policy spaces obtained by successively enlarging information while retaining the same objective \(J\) and all other constraints. Define \(v_i:=\inf_{x\in\Pi_i}J(x)\). For minimization, \(v_2\le v_1\le v_0\); for maximization with \(v_i:=\sup_{x\in\Pi_i}J(x)\), the inequalities reverse. Equality of adjacent values does not imply equality of the corresponding policy spaces.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: For minimization, enlarging information cannot increase the optimal value; for maximization, it cannot decrease it. Equal optimal values do not require equal policy spaces.
assumptions_latex: The same objective functional \(J\) and the same non-information constraints are used for every policy space.
The policy spaces satisfy \(\Pi_0\subseteq\Pi_1\subseteq\Pi_2\) and are nonempty.
The relevant infima or suprema are well defined.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: For minimization, \(v_2\le v_1\le v_0\); for maximization, the corresponding inequalities reverse.

notation.meaning: Nested policy spaces ordered by increasing information
Minimization value over policy space i

source_refs.locator: 2.9.3 Expected Value of Perfect Information p. 154

children.title: Nonanticipativity-Violation Boundaries
children.top_down_role: Limits separating admissible policies from informational relaxations.

knowledge_statements.title: Nonanticipativity-Violation Boundaries
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Implementability boundary for scenario-wise decisions admitted by an information relaxation.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(\omega^a\sim_t\omega^b\) mean that two scenarios share the same observable history at stage \(t\) under the original information pattern. Original admissibility requires \(x_t(\omega^a)=x_t(\omega^b)\). A policy admitted by an information relaxation violates stage-\(t\) nonanticipativity whenever \(x_t(\omega^a)\ne x_t(\omega^b)\), and such a policy is not implementable under the original information pattern. If every optimizer of an attained relaxation violates at least one shared-history class, none of its optimizers is originally admissible. Equal relaxed and original optimal values can nevertheless occur when the relaxation has an optimal policy that remains nonanticipative, even if other relaxed optimizers violate nonanticipativity.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A relaxed policy is nonimplementable when it assigns different current actions to scenarios that the original information cannot distinguish. Equal optimal values can still occur if a nonanticipative relaxed optimizer also exists.
assumptions_latex: At stage \(t\), the relation \(\omega^a\sim_t\omega^b\) denotes equality of observable histories under the original information pattern.
The relaxed policy space contains the original policy space and may permit separate decisions on scenarios in one original information class.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: Any relaxed policy satisfying \(x_t(\omega^a)\ne x_t(\omega^b)\) for some \(\omega^a\sim_t\omega^b\) violates original nonanticipativity and is not originally implementable.

notation.meaning: Shared-history equivalence under the original stage-t information
Stage-t decision under a relaxed policy

children.title: Two-Stage Recourse Models
children.top_down_role: Here-and-now decisions followed by uncertainty-dependent corrective decisions.

children.title: Core Two-Stage Representations
children.top_down_role: Equivalent organizations of first-stage and recourse decisions.

children.title: Implicit Recourse-Function Form
children.top_down_role: Second-stage optimization represented by its value mapping.

assumptions_latex: The first-stage feasible set is \(X\subseteq\mathbb{R}^n\), and \(c\in\mathbb{R}^n\).
The random vector \(\xi\) is defined on \((\Omega,\mathcal F,\mathbb P)\), and the negative part of \(Q(x,\xi)\) is integrable for every \(x\in X\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \[\inf_{x\in X}\left\{c^\top x+\mathbb E[Q(x,\xi)]\right\}\]

notation.meaning: Second-stage value at first-stage decision x and realization z.
Feasible recourse set for x under realization z.

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Risk-neutral two-stage minimization with the second stage eliminated through its extended-real value function.

source_refs.locator: 1.1.1 Recourse problems p. 5
2.1.6 Two-stage stochastic programming p. 40

knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For \(x\in X\) and a realization \(z\), define the extended-real recourse function by \[Q(x,z):=\inf_{y\in Y(x,z)}q(x,y,z),\] with the convention \(\inf\varnothing=+\infty\). The implicit risk-neutral two-stage problem is \[\inf_{x\in X}\left\{c^\top x+\mathbb E[Q(x,\xi)]\right\}.\] Thus all second-stage decisions and constraints enter the first-stage problem only through the random value mapping \(Q(x,\xi)\); a first-stage point having infeasible recourse on an event of positive probability has objective value \(+\infty\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The second-stage optimization is replaced by its optimal-value function, whose expectation is added to the first-stage cost.
knowledge_statements.title: Implicit Recourse-Function Form

source_witnesses.locator: 1.1.1 Recourse problems p. 5
2.1.6 Two-stage stochastic programming p. 40

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Implicit recourse-function form of a two-stage stochastic linear program with fixed recourse
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Represents scenario-wise recourse by its value function and the two-stage model by a first-stage problem involving expected recourse cost.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
For deterministic first-stage data \((c,A,b)\), a scenario-independent recourse matrix \(W\), and random second-stage data \(\xi(\omega)=(q(\omega),h(\omega),T(\omega))\), define
\[
Q(x,\xi(\omega)):=\min_{y\ge 0}\left\{q(\omega)^Ty:Wy=h(\omega)-T(\omega)x\right\},
\qquad
\mathcal Q(x):=\mathbb E_{\xi}[Q(x,\xi(\omega))].
\]
Where these quantities are well-defined, the fixed-recourse two-stage stochastic linear program has the implicit recourse-function representation
\[
\min_{x\ge 0}\left\{c^Tx+\mathcal Q(x):Ax=b\right\}.
\]
The underlying scenario-dependent recourse constraints are required to hold almost surely.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: With a deterministic, scenario-independent recourse matrix W, each realization's second-stage linear program defines a recourse value Q. Its expectation defines the expected recourse function, yielding a first-stage problem whose objective is first-stage cost plus expected recourse cost. The random recourse constraints hold almost surely.
assumptions_latex: c\in\mathbb R^{n_1},\quad A\in\mathbb R^{m_1\times n_1},\quad b\in\mathbb R^{m_1}
W\in\mathbb R^{m_2\times n_2}\text{ is deterministic and scenario-independent}
q(\omega)\in\mathbb R^{n_2},\quad h(\omega)\in\mathbb R^{m_2},\quad T(\omega)\in\mathbb R^{m_2\times n_1}
Ax=b,\quad x\ge 0
T(\omega)x+Wy(\omega)=h(\omega),\quad y(\omega)\ge 0\quad\text{a.s.}
Q(x,\xi(\omega))\text{ and }\mathbb E_{\xi}[Q(x,\xi(\omega))]\text{ are well-defined}
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \min_{x\ge 0}\left\{c^Tx+\mathbb E_{\xi}[Q(x,\xi(\omega))]:Ax=b\right\}

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Implicit fixed-recourse form of a two-stage stochastic linear program
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Two-stage stochastic linear programming in which the first-stage decision precedes observation of the random cost, right-hand-side, and interstage-coupling data, while the recourse matrix is deterministic.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(x\) be selected before observing \(\boldsymbol\xi=(\boldsymbol q,\boldsymbol h,\boldsymbol T)\), and let \(y\) be selected afterward. Under fixed recourse, \[Q(x,\boldsymbol\xi)=\min\{\boldsymbol q^{T}y\mid Wy=\boldsymbol h-\boldsymbol T x,\ y\ge 0\},\qquad \mathcal Q(x)=\mathbb E_{\boldsymbol\xi}[Q(x,\boldsymbol\xi)].\] The implicit recourse-function representation is \[\min\{c^{T}x+\mathcal Q(x)\mid Ax=b,\ x\ge 0\}.\]
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The first-stage decision is made before the random data are observed. After observation, a second-stage corrective decision solves a linear recourse problem. When the recourse matrix is fixed, the expected optimal second-stage value defines the recourse function, and the implicit formulation minimizes first-stage cost plus that function.
assumptions_latex: Ax=b,\quad x\ge 0
\boldsymbol\xi=(\boldsymbol q,\boldsymbol h,\boldsymbol T)\text{ is observed after }x\text{ is selected}
W\text{ is deterministic (fixed recourse)}
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \min_{x\ge 0,\ Ax=b}\left\{c^{T}x+\mathbb E_{\boldsymbol\xi}\left[\min_{y\ge 0}\{\boldsymbol q^{T}y\mid Wy=\boldsymbol h-\boldsymbol T x\}\right]\right\}

children.title: Scenario-Expanded Form
children.top_down_role: Scenario-indexed recourse decisions for finite support.

assumptions_latex: The distribution of \(\xi\) has finite support \(\{z_1,\ldots,z_S\}\) with probabilities \(p_s>0\) and \(\sum_{s=1}^S p_s=1\).
Each scenario has a recourse set \(Y(x,z_s)\) and objective \(q(x,y_s,z_s)\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \[\inf_{x,y_1,\ldots,y_S}\left\{c^\top x+\sum_{s=1}^S p_s q(x,y_s,z_s):x\in X,\ y_s\in Y(x,z_s)\ \forall s\right\}\]

knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For finite support \(\{z_1,\ldots,z_S\}\), introduce one recourse decision \(y_s\) per scenario. The scenario-expanded problem is \[\inf_{x,y_1,\ldots,y_S}\left\{c^\top x+\sum_{s=1}^S p_s q(x,y_s,z_s):x\in X,\ y_s\in Y(x,z_s)\ \text{for all }s\right\}.\] Its feasible tuples use one common first-stage decision \(x\), while second-stage decisions may depend on the observed scenario. Its optimal value equals that of the implicit formulation whenever the scenario subproblem values and the finite expectation are well defined.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Finite-support uncertainty yields one recourse decision per scenario, all sharing a common first-stage decision.

children.title: Split-Variable Nonanticipative Form
children.top_down_role: Scenario copies coupled at the first stage.

assumptions_latex: The uncertainty has finite scenarios \(s=1,\ldots,S\) with probabilities \(p_s>0\).
For each scenario, \(D_s\subseteq\mathbb R^n\times\mathbb R^{m_s}\) is the feasible set and \(f_s\) is its total scenario cost.

knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Replace the common first-stage decision by scenario copies \(x_1,\ldots,x_S\) and impose consensus. knowledge_statements.statement_title: Two-stage stochastic formulation of supply-chain network design
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Finite supply-chain networks with binary facility or machine decisions, nonnegative multicommodity flows, random operational data, and optional penalized shortage recourse.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Let \(x\in\mathcal X\subseteq\{0,1\}^{|\mathcal P|}\) be first-stage facility and machine decisions and let \(y\ge0\) be second-stage product flows. For \(\xi=(q,d,s,R,M)\), define
\[
Q(x,\xi)=\inf_{y\ge0}\{q^\top y:Ny=0,\ Cy\ge d,\ Sy\le s,\ Ry\le Mx\},
\]
with \(Q(x,\xi)=+\infty\) when the recourse constraints are infeasible. If \(\xi\) has a specified joint probability distribution, the risk-neutral two-stage model is
\[
\min_{x\in\mathcal X}\ c^\top x+\mathbb E[Q(x,\xi)].
\]
Viewed on \(\mathbb R^{|\mathcal P|}\), \(Q(\cdot,\xi)\) is an extended-real convex function. Demand-shortage recourse replaces \(Cy\ge d\) by \(Cy+z\ge d\), introduces \(z\ge0\), and minimizes \(q^\top y+h^\top z\) with \(h>0\); under the usual nonnegative supply, demand, and capacity data, this recourse problem is feasible for every admissible \(x\), since \(y=0\) and any \(z\ge d\) are feasible.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Binary facility and machine choices form the first stage, while nonnegative product flows form the second stage. When operating costs, demands, supplies, processing requirements, or capacities are random with a specified joint distribution, expected recourse cost is added to first-stage investment cost. An infeasible second stage has value positive infinity. The recourse value is convex in the continuous extension of the first-stage vector. Adding nonnegative shortage variables with positive penalty costs makes the second stage feasible for every admissible design under nonnegative supply, demand, and capacity data.
assumptions_latex: \mathcal S,\mathcal P,\mathcal C,\mathcal K,\mathcal A\text{ are finite.}
\mathcal X\subseteq\{0,1\}^{|\mathcal P|},\quad y\ge0.
\xi=(q,d,s,R,M)\text{ has a specified joint probability distribution.}
N,C,S,R,M\text{ encode flow conservation, demand, supply, and installed-capacity constraints.}
h>0\text{ for penalized shortage recourse; supply, demand, and installed capacities are nonnegative.}
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \min_{x\in\mathcal X}\bigl(c^\top x+\mathbb E[Q(x,\xi)]\bigr),\qquad Q(x,\xi)=+\infty\text{ if recourse is infeasible};\quad Q(\cdot,\xi)\text{ is convex, and shortage recourse makes the second stage feasible for every }x\in\mathcal X.

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Expected downside-risk constraint for recourse profit
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Two-stage profit maximization with a target imposed on scenario-dependent recourse profit.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For each scenario \(\omega\), introduce \(u(\xi(\omega))\) satisfying \(u(\xi(\omega))\ge g-q(\omega)^Ty(\omega)\) and \(u(\xi(\omega))\ge0\), and impose \(\mathbb E_{\xi}[u(\xi)]\le l\). Thus \(u\) is an epigraph variable for the target shortfall \((g-q(\omega)^Ty(\omega))_+\). For a discrete random vector, the expectation constraint is linear and acts as a first-stage, all-scenario constraint; it may be included directly in the extensive form or imposed sequentially when violated.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: In a two-stage profit model, downside risk relative to target g is represented scenario-wise by a nonnegative variable at least as large as the target minus recourse profit. Bounding its expectation by l limits expected downside risk. With discrete uncertainty this is a linear, first-stage constraint spanning all scenarios, usable directly in the extensive form or added sequentially as needed.
assumptions_latex: \max\; c^Tx+\mathbb E_{\xi}[\max\;q(\omega)^Ty(\omega)]\text{ is a two-stage profit model with its recourse constraints}
g\in\mathbb R\text{ is the target recourse-profit level}
l\in\mathbb R\text{ is the prescribed expected-downside-risk bound}
u(\xi(\omega))\ge g-q(\omega)^Ty(\omega),\quad u(\xi(\omega))\ge0\quad\forall\omega
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \mathbb E_{\xi}[u(\xi)]\le l;\quad \text{if }\xi\text{ is discrete, this is a linear all-scenario first-stage constraint.}

knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(\xi\) take values in a measurable space \((\Xi,\mathcal A)\). In the linear-cost case, let \(X\subseteq\mathbb R^n\), let \(Y(x)\subseteq\mathbb R^m\) be deterministic for each \(x\in X\), and let \(c:\Xi\to\mathbb R^n\) and \(q:\Xi\to\mathbb R^m\) be measurable coefficient maps. knowledge_statements.statement_title: Joint chance constraint and fixed-set robust restriction
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Multiproduct assembly service-level model with vector demand.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Let W=A^\top D\in\mathbb{R}^m and \alpha\in(0,1). The joint chance-constrained model is
\min_{x\ge0}c^\top x\quad\text{s.t.}\quad \Pr\{A^\top D\le x\}=H_W(x)\ge1-\alpha.
Equivalently, x is feasible iff there exists a measurable \mathfrak D with \Pr\{D\in\mathfrak D\}\ge1-\alpha such that A^\top d\le x for every d\in\mathfrak D. Fixing one such set \mathfrak D_\alpha yields the sufficient robust restriction A^\top d\le x for all d\in\mathfrak D_\alpha. When c\ge0, its coordinatewise minimal solution is
x_j=\sup_{d\in\mathfrak D_\alpha}\sum_{i=1}^n a_{ij}d_i,\quad j=1,\ldots,m.
For m=1 and c>0, an optimizer is the left (1-\alpha)-quantile H_W^{-1}(1-\alpha). In higher dimensions the selected minimal quantile generally depends on c, and dependence among coordinates of W prevents replacement of the joint constraint by marginal constraints without additional assumptions.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The service requirement is a joint chance constraint requiring enough parts to cover all product demands with probability at least one minus alpha. It can be expressed through the multivariate distribution of required parts or through a measurable set containing sufficient probability mass. Fixing such a set gives a conservative robust formulation whose coordinatewise smallest order quantities are worst-case part requirements over that set. The scalar case reduces to a quantile, whereas the multivariate case generally depends on costs and cannot be recovered from marginal distributions alone.
assumptions_latex: A\in\mathbb{R}_+^{n\times m},\quad D\in\mathbb{R}_+^n,\quad W=A^\top D
\alpha\in(0,1),\quad x\in\mathbb{R}_+^m
\mathfrak D_\alpha\text{ is measurable and }\Pr\{D\in\mathfrak D_\alpha\}\ge1-\alpha
c\ge0\text{ for the coordinatewise robust optimizer; }c>0\text{ in the scalar quantile claim}
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \Pr\{A^\top D\le x\}\ge1-\alpha\text{ has the stated measurable-set representation, and any fixed qualifying }\mathfrak D_\alpha\text{ induces the stated robust sufficient condition.}

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Two-stage multiproduct assembly recourse formulation
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Random-demand assembly model, finite-scenario extensive form, decision timing, and relatively complete recourse.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
For ordered parts \(x\in\mathbb{R}_+^m\) and realized demand \(d\in\mathbb{R}_+^n\), define
\[
Q(x,d)=\min_{z,y}\left\{(l-q)^\top z-s^\top y:y=x-A^\top z,\ 0\le z\le d,\ y\ge0\right\}.
\]
The first-stage problem is
\[
\min_{x\ge0}\left\{c^\top x+\mathbb{E}[Q(x,D)]\right\}.
\]
If \(D\) has scenarios \(d^k\) with probabilities \(p_k>0\), \(\sum_{k=1}^Kp_k=1\), the problem is equivalently
\[
\min_{x,z^k,y^k}c^\top x+\sum_{k=1}^Kp_k\bigl[(l-q)^\top z^k-s^\top y^k\bigr]
\]
subject to \(y^k=x-A^\top z^k\), \(0\le z^k\le d^k\), \(y^k\ge0\), and \(x\ge0\) for every \(k\). The vector \(x\) is scenario-independent, whereas \((z^k,y^k)\) may depend on \(k\). For every \(x\ge0\) and every demand realization, \(z=0\), \(y=x\) is feasible, so the model has relatively complete recourse.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Parts are ordered before demand is known, whereas production and residual inventory are chosen after demand is observed. Under finite demand support, the expected-cost problem has an extensive linear-programming formulation with a common first-stage order vector and scenario-dependent recourse variables. Zero production with all ordered parts retained is feasible for every demand realization, so recourse is relatively complete.
assumptions_latex: n,m\in\mathbb{N},\quad A\in\mathbb{R}_+^{n\times m},\quad D\in\mathbb{R}_+^n
x\in\mathbb{R}_+^m,\quad 0\le z\le d,\quad y\in\mathbb{R}_+^m
s_j<c_j\quad(j=1,\ldots,m)
\Pr(D=d^k)=p_k>0,\quad \sum_{k=1}^Kp_k=1\quad\text{for the finite-scenario representation}
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \min_{x\ge0}\{c^\top x+\mathbb{E}[Q(x,D)]\}\text{ has the stated extensive LP representation under finite support, and its recourse is relatively complete.}

knowledge_statements.title: Convex Nonlinear Recourse
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Jointly convex continuous recourse with nonlinear objectives or constraints.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(X\subseteq\mathbb R^n\) be convex. For each realization \(\xi\), define \[Q(x,\xi)=\inf_{y\in\\mathbb R^m}\{f(x,y,\xi):g_i(x,y,\xi)\leq0,\ i=1,\ldots,r\}.\] This is convex nonlinear recourse when \(f(\cdot,\cdot,\xi)\) and every \(g_i(\cdot,\cdot,\xi)\) are proper convex functions and at least one defining function need not be affine. knowledge_statements.title: Continuous Nonconvex Recourse
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Continuous second-stage optimization lacking the convexity needed for convex value geometry.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For a realization \(\xi\), let \[Q(x,\xi)=\inf\{f(x,y,\xi):y\in Y(x,\xi)\subseteq\mathbb R^m\}.\] The recourse is continuous nonconvex when every component of \(y\) is real-valued and, for some \((x,\xi)\), either \(Y(x,\xi)\) is nonconvex or \(f(x,\cdot,\xi)\) is nonconvex on that set. Consequently, convexity of \(Q(\cdot,\xi)\), global optimality of local minimizers, and exact recovery by convex relaxation are not guaranteed without additional structure.

knowledge_statements.title: Discrete Recourse
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Second-stage correction restricted to integer-valued actions.

knowledge_statements.title: Mixed-Discrete Nonconvex Recourse
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Recourse combining continuous and discrete actions in a generally nonconvex second-stage model.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For each realization \(\xi\), mixed-discrete nonconvex recourse has the form \[Q(x,\xi)=\inf\{f(x,u,v,xi):(u,v)\in Y(x,xi),\ u\in\mathbb R^p,\ v\in\mathbb Z^q\},\qquad q\geq1.\] The class permits nonconvexity in \(f\) or \(Y(x,xi)\) in addition to integrality of \(v\). knowledge_statements.title: Convexification Boundaries
knowledge_statements.scope_note: A binary-recourse example where convex relaxation changes the recourse value.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Consider \[Q(t)=\min_{y\in\{0,1\}}(t-y)^2=\min\{t^2,(t-1)^2\},\qquad 0\leq t\leq1.\] Although each branch is convex, \(Q\) is not convex because \(Q(0)=Q(1)=0\) while \(Q(1/2)=1/4\). Replacing \(y\in\{0,1\}\) by its convex hull \(0\leq y\leq1\) gives \[Q_{\mathrm{rel}}(t)=\min_{0\leq y\leq1}(t-y)^2=0.\] Hence convexifying the feasible actions before taking the value function can yield a strict lower bound and does not generally preserve discrete recourse.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Binary recourse can have a nonconvex value function, and relaxing the binary action to its convex hull can strictly lower that value.
assumptions_latex: The second-stage objective is \((t-y)^2\)
The original action satisfies \(y\in\{0,1\}\)
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(Q_{\mathrm{rel}}(t)<Q(t)\) for every \(t\in(0,1)\).

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Relatively Complete, Complete, and Simple Recourse
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Definitions and structural relationships among three classical recourse regimes.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: A two-stage stochastic program has relatively complete recourse when \(K_1\subseteq K_2\). It has complete recourse when \(\forall t\in\mathbb R^{m_2}\,\exists y\ge 0\) such that \(Wy=t\), equivalently \(\operatorname{pos}W=\mathbb R^{m_2}\), or equivalently the columns of \(W\) contain a positive linear basis of \(\mathbb R^{m_2}\); complete recourse is a special case of relatively complete recourse. It has simple recourse when \(W=[I,-I]\), with \(y=(y^+,y^-)\) and \(q=(q^+,q^-)\). In the simple-recourse case, if \(q_i^++q_i^-\ge 0\) almost surely, the optimal values of \(y_i^+(\omega)\) and \(y_i^-(\omega)\) are determined by the sign of \(h_i(\omega)-T_{i\cdot}(\omega)x\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Relatively complete recourse means every first-stage feasible decision has a feasible second-stage completion. Complete recourse means every right-hand side can be generated by a nonnegative recourse vector, equivalently the positive cone of W is the whole second-stage space; it implies relatively complete recourse. Simple recourse uses W equal to [I,-I], and under nonnegative paired recourse costs its optimal positive and negative corrections are determined by the sign of the residual.
assumptions_latex: K_1\text{ is the first-stage feasible set and }K_2\text{ is the set admitting feasible recourse.}
\text{For the simple-recourse sign property, }q_i^++q_i^-\ge 0\text{ almost surely.}
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: K_1\subseteq K_2\text{ characterizes relatively complete recourse};\quad \operatorname{pos}W=\mathbb R^{m_2}\text{ characterizes complete recourse};\quad W=[I,-I]\text{ characterizes simple recourse, with corrections selected by residual sign under the stated cost condition.}

knowledge_statements.title: Fixed Recourse
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Linear recourse whose technology matrix is independent of the realized scenario.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(\xi\) range over a scenario set \(\Xi\). A linear two-stage model has fixed recourse when its second-stage technology matrix is scenario-invariant. knowledge_statements.statement_title: Almost-Sure Optimality Conditions for the L-Infinity Formulation
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Functional-space optimality characterization for a fixed-recourse two-stage stochastic linear program.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Assume that the formulation with \(X=L_\infty(\Omega,\mathcal B,\mu;\mathbb R^{n_1+n_2})\) is feasible, has a bounded optimal value, and satisfies relatively complete recourse. A feasible pair \((x^*(\omega),y^*(\omega))\) is optimal if and only if there exist integrable functions \(\lambda^*(\omega),\rho^*(\omega),\pi^*(\omega)\) such that, almost surely, for \(j=1,\ldots,n_1\), \[c_j-\lambda^*(\omega)A_{\cdot j}-\rho^*(\omega)-\pi^*(\omega)^TT_{\cdot j}(\omega)\geq 0,\] \[\bigl(c_j-\lambda^*(\omega)A_{\cdot j}-\rho^*(\omega)-\pi^*(\omega)^TT_{\cdot j}(\omega)\bigr)x_j^*(\omega)=0,\] and, almost surely, for \(j=1,\ldots,n_2\), \[q_j(\omega)-\pi^*(\omega)^TW_{\cdot j}\geq 0,\] \[\bigl(q_j(\omega)-\pi^*(\omega)^TW_{\cdot j}\bigr)y_j^*(\omega)=0,\] together with \[\mathbb E_{\omega}[\rho^*(\omega)]=0.\]
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: For the feasible, bounded L-infinity formulation with relatively complete fixed recourse, a feasible policy pair is optimal exactly when integrable multipliers satisfy the stated almost-sure dual inequalities and complementary-slackness equations for both stages, together with zero expectation of rho.

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Deterministic-equivalent representation of a fixed-recourse two-stage stochastic linear program
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Represents the expected scenario-wise recourse value and, when the coupling matrix is deterministic, its tender-variable form. It applies to discrete or continuous uncertainty.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Let \(A,W,c,b\) be deterministic and let the recourse matrix \(W\) be scenario-invariant. For random data \(\xi(\omega)=(q(\omega),h(\omega),T(\omega))\), the two-stage model has deterministic-equivalent form
\[
\min_{x\ge 0,\,Ax=b}\{c^Tx+\mathcal Q(x)\},\qquad \mathcal Q(x)=\mathbb E_\xi[Q(x,\xi)],
\]
where
\[
Q(x,\xi(\omega))=\min_{y\ge0}\{q(\omega)^Ty\mid Wy=h(\omega)-T(\omega)x\}.
\]
If \(T\) is deterministic, it also admits the tender representation
\[
\min_{x,\chi}\{c^Tx+\Psi(\chi)\mid Ax=b,\ Tx-\chi=0,\ x\ge0\},
\]
with
\[
\Psi(\chi)=\mathbb E_\xi\!\left[\min_{y\ge0}\{q(\omega)^Ty\mid Wy=h(\omega)-\chi\}\right].
\]
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A two-stage stochastic linear program with scenario-invariant recourse matrix W can be written as a first-stage linear cost plus the expected optimal value of a scenario recourse problem. If T is deterministic, the recourse dependence can instead be expressed through the tender χ = Tx.
assumptions_latex: A,W,c,b\text{ are deterministic and }W\text{ is scenario-invariant}.
\xi(\omega)=(q(\omega),h(\omega),T(\omega))\text{ has dimensionally compatible components}.
Ax=b,\ x\ge0,\quad T(\omega)x+Wy(\omega)=h(\omega),\ y(\omega)\ge0\quad\text{are imposed almost surely}.
T\text{ is deterministic for the tender-variable specialization}.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \min_{x\ge0,\,Ax=b}\{c^Tx+\mathcal Q(x)\},\quad \mathcal Q(x)=\mathbb E[Q(x,\xi)],\quad Q(x,\xi)=\min_{y\ge0}\{q^Ty\mid Wy=h-Tx\},\quad T\text{ deterministic}\Rightarrow \chi=Tx\text{ tender representation}.

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Regularity of the Fixed-Recourse Function
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Convexity, Lipschitz continuity, finiteness, and conditional differentiability of the expected recourse function under fixed recourse.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For a stochastic program with fixed recourse, if \(\xi\) has finite second moments, then \(\mathcal Q\) is a Lipschitzian convex function and is finite on \(K_2\). If, additionally, the distribution of \(\xi\) is absolutely continuous, then \(\mathcal Q\) is differentiable on \(\operatorname{ri}K_2\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Under fixed recourse and finite second moments, the expected recourse function is Lipschitz and convex and is finite on K2. Absolute continuity of the distribution additionally gives differentiability on the relative interior of K2.
assumptions_latex: \text{The stochastic program has fixed recourse.}
\mathbb E[\|\xi\|^2]<\infty.
\text{Differentiability additionally requires that the distribution of }\xi\text{ be absolutely continuous.}
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \mathcal Q\text{ is Lipschitzian and convex and is finite on }K_2;\qquad \mathcal Q\text{ is differentiable on }\operatorname{ri}K_2\text{ under the additional absolute-continuity assumption.}

knowledge_statements.title: Random Recourse
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Linear recourse whose second-stage technology depends on the realized scenario.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(\xi\) range over a scenario set \(\Xi\). A linear two-stage model has random recourse when the matrix multiplying the second-stage decision depends on the realization. Its scenario value has the form \[Q(x,\xi)=\inf\{q(\xi)^{\mathsf T}y:W(\xi)y=h(\xi)-T(\xi)x,\ y\geq0\},\] where \(W:\Xi\to\mathbb R^{m\times r}\) is not scenario-invariant. Consequently, the attainable recourse cone and feasibility of a residual may vary across scenarios.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Random recourse has a second-stage technology matrix that varies across scenarios, so attainable corrections and feasibility may vary as well.
assumptions_latex: \(\Xi\) is the scenario set
\(W:\Xi\to\mathbb R^{m\times r}\) has compatible finite dimensions
There exist \(\xi_1,\xi_2\in\Xi\) such that \(W(\xi_1)\ne W(\xi_2)\)
Second-stage decisions are selected after observing \(\xi\)
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The recourse technology \(W(\xi)\) is scenario-dependent.

children.title: Simple Recourse

knowledge_statements.title: Simple Recourse
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Coordinatewise correction by separate positive and negative deviation variables.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(r=h(\xi)-T(\xi)x\in\mathbb R^m\), and let \(q^+,q^-\in\mathbb R_+^m\). Simple recourse is represented by \[Q(x,\xi)=\min_{y^+,y^-\geq0}\{(q^+)^{\mathsf T}y^++(q^-)^{\mathsf T}y^-:y^+-y^-=r\}.\] Because the coordinates are independent, an optimal solution is \(y^+=r_+\) and \(y^-=r_-\), where \((r_+)_i=\max\{r_i,0\}\) and \((r_-)_i=\max\{-r_i,0\}\). Therefore, \[Q(x,\xi)=(q^+)^{\mathsf T}r_++(q^-)^{\mathsf T}r_-.\]
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Simple recourse corrects each residual coordinate independently with positive and negative deviations, giving a weighted piecewise-linear value.
assumptions_latex: \(q^+,q^-\geq0\) componentwise
Positive and negative deviations are unbounded above
The recourse equation is \(y^+-y^-=r\)
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(Q(x,\xi)=(q^+)^{\mathsf T}r_++(q^-)^{\mathsf T}r_-\).

notation.meaning: componentwise positive and negative parts of the residual

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Frank–Wolfe Algorithm for Simple-Recourse Problems
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Extraction-grounded algorithm for source problem (7.1); notation is retained from the source formulation.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Given a feasible \(x^0\) for \((7.1)\), set \(v=0\). At iteration \(v\), define \(\bar F^v=\operatorname{diag}\{F_i(T_{i\cdot}x^v)\}\) and let \(\widehat x^v\) solve
\[
\min_x\ \bigl(c^T+(q^+-q)^T\bar F^vT\bigr)x\quad\text{s.t. }Ax=b,\ x\geq0.
\]
Choose \(\lambda\in[0,1]\) minimizing
\[
c^T\bigl(x^v+\lambda(\widehat x^v-x^v)\bigr)+\sum_{i=1}^{m_2}\Psi_i\!\left(T\bigl(x^v+\lambda(\widehat x^v-x^v)\bigr)\right),
\]
and set \(x^{v+1}=x^v+\lambda(\widehat x^v-x^v)\). If \(x^{v+1}=x^v\), stop with an optimal solution; otherwise increment \(v\) and repeat.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Starting from a feasible point, solve the stated linearized simple-recourse subproblem and minimize the original objective along the segment to that solution. A null update terminates with an optimal solution; otherwise iterate.
assumptions_latex: x^0\text{ is feasible for problem }(7.1).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: x^{v+1}=x^v\ \Longrightarrow\ x^v\text{ is an optimal solution of }(7.1).

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Distributional Optimality Condition for Simple Recourse
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Necessary and sufficient multiplier and distribution-function characterization of first-stage optimality under simple recourse.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Suppose problem \((1.1)\) has simple recourse and a finite optimal value. A point \(x^*\in K_1\) is optimal in the corresponding problem \((1.2)\) if and only if there exist \(\lambda^*\in\mathbb R^{m_1}\), \(\mu^*\in\mathbb R_+^{n_1}\), and \(\pi_i^*\) such that \((\mu^*)^Tx^*=0\), \[-\left(q_i^+-q_iF_i^-(T_{i\cdot}x^*)\right)\le \pi_i^*\le-\left(q_i^+-q_iF_i^+(T_{i\cdot}x^*)\right)\quad\text{for every }i,\] and \[-c+A^T\lambda^*+\mu^*-(\pi^*)^TT=0.\]
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: For a simple-recourse problem with finite optimal value, first-stage optimality is equivalent to complementary first-stage multipliers, distribution-dependent bounds on the recourse coefficients, and the stated stationarity equation.
assumptions_latex: \text{Problem }(1.1)\text{ has simple recourse and a finite optimal value.}
x^*\in K_1.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: x^*\text{ is optimal in }(1.2)\Longleftrightarrow\exists\lambda^*,\mu^*,\pi^*\text{ satisfying }(\mu^*)^Tx^*=0,\ -\left(q_i^+-q_iF_i^-(T_{i\cdot}x^*)\right)\le\pi_i^*\le-\left(q_i^+-q_iF_i^+(T_{i\cdot}x^*)\right),\text{ and }-c+A^T\lambda^*+\mu^*-(\pi^*)^TT=0.

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Alternating Algorithm for Simple-Recourse Problems
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Extraction-grounded procedure using the source-defined formulations (7.19) and (7.20).
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Set \(v=0\), choose a feasible \(x^0\) for \((7.20)\), and let \(\chi^0\) be part of a solution of \((7.20)\) with \(N\) defined according to \(x^0\). Solve \((7.19)\) and let \(X^{v+1}\) be its set of optimal \(x\)-solutions. If there exists \(x^{v+1}\in X^{v+1}\) such that
\[
c^Tx^{v+1}+\Psi(Tx^{v+1})<c^Tx^v+\Psi(Tx^v),
\]
choose one, solve \((7.20)\) with \(N\) defined according to \(x^{v+1}\) to obtain \(\chi^{v+1}\), increment \(v\), and repeat. If no such improving \(x^{v+1}\) exists, stop.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Initialize with a feasible x and a compatible chi. Repeatedly solve formulation (7.19), choose an optimal x that strictly improves the stated objective, and solve formulation (7.20) after updating N from that x. Stop if no strictly improving member of the optimal set exists.
assumptions_latex: x^0\text{ is feasible for }(7.20).
\chi^0\text{ is part of a solution of }(7.20)\text{ with }N\text{ defined according to }x^0.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \nexists x\in X^{v+1}:c^Tx+\Psi(Tx)<c^Tx^v+\Psi(Tx^v)\ \Longrightarrow\ \text{the algorithm stops}.

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Finiteness Criterion for Simple Recourse
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Necessary and sufficient paired-cost condition for real-valued expected recourse under simple recourse.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Suppose a two-stage stochastic program is feasible, has simple recourse, and \(\xi\) has finite second moments. Then \(\mathcal Q(x)\) is finite if and only if \(q_i^+ + q_i^-\ge 0\) almost surely for every recourse component \(i\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: For a feasible simple-recourse program with finite second moments, the expected recourse value is finite exactly when each paired positive and negative recourse cost has an almost-surely nonnegative sum.
assumptions_latex: \text{The two-stage stochastic program is feasible and has simple recourse.}
\mathbb E[\|\xi\|^2]<\infty.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \mathcal Q(x)\in\mathbb R\quad\Longleftrightarrow\quad q_i^+ + q_i^-\ge 0\text{ almost surely for every }i.

children.title: Network Recourse
children.top_down_role: Recourse inheriting network structure.

knowledge_statements.title: Network Recourse
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Second-stage correction represented as a capacitated network-flow problem.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(G=(V,A)\) be a directed graph with node-arc incidence matrix \(B\). Network recourse has scenario value \[Q(x,xi)=\inf\{q(xi)^{\mathsf T}y:By=h(xi)-T(xi)x,\ 0\leq y\leq u(xi)\},\] where \(y\) is the vector of recourse flows and the residual is a node-supply vector. Thus second-stage feasibility is precisely the existence of a flow satisfying conservation and capacity constraints; omitted upper bounds are interpreted as \(+\infty\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Network recourse models corrective actions as flows satisfying node conservation and optional arc capacities on a directed network.
assumptions_latex: \(B\) is a directed node-arc incidence matrix
\(h(xi)-T(xi)x\) has dimension \(|V|\)
Arc capacities satisfy \(u(xi)\geq0\)
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: Second-stage feasibility is equivalent to existence of a capacitated flow with balance vector \(h(xi)-T(xi)x\).
