children.title: Block-Separable Recourse
children.top_down_role: Recourse separable across subsystems or resources.

knowledge_statements.title: Block-Separable Recourse
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Independent second-stage subsystems whose values add across blocks.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let the recourse variables and constraints decompose into \(K\) uncoupled blocks. For each realization \(xi\), suppose \[Y(x,xi)=\prod_{k=1}^K Y_k(x,xi),\qquad f(x,y,xi)=\sum_{k=1}^K f_k(x,y_k,xi).\] Then the recourse value separates as \[Q(x,xi)=\inf_{y\in Y(x,xi)}f(x,y,xi)=\sum_{k=1}^K Q_k(x,xi),\qquad Q_k(x,xi)=\inf_{y_k\in Y_k(x,xi)}f_k(x,y_k,xi),\] using extended-real arithmetic whenever a block is infeasible.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: When second-stage feasible sets form a Cartesian product and costs add by block, the recourse value is the sum of independent block values.
assumptions_latex: \(K<\infty\)
The feasible set is the Cartesian product of block feasible sets
The objective is additively separable across blocks
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(Q(x,xi)=\sum_{k=1}^K Q_k(x,xi)\).

notation.meaning: feasible set of recourse block k

review_flags: no supplied locator specifically supports block-separable recourse

children.title: Complete Recourse
children.top_down_role: Global second-stage feasibility.

knowledge_statements.title: Complete Recourse
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Linear recourse feasible for every possible right-hand side.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For a fixed linear recourse matrix \(W\in\mathbb R^{m\times r}\) with nonnegative recourse variables, complete recourse is the condition \[\forall z\in\mathbb R^m\quad\exists y\in\mathbb R_+^r\quad Wy=z.\] Equivalently, the cone generated by the columns of \(W\) is the entire right-hand-side space: \[\operatorname{cone}(W)=\{Wy:y\geq0\}=\mathbb R^m.\] Consequently, every dimensionally compatible residual \(h(\xi)-T(\xi)x\) admits a feasible second-stage action, independently of \(x\) and \(\xi\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Complete recourse means every possible right-hand side can be generated by a nonnegative second-stage action, equivalently the columns of the recourse matrix generate the whole space as a cone.
assumptions_latex: \(W\in\mathbb R^{m\times r}\) is fixed
Recourse variables satisfy \(y\in\mathbb R_+^r\)
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\operatorname{cone}(W)=\mathbb R^m\).

notation.meaning: cone generated by the columns of W

knowledge_statements.title: Relatively Complete Recourse
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Supportwise feasibility relative to the admissible first-stage set.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Let \(X\subseteq\mathbb R^n\) be the admissible first-stage set, let \(\Xi\) be the support of \(\xi\), and define \(Y(x,\xi)=\{y\in\mathbb R_+^m:W(\xi)y=h(\xi)-T(\xi)x\}\). The two-stage model has relatively complete recourse when
\[Y(x,\xi)\ne\varnothing\qquad\text{for every }x\in X\text{ and every }\xi\in\Xi.\]
Thus every admissible first-stage decision admits a feasible corrective decision under every supported realization.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Recourse is relatively complete when every admissible first-stage decision has a feasible second-stage correction for every realization in the uncertainty support.
assumptions_latex: \(X\ne\varnothing\).
\(\Xi=\operatorname{supp}(\mathbb P_\xi)\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(Y(x,\xi)\ne\varnothing\) for all \((x,\xi)\in X\times\Xi\).

notation.meaning: feasible recourse decisions after choosing x and observing xi

children.title: Almost-Sure Recourse Feasibility
children.top_down_role: Feasibility outside probability-null exceptions.

knowledge_statements.title: Almost-Sure Recourse Feasibility
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Probability-one feasibility for a specified first-stage decision.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
On a probability space \((\Omega,\mathcal F,\mathbb P)\), fix \(x\in X\) and let \(Y(x,\xi(\omega))\) be the recourse-feasible set. Recourse is almost surely feasible at \(x\) when
\[\mathbb P\bigl(\{\omega\in\Omega:Y(x,\xi(\omega))\ne\varnothing\}\bigr)=1.\]
Almost-sure feasibility permits infeasible realizations on a measurable probability-null set and is therefore weaker than supportwise feasibility at \(x\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A first-stage decision has almost-sure feasible recourse when a feasible correction exists with probability one, allowing infeasibility only on a null set.
assumptions_latex: \((\Omega,\mathcal F,\mathbb P)\) is a probability space.
\(\{\omega:Y(x,\xi(\omega))\ne\varnothing\}\in\mathcal F\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\mathbb P(Y(x,\xi)\ne\varnothing)=1\).

children.title: Incomplete Recourse

knowledge_statements.title: Incomplete Recourse
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Failure of supportwise recourse feasibility for at least one admissible decision.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Let \(X\) be the admissible first-stage set, \(\Xi\) the support of \(\xi\), and \(Y(x,\xi)\) the feasible recourse set. Recourse is incomplete relative to \(X\) and \(\Xi\) when
\[\exists(x,\bar\xi)\in X\times\Xi\quad\text{such that}\quad Y(x,\bar\xi)=\varnothing.\]
For a fixed \(x\), the stronger probabilistically relevant failure condition is \(\mathbb P(Y(x,\xi)=\varnothing)>0\). Under the extended-value convention, that condition makes the recourse value \(+\infty\) with positive probability.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Recourse is incomplete when some admissible first-stage decision and supported realization admit no feasible correction; positive-probability failure is the stronger stochastic form.
assumptions_latex: \(X\ne\varnothing\).
\(\Xi=\operatorname{supp}(\mathbb P_\xi)\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(Y(x,\bar\xi)=\varnothing\) for some \((x,\bar\xi)\in X\times\Xi\).

knowledge_statements.title: Sufficiently Expensive Recourse
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Dual feasibility excluding unboundedly favorable recourse costs.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
For the linear recourse problem
\[Q(x,\xi)=\inf\{q(\xi)^{\mathsf T}y:W(\xi)y=h(\xi)-T(\xi)x,\ y\ge0\},\]
recourse is sufficiently expensive at \(\xi\) when its dual feasible set
\[D(\xi)=\{\pi:W(\xi)^{\mathsf T}\pi\le q(\xi)\}\]
is nonempty. It is sufficiently expensive almost surely when \(\mathbb P(D(\xi)\ne\varnothing)=1\). Whenever the primal feasible set is nonempty and \(D(\xi)\ne\varnothing\), weak duality excludes \(Q(x,\xi)=-\infty\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Linear recourse is sufficiently expensive when its dual constraints are feasible; together with primal feasibility, this prevents the recourse value from being minus infinity.
assumptions_latex: \(W(\xi),T(\xi),h(\xi),q(\xi)\) have compatible finite dimensions.
\(y\) is constrained componentwise by \(y\ge0\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(D(\xi)\ne\varnothing\), and primal feasibility implies \(Q(x,\xi)>-\infty\).

notation.meaning: dual multiplier for the recourse equality

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Measurable Closed-Valued Multifunction
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Defines measurability through inverse images under intersection with closed subsets of Euclidean space.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let $(\Xi,\mathcal A)$ be a measurable space and let $G:\Xi\rightrightarrows\mathbb R^n$ be closed-valued. The multifunction $G$ is measurable if, for every closed set $C\subseteq\mathbb R^n$, the hit set $G^{-1}(C):=\{\xi\in\Xi:G(\xi)\cap C\neq\varnothing\}$ belongs to $\mathcal A$.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A closed-valued multifunction from a measurable space into Euclidean space is measurable when, for every closed set, the scenarios whose images intersect that set form a measurable set.
assumptions_latex: $(\Xi,\mathcal A)$ is a measurable space.
$G:\Xi\rightrightarrows\mathbb R^n$ is closed-valued.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: G\text{ is measurable}\iff \forall C\subseteq\mathbb R^n\text{ closed},\ \{\xi\in\Xi:G(\xi)\cap C\neq\varnothing\}\in\mathcal A.

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Decomposable Space of Measurable Functions
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Closure under measurable pasting, together with the standard vector-valued \(L_p\) examples.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \((\Omega,\mathcal F,P)\) be a probability space and let \(\mathfrak M\) be a linear space of \(\mathcal F\)-measurable mappings \(\psi:\Omega\to\mathbb R^m\). The space \(\mathfrak M\) is decomposable if, for every \(\psi\in\mathfrak M\), \(A\in\mathcal F\), and bounded \(\mathcal F\)-measurable \(\gamma:\Omega\to\mathbb R^m\), the function \(\eta=\mathbf 1_{\Omega\setminus A}\psi+\mathbf 1_A\gamma\) belongs to \(\mathfrak M\). For every \(p\in[1,+\infty]\), \(\mathcal L_p(\Omega,\mathcal F,P;\mathbb R^m)\) is decomposable.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A linear space of measurable vector-valued functions is decomposable when it remains closed after replacing a member on any measurable event by a bounded measurable function. Every vector-valued Lp space for p from 1 through infinity is decomposable.
assumptions_latex: \((\Omega,\mathcal F,P)\) is a probability space.
\(\mathfrak M\) is a linear space of \(\mathcal F\)-measurable mappings \(\Omega\to\mathbb R^m\).

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Interchangeability Principle for Expected Integral Functionals
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Equality between the expected pointwise infimum and the infimum over measurable decisions, with an optimizer characterization under the stated value boundary.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(\mathfrak M\) be a decomposable space and let \(f:\mathbb R^m\times\Omega\to\mathbb R\) be a random lower semicontinuous function. For \(\chi\in\mathfrak M\), define \(F_\chi(\omega)=f(\chi(\omega),\omega)\). If \(\inf_{\chi\in\mathfrak M}\mathbb E[F_\chi]<+\infty\), then \[\mathbb E\!\left[\inf_{x\in\mathbb R^m}f(x,\omega)\right]=\inf_{\chi\in\mathfrak M}\mathbb E[F_\chi].\] If the common value is not \(-\infty\), then \[\bar\chi\in\operatorname*{argmin}_{\chi\in\mathfrak M}\mathbb E[F_\chi]\iff \bar\chi\in\mathfrak M\ \text{and}\ \bar\chi(\omega)\in\operatorname*{argmin}_{x\in\mathbb R^m}f(x,\omega)\ \text{for almost every }\omega.\]
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: For a random lower-semicontinuous function and a decomposable decision space, the expectation of the pointwise infimum equals the infimum of the expected values when the latter is below positive infinity. If the common value is not negative infinity, a decision minimizes the expectation exactly when it minimizes pointwise almost surely.

\(f:\mathbb R^m\times\Omega\to\mathbb R\) is a random lower semicontinuous function.
\(F_\chi(\omega)=f(\chi(\omega),\omega)\).
\(\inf_{\chi\in\mathfrak M}\mathbb E[F_\chi]<+\infty\).

children.title: Recourse-Value Measurability
children.top_down_role: Measurable organization of scenario-indexed recourse values.

knowledge_statements.title: Recourse-Value Measurability
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Measurable minimum theorem for compact-valued recourse systems.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Let \((\Omega,\mathcal F)\) be a measurable space, let \(Y:\Omega\rightrightarrows\mathbb R^m\) be nonempty, compact-valued, and weakly measurable, and let \(f:\Omega\times\mathbb R^m\to\mathbb R\) be Carathéodory. Define
\[Q(\omega)=\min_{y\in Y(\omega)}f(\omega,y).\]
Then \(Q:\Omega\to\mathbb R\) is \(\mathcal F\)-measurable. Consequently, the scenario recourse value is a random variable whenever its feasible-set multifunction and objective satisfy these measurable-minimum hypotheses.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A compact-valued measurable feasible-set mapping and a Carathéodory objective produce a measurable scenario-wise optimal recourse value.
assumptions_latex: \(Y\) is nonempty, compact-valued, and weakly measurable.
\(f(\cdot,y)\) is measurable and \(f(\omega,\cdot)\) is continuous.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(Q(\omega)=\min_{y\in Y(\omega)}f(\omega,y)\) is \(\mathcal F\)-measurable.

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The theorem is mathematically plausible and fits the measurability leaf, but its exact measurable-multifunction hypotheses require an authoritative theorem or section locator.

children.title: Measurable Decision Selection
children.top_down_role: Scenario-indexed recourse choices admitting measurable representatives.

knowledge_statements.title: Measurable Decision Selection
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Measurable selection from the scenario-wise recourse argmin mapping.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Under the hypotheses of the measurable minimum theorem, define
\[S(\omega)=\operatorname*{argmin}_{y\in Y(\omega)}f(\omega,y).\]
Then \(S(\omega)\) is nonempty and compact for every \(\omega\), and there exists an \(\mathcal F\)-measurable mapping \(y^*:\Omega\to\mathbb R^m\) satisfying
\[y^*(\omega)\in S(\omega)\qquad\text{for every }\omega\in\Omega.\]
Thus scenario-wise optimal recourse decisions can be represented by a measurable decision rule.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Under measurable compact feasibility and objective continuity, the scenario-wise argmin admits a measurable selector that is optimal in every scenario.
assumptions_latex: \(Y\) is nonempty, compact-valued, and weakly measurable.
\(f\) is Carathéodory.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: There exists measurable \(y^*\) with \(y^*(\omega)\in\operatorname*{argmin}_{y\in Y(\omega)}f(\omega,y)\).

notation.meaning: scenario-wise set of optimal recourse decisions

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The theorem role fits the terminal container, but the exact hypotheses guaranteeing measurability of the argmin multifunction and existence of an everywhere-defined selector need authoritative support.

children.title: Selection Failure Regimes
children.top_down_role: Cases where pointwise recourse choices lack suitable measurable organization.

knowledge_statements.title: Selection Failure Regimes
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Failure caused by a nonmeasurable feasible-set graph.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Let \((\Omega,\mathcal F)\) be a measurable space containing a set \(A\subseteq\Omega\) with \(A\notin\mathcal F\), and define
\[Y(\omega)=\begin{cases}\{0\},&\omega\in A,\\\{1\},&\omega\notin A.\end{cases}\]
Every pointwise feasible selector \(y\) is forced to satisfy \(y^{-1}(\{0\})=A\), so no such selector is \(\mathcal F\)-measurable. Hence nonempty singleton recourse sets alone do not ensure measurable decisions; measurability of the multifunction or its graph is essential.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Nonempty scenario-wise feasible sets need not admit a measurable decision rule when their dependence on the scenario is nonmeasurable.
assumptions_latex: \(A\notin\mathcal F\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: No \(\mathcal F\)-measurable selector \(y\) satisfies \(y(\omega)\in Y(\omega)\) for every \(\omega\).

notation.meaning: a nonmeasurable subset of the scenario space

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The counterexample is internally coherent and the counterexample content kind exactly fits a selection-failure leaf, but no evidence or standard-field rationale is supplied.

children.title: Recourse-Value Integrability

knowledge_statements.title: Recourse-Value Integrability
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Absolute integrability of the measurable scenario recourse value.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Let \(Q(x,\xi)\) be a real-valued measurable recourse value for a fixed first-stage decision \(x\). It is integrable when
\[\mathbb E[|Q(x,\xi)|]=\int_\Omega |Q(x,\xi(\omega))|\,d\mathbb P(\omega)<\infty.\]
Equivalently, both positive and negative parts \(Q(x,\xi)^+\) and \(Q(x,\xi)^-\) have finite expectations. Under this condition, \(\mathbb E[Q(x,\xi)]\) is a finite, unambiguously defined real number.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A measurable recourse value is integrable when its absolute value has finite expectation, equivalently when both positive and negative parts have finite expectations.
assumptions_latex: \(Q(x,\xi)\) is real-valued and measurable.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(Q(x,\xi)\in L^1(\mathbb P)\) and \(\mathbb E[Q(x,\xi)]\in\mathbb R\).

notation.meaning: scenario recourse value at fixed x
positive and negative parts of the recourse value

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The definition and positive/negative-part equivalence are standard and precise, but the record supplies no source or explicit standard-field rationale.

children.title: Finite Expected Recourse Values
children.top_down_role: Regimes yielding finite expected recourse costs.

knowledge_statements.title: Finite Expected Recourse Values
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Integrable domination as a sufficient condition for finite expectation.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Fix \(x\in X\). Suppose \(Q(x,\xi)\) is measurable and finite almost surely, and there exists a nonnegative random variable \(G\) such that
\[|Q(x,\xi)|\le G\quad\text{almost surely},\qquad \mathbb E[G]<\infty.\]
Then \(Q(x,\xi)\) is integrable and
\[|\mathbb E[Q(x,\xi)]|\le\mathbb E[|Q(x,\xi)|]\le\mathbb E[G]<\infty.\]
Hence the expected recourse term is a finite real number at \(x\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: An almost-surely finite recourse value dominated in absolute value by an integrable random variable has a finite expected value.
assumptions_latex: \(Q(x,\xi)\) is measurable and finite almost surely.
\(|Q(x,\xi)|\le G\) almost surely for some \(G\in L^1_+(\mathbb P)\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(Q(x,\xi)\in L^1(\mathbb P)\) and \(\mathbb E[Q(x,\xi)]\in\mathbb R\).

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The domination condition correctly implies integrability and a finite expected recourse value, and the property content kind is suitable. A supporting probability or integration reference is required.

knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Under fixed recourse and the stated moment conditions, the expected positive part of the recourse value at a decision is finite exactly when the recourse right-hand side belongs to the positive cone generated by W almost surely.
assumptions_latex: \text{The recourse matrix }W\text{ is fixed}.
\mathbb E[\|q\|\,\|h\|]<\infty.

x\in\mathbb R^n.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \mathbb E[Q(x,\xi)_+]<\infty\iff h-Tx\in\operatorname{pos}W\quad\text{almost surely}.

knowledge_statements.title: Infinite-Value Regimes
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Positive-probability infeasibility or nonintegrable positive tails force infinite expectation.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Adopt the extended-value convention \(Q(x,\xi)=+\infty\) whenever the recourse problem is infeasible. If
\[\mathbb P(Q(x,\xi)=+\infty)>0,\]
then \(\mathbb E[Q(x,\xi)]=+\infty\), provided the negative part has finite expectation. More generally, even when \(Q(x,\xi)<\infty\) almost surely, the same conclusion holds if
\[\mathbb E[Q(x,\xi)^+]=+\infty\quad\text{and}\quad\mathbb E[Q(x,\xi)^-]<\infty.\]
If both part-expectations are infinite, the expectation is undefined rather than equal to an extended real value.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Positive-probability infeasibility or a nonintegrable positive tail yields infinite expected recourse when the negative part is integrable; two infinite parts make expectation undefined.
assumptions_latex: \(Q(x,\xi)\) is extended-real-valued and measurable.
\(\mathbb E[Q(x,\xi)^-]<\infty\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: Either stated positive-value failure condition implies \(\mathbb E[Q(x,\xi)]=+\infty\).

notation.meaning: positive part of the recourse value
negative part of the recourse value

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The extended-expectation distinctions are mathematically consistent and the failure-boundary kind fits the leaf, but the claims require a source locator.

children.title: Tail-Driven Finiteness Boundaries
children.top_down_role: Finiteness limits arising from extreme scenario behavior.

knowledge_statements.title: Tail-Driven Finiteness Boundaries
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Exact tail-integral criterion for nonnegative recourse values.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Let \(Q(x,\xi)\) be a nonnegative measurable recourse value. Its expectation satisfies the tail representation
\[\mathbb E[Q(x,\xi)]=\int_0^\infty \mathbb P(Q(x,\xi)>t)\,dt.\]
Consequently,
\[\mathbb E[Q(x,\xi)]<\infty\quad\Longleftrightarrow\quad\int_0^\infty \mathbb P(Q(x,\xi)>t)\,dt<\infty.\]
Thus the integrability of the survival function is the exact boundary between finite and infinite expected nonnegative recourse values.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: For nonnegative recourse, the expectation is finite exactly when the integral of its tail probabilities is finite.
assumptions_latex: \(Q(x,\xi):\Omega\to[0,+\infty]\) is measurable.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\mathbb E[Q(x,\xi)]<\infty\) if and only if \(\int_0^\infty\mathbb P(Q(x,\xi)>t)\,dt<\infty\).

notation.meaning: survival probability of the recourse value above threshold t

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The tail-integral criterion is correctly restricted to nonnegative measurable recourse values and fits the finiteness-boundary container, but no authoritative source is cited.

children.title: Recourse-Solution Attainment

knowledge_statements.title: Recourse-Solution Attainment
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Attainment under compact feasibility and lower semicontinuity.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Fix a first-stage decision \(x\) and realization \(\xi\). Let \(Y(x,\xi)\subseteq\mathbb R^m\) be nonempty and compact, and let \(f(x,\xi,\cdot):Y(x,\xi)\to(-\infty,+\infty]\) be proper and lower semicontinuous. Then there exists \(y^*\in Y(x,\xi)\) such that
\[f(x,\xi,y^*)=\min_{y\in Y(x,\xi)}f(x,\xi,y)=Q(x,\xi).\]
Hence the scenario recourse infimum is attained by a feasible corrective decision.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A proper lower-semicontinuous recourse objective attains its minimum on every nonempty compact scenario-feasible set.
assumptions_latex: \(Y(x,\xi)\) is nonempty and compact.
\(f(x,\xi,\cdot)\) is proper and lower semicontinuous on \(Y(x,\xi)\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: There exists \(y^*\in Y(x,\xi)\) with \(f(x,\xi,y^*)=Q(x,\xi)\).

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The compactness and lower-semicontinuity hypotheses support the stated attainment result, and theorem is the correct content kind. An authoritative attainment-theorem locator is still required.

children.title: Closed Feasible-Set Structure

knowledge_statements.title: Closed Feasible-Set Structure
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Closedness of the second-stage feasible multifunction induced by a closed joint constraint set.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(X\) and \(Y\) be finite-dimensional Euclidean spaces, let \(C\subseteq X\times Y\) be closed, and define \(F(x):=\{y\in Y:(x,y)\in C\}\). Then \(\operatorname{gph}F=C\) is closed, every fiber \(F(x)\) is closed, and feasibility is preserved under convergent primal sequences: if \(x_k\to x\), \(y_k\to y\), and \(y_k\in F(x_k)\) for every \(k\), then \(y\in F(x)\). This conclusion does not assert that the projection \(\operatorname{dom}F=\{x:F(x)\neq\varnothing\}\) is closed.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A closed joint constraint set gives closed recourse fibers and preserves feasibility under convergent first- and second-stage decisions, although its first-stage projection need not be closed.
assumptions_latex: \(X\) and \(Y\) are finite-dimensional Euclidean spaces.
\(C\subseteq X\times Y\) is closed.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\operatorname{gph}F\) and every \(F(x)\) are closed, with sequential feasibility preservation.

notation.meaning: second-stage feasible set at first-stage decision x

knowledge_statements.title: Closed Recourse-Value Structure
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Lower semicontinuity and finite-value attainment for a parametric recourse problem under local uniform level-boundedness.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(X\) and \(Y\) be finite-dimensional Euclidean spaces, let \(C\subseteq X\times Y\) be closed, and let \(g:X\times Y\to(-\infty,+\infty]\) be lower semicontinuous. Define \(Q(x):=\inf\{g(x,y):(x,y)\in C\}\), with the infimum of an empty set equal to \(+\infty\). Suppose that for every \(\bar x\in X\) and \(\alpha\in\mathbb R\), there is a neighborhood \(U\) of \(\bar x\) such that \(\{y\in Y:\exists x\in U,\ (x,y)\in C,\ g(x,y)\leq\alpha\}\) is bounded. Then \(Q\) is lower semicontinuous, equivalently \(\operatorname{epi}Q\) is closed. Moreover, whenever \(Q(x)\in\mathbb R\), the infimum defining \(Q(x)\) is attained.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: In finite dimensions, a lower-semicontinuous recourse objective over closed constraints has a closed value function and attained finite minima when nearby feasible sublevel sets are uniformly bounded in the recourse variable.
assumptions_latex: \(X\) and \(Y\) are finite-dimensional Euclidean spaces.
\(C\subseteq X\times Y\) is closed.
\(g:X\times Y\to(-\infty,+\infty]\) is lower semicontinuous.
Feasible sublevel sets are locally uniformly bounded in \(y\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(Q\) is lower semicontinuous, \(\operatorname{epi}Q\) is closed, and every finite value of \(Q\) is attained.

children.title: Nonattainment Boundaries

knowledge_statements.title: Nonattainment Boundaries
knowledge_statements.scope_note: A continuous recourse objective on a closed, noncompact feasible set may have no optimizer.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Consider the recourse problem \(Q:=\inf_{y\in\mathbb R}e^y\). Its feasible set \(\mathbb R\) is nonempty and closed, and its objective is continuous, strictly positive, and bounded below. Nevertheless, \(Q=0\) because \(e^y\downarrow0\) as \(y\to-\infty\), while no \(y\in\mathbb R\) satisfies \(e^y=0\). Thus closed feasibility and continuity alone do not ensure attainment; compactness, coercivity, or an appropriate level-boundedness condition is essential.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Continuous minimization over a closed but noncompact recourse set can fail to attain its finite infimum because minimizing sequences escape to infinity.
assumptions_latex: \(Y=\mathbb R\).
The feasible set is \(Y\), and the objective is \(e^y\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\inf_{y\in\mathbb R}e^y=0\), but \(\operatorname*{argmin}_{y\in\mathbb R}e^y=\varnothing\).

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Closed Convex Geometry of the Expected Fixed-Recourse Function
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Domain, continuity, and subdifferential properties of expected polyhedral recourse under fixed recourse and integrability.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(\phi(x)=\mathbb E[Q(x,\omega)]\). Suppose recourse is fixed, \(\Pi(\omega)\ne\varnothing\) almost surely, and, for \(j=1,\ldots,J_2\), \[\mathbb E|\gamma_j|<+\infty,\qquad \mathbb E[\|q_j\|\,\|h\|]<+\infty,\qquad \mathbb E[\|q_j\|\,\|T\|]<+\infty.\] Then \(\phi\) is well defined and \(\phi(x)>-\infty\) for every \(x\in\mathbb R^n\). Moreover, \(\phi\) is convex and lower semicontinuous and is Lipschitz continuous on \(\operatorname{dom}\phi\); its domain is closed and convex and satisfies \[\operatorname{dom}\phi=\{x\in\mathbb R^n:h-Tx\in W(\mathcal Y)\text{ almost surely}\}.\] For every \(x_0\in\operatorname{dom}\phi\), \[\partial\phi(x_0)=-\mathbb E[T^\top\mathfrak D(x_0,\omega)]+\mathcal N_{\operatorname{dom}\phi}(x_0),\] where the expectation of the set-valued term is understood in the set-valued sense.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Under fixed recourse, almost-sure nonemptiness of the stated feasible set, and the given integrability conditions, the expected recourse function never equals negative infinity. It is closed convex and Lipschitz on its closed convex domain, its domain is characterized by almost-sure recourse feasibility, and its subdifferential is the expected dual contribution plus the domain normal cone.
assumptions_latex: \phi(x)=\mathbb E[Q(x,\omega)]
\text{Recourse is fixed}
\Pi(\omega)\ne\varnothing\quad\text{almost surely}
\mathbb E|\gamma_j|<+\infty,\quad \mathbb E[\|q_j\|\|h\|]<+\infty,\quad \mathbb E[\|q_j\|\|T\|]<+\infty\quad(j=1,\ldots,J_2)
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \phi(x)>-\infty\ \forall x;\quad \phi\text{ is convex, lower semicontinuous, and Lipschitz on }\operatorname{dom}\phi;\quad \operatorname{dom}\phi=\{x:h-Tx\in W(\mathcal Y)\ \mathrm{a.s.}\}\text{ is closed and convex};\quad \partial\phi(x_0)=-\mathbb E[T^\top\mathfrak D(x_0,\omega)]+\mathcal N_{\operatorname{dom}\phi}(x_0).

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Piecewise Convex Program
knowledge_statements.scope_note: General cellwise-smooth representation of a convex optimization problem; objective notation is normalized consistently as z.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: The problem \(\inf\{z(x)\mid x\in S\}\) is piecewise convex when \(z:\mathbb R^n\to\overline{\mathbb R}\) is convex, \(S\subseteq\operatorname{dom}z\) is closed and convex with nonempty interior, and there is a finite closed convex complex \(\mathcal K\) whose \(n\)-dimensional cells cover \(S\), such that either \(z\equiv-\infty\), or for every cell \(C_v\) there is a convex function \(z_v\) on \(S\), continuously differentiable on an open neighborhood of \(C_v\), satisfying \(z(x)=z_v(x)\) and \(\nabla z_v(x)\in\partial z(x)\) for every \(x\in C_v\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A piecewise convex program minimizes a convex objective z over a closed convex set S with nonempty interior. A finite closed convex complex covers S by full-dimensional cells, and, unless z is identically minus infinity, each cell has a convex local representation z_v that is continuously differentiable near the cell, agrees with z there, and has gradient belonging to the subdifferential of z.

S\subseteq\operatorname{dom}z\text{ is closed and convex, with }\operatorname{int}S\ne\varnothing.
\mathcal K\text{ is a finite closed convex complex whose }n\text{-dimensional cells cover }S.
z\equiv-\infty\text{, or each cell }C_v\text{ admits the stated convex }C^1\text{ representation }z_v.

knowledge_statements.title: Recourse-Function Convexity
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Convexity of a value function obtained by partial minimization of a jointly convex recourse model.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(X\) and \(Y\) be real vector spaces, let \(C\subseteq X\times Y\) be convex, and let \(g:C\to(-\infty,+\infty]\) be convex. knowledge_statements.scope_note: Closedness of a convex recourse function under inf-compactness in the eliminated variable.

knowledge_statements.title: Convexity Preservation Regimes
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Scenario aggregation preserves convexity for proper expectations and nonnegative weighted sums of convex recourse values.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \((\Omega,\mathcal F,\mathbb P)\) be a probability space, let \(X\) be a real vector space, and let \(Q_\xi:X\to(-\infty,+\infty]\) be convex for almost every scenario \(\xi\). Suppose \(Q(x):=\mathbb E[Q_\xi(x)]\) is well defined for every \(x\in X\), never equals \(-\infty\), and is finite at some point. Then \(Q\) is convex. In particular, if \(Q_s:X\to(-\infty,+\infty]\) is convex for \(s=1,\ldots,S\) and \(p_s\geq0\) with \(\sum_{s=1}^S p_s=1\), then \(x\mapsto\sum_{s=1}^S p_sQ_s(x)\) is convex wherever the extended-real sum is well defined. Adding a convex first-stage cost and minimizing over a convex first-stage feasible set preserves the convex optimization structure.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Proper expectations and well-defined nonnegative weighted sums preserve scenario-wise recourse convexity; convex first-stage costs and feasible sets preserve the overall convex model.

\(Q(x)=\mathbb E[Q_\xi(x)]\) is well defined, never equals \(-\infty\), and is finite at some point.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(x\mapsto\mathbb E[Q_\xi(x)]\) is convex, and every well-defined finite nonnegative scenario aggregation is convex.

notation.meaning: nonnegative probability weight of scenario s

knowledge_statements.title: Closedness Failure Boundaries
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Closed joint feasibility does not ensure a closed marginal value without bounded near-optimal recourse decisions.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(C:=\{(x,y)\in\mathbb R^2:x\geq0,\ xy\geq1\}\), which is closed, and minimize the continuous objective \(g(x,y):=0\) over each fiber. The resulting value is \(Q(x)=0\) for \(x>0\) and \(Q(x)=+\infty\) for \(x\leq0\). Hence \(Q\) is not lower semicontinuous at \(0\), although \(C\) is closed. Indeed, feasible points \((x,1/x)\) escape to infinity as \(x\downarrow0\), showing precisely why projection or marginalization requires compactness or level-boundedness.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A closed joint feasible set can produce a nonclosed value function when feasible recourse decisions diverge as the parameter approaches a boundary.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(Q(0)=+\infty\) while \(\liminf_{x\downarrow0}Q(x)=0\), so \(Q\) is not lower semicontinuous.

knowledge_statements.title: Polyhedral Epigraph Structure
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Epigraph representation for finite-valued linear recourse through extreme points of the dual feasible polyhedron.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(X\subseteq\mathbb R^n\) be polyhedral, let \(q\in\mathbb R^m\), \(h\in\mathbb R^r\), \(T\in\mathbb R^{r\times n}\), and \(W\in\mathbb R^{r\times m}\), and define \(Q(x):=\min\{q^\top y:Wy=h-Tx,\ y\in\mathbb R_+^m\}\) for \(x\in X\). Assume the primal problem is feasible with finite value for every \(x\in X\), strong linear-programming duality holds, and every relevant dual optimum is represented by one of finitely many extreme points \(\pi^1,\ldots,\pi^K\) of \(D:=\{\pi\in\mathbb R^r:W^\top\pi\leq q\}\). Then \[Q(x)=\max_{1\leq k\leq K}(\pi^k)^\top(h-Tx),\qquad x\in X,\] and \[\operatorname{epi}_XQ=\{(x,t)\in X\times\mathbb R:t\geq(\pi^k)^\top(h-Tx),\ k=1,\ldots,K\}.\] Hence \(\operatorname{epi}_XQ\) is polyhedral.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Finite-valued linear recourse has a polyhedral restricted epigraph when finitely many dual extreme points generate every relevant optimal value.
assumptions_latex: \(X\subseteq\mathbb R^n\) is polyhedral, and the recourse linear program is feasible with finite value on \(X\).
Strong linear-programming duality holds.
Finitely many extreme points of \(D\) represent all dual optima relevant on \(X\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(Q\) is a finite maximum of affine functions on \(X\), and \(\operatorname{epi}_XQ\) is polyhedral.

knowledge_statements.title: Piecewise-Linear Value Structure
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Finite affine-piece representation of a linear recourse value on its finite-valued domain.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(X\subseteq\mathbb R^n\) be a polyhedron, let \(a_k\in\mathbb R^n\) and \(b_k\in\mathbb R\) for \(k=1,\ldots,K\), and suppose \(Q(x)=\max_{1\leq k\leq K}\{a_k^\top x+b_k\}\) for every \(x\in X\). Then \(Q\) is convex and piecewise affine on \(X\). For every \(x\in X\), at least one index \(k\) is active, meaning \(Q(x)=a_k^\top x+b_k\), and \(Q\) agrees with that affine function on every subset where the same piece remains maximal. At points in \(\operatorname{ri}X\), failure of differentiability can occur only where active pieces with distinct gradients tie.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A finite affine maximum makes linear recourse convex and piecewise affine, with possible interior kinks only where active pieces having different gradients tie.
assumptions_latex: \(X\subseteq\mathbb R^n\) is polyhedral.
\(a_k\in\mathbb R^n\), \(b_k\in\mathbb R\), and \(Q(x)=\max_{1\leq k\leq K}(a_k^\top x+b_k)\) on \(X\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(Q\) is convex and piecewise affine on \(X\), and its relative-interior nondifferentiability locus is contained in the affine-piece tie sets.

knowledge_statements.title: Critical-Region Geometry
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Polyhedral regions on which one affine dual piece determines the recourse value.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(X\subseteq\mathbb R^n\) be a polyhedron, let \(a_k\in\mathbb R^n\) and \(b_k\in\mathbb R\) for \(k=1,\ldots,K\), and let \(Q(x)=\max_{1\leq k\leq K}(a_k^\top x+b_k)\) on \(X\). For each \(k\), define \[R_k:=\{x\in X:(a_k-a_j)^\top x\geq b_j-b_k\ \text{for every }j=1,\ldots,K\}.\] Then each \(R_k\) is a possibly empty polyhedron, \(X=\bigcup_{k=1}^K R_k\), and \(Q(x)=a_k^\top x+b_k\) for every \(x\in R_k\). For \(k\neq j\), the intersection \(R_k\cap R_j\) lies in the tie hyperplane \(\{x:(a_k-a_j)^\top x=b_j-b_k\}\). The nondifferentiability locus of \(Q\) in \(\operatorname{ri}X\) is contained in the union of tie sets for active pieces with distinct gradients.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Each affine piece defines a polyhedral critical region; these regions cover the domain, and shared active-region boundaries lie in affine-piece tie hyperplanes.
assumptions_latex: \(X\subseteq\mathbb R^n\) is polyhedral.
\(a_k\in\mathbb R^n\), \(b_k\in\mathbb R\), and \(Q\) is the maximum of the resulting finitely many affine functions on \(X\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The sets \(R_k\) form a polyhedral covering of \(X\) on whose members \(Q\) is affine, and intersections of active regions lie in affine-piece tie hyperplanes.

knowledge_statements.title: Nonpolyhedral Boundaries
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Convex recourse need not be polyhedral when the second-stage objective is nonpolyhedral.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For \(x\in\mathbb R\), consider \(Q(x):=\min\{y^2:y=x\}\). The feasible set is affine and the unique optimizer is \(y=x\), so \(Q(x)=x^2\). This recourse function is finite, closed, strictly convex, and smooth, but its epigraph \(\{(x,t):t\geq x^2\}\) is not a polyhedron and \(Q\) is not piecewise affine on any finite polyhedral partition of \(\mathbb R\). Thus polyhedral constraints alone do not yield polyhedral recourse geometry; a polyhedral objective or equivalent finite affine dual representation is also required.

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Convex scenario recourse at a fixed scenario and right-hand-side parameter.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Fix \(\omega\in\Omega\) and \(\chi_\omega\), and assume the stated convexity hypotheses. Then \(\vartheta(\cdot,\omega)\) and \(F(\cdot,\omega)\) are convex. If the primal problem (2.71) is subconsistent, it has no duality gap with (2.72) iff \(\vartheta(\cdot,\omega)\) is lower semicontinuous at \(\chi_\omega\). knowledge_statements.title: Two-Stage Nonanticipativity Duality
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Lagrangian dual decomposition of finite-scenario first-stage consensus constraints.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(S\) be a finite scenario set with \(p_s>0\) and \(\sum_{s\in S}p_s=1\). For each \(s\in S\), let \(F_s\) be the feasible set for the scenario variables \((x_s,y_s)\), and consider \[v=\min_{z,\{x_s,y_s\}_{s\in S}}\sum_{s\in S}p_s\bigl(c^{\mathsf T}x_s+q_s^{\mathsf T}y_s\bigr)\quad\text{subject to }(x_s,y_s)\in F_s\text{ and }x_s-z=0.\] Assign multiplier \(p_s\lambda_s\) to \(x_s-z=0\). If strong Lagrangian duality holds and the primal optimum is finite and attained, then \[v=\max_{\{\lambda_s\}_{s\in S}:\,\sum_{s\in S}p_s\lambda_s=0}\sum_{s\in S}p_s\inf_{(x_s,y_s)\in F_s}\bigl(c^{\mathsf T}x_s+q_s^{\mathsf T}y_s+\lambda_s^{\mathsf T}x_s\bigr).\]
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Dualizing the oriented consensus constraints x_s−z=0 separates the extensive form into scenario subproblems, while the probability-weighted multipliers must sum to zero.

\(F_s\) is the feasible set for scenario variables \((x_s,y_s)\), and nonanticipativity is imposed as \(x_s-z=0\).
The extensive-form primal has a finite attained optimum and strong Lagrangian duality holds.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The extensive-form value equals the separable nonanticipativity dual value over multipliers satisfying \(\sum_{s\in S}p_s\lambda_s=0\).

knowledge_statements.title: Scenario-Tree Form
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Deterministic-equivalent representation on a finite, rooted scenario tree.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(\mathcal T=(V,E)\) be a finite rooted tree with stages \(t(v)\), node probabilities \(p_v\), data \(\xi_v\), and parent map \(a(v)\). A scenario-tree multistage problem has the form \[\min_{(x_v)_{v\in V}}\ \sum_{v\in V}p_v c_v(x_{a(v)},x_v;\xi_v)\quad\text{subject to}\quad x_v\in X_v(x_{a(v)},\xi_v),\ v\in V,\] with the root-parent argument omitted. Each node has one decision variable, so scenarios sharing the history represented by \(v\) automatically share the same decision. Thus node indexing enforces nonanticipativity without additional pairwise equalities.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A finite scenario tree yields a deterministic equivalent whose node decisions, weighted costs, and parent-child constraints represent recourse; shared nodes automatically enforce nonanticipativity.
assumptions_latex: \(\mathcal T\) is finite and rooted.
\(p_v\ge 0\), and leaf probabilities sum to one.
Each node records all information available when \(x_v\) is selected.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The node-indexed program is a finite deterministic equivalent with nonanticipativity encoded by common tree nodes.

children.title: Adapted Policy-Space Form

knowledge_statements.title: Adapted Policy-Space Form
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Policy formulation over stochastic histories and their natural information filtration.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: On a probability space \((\Omega,\mathcal F,\mathbb P)\), let \(\xi=(\xi_t)_{t=1}^T\) generate \(\mathcal F_t=\sigma(\xi_1,\ldots,\xi_t)\). The adapted policy-space formulation is \[\inf_{x\in\mathcal X_{\mathrm{ad}}}\ \mathbb E\!\left[\sum_{t=1}^T c_t(x_t,\xi_{1:t})\right],\qquad \mathcal X_{\mathrm{ad}}=\{x:x_t\text{ is }\mathcal F_t\text{-measurable and }x_t(\omega)\in X_t(x_{1:t-1}(\omega),\xi_{1:t}(\omega))\ \mathbb P\text{-a.s.}\}.\] Measurability makes each decision a function only of information revealed through its decision stage.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The decision variable is an adapted policy: each stage decision is measurable with respect to observed history and satisfies the history-dependent constraints almost surely.
assumptions_latex: \(T<\infty\).
Stage costs are measurable and have a well-defined extended expectation.
The feasible policy class is nonempty.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: Every feasible \(x\in\mathcal X_{\mathrm{ad}}\) is nonanticipative with respect to \((\mathcal F_t)_{t=1}^T\).

children.title: Scenario Trees

knowledge_statements.title: Scenario Trees
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Finite, nonrecombining representation of discrete uncertainty histories.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: A scenario tree of horizon \(T\) is a finite rooted directed tree \(\mathcal T=(V,E)\) with stage partition \(V=V_0\mathbin{\dot\cup}\cdots\mathbin{\dot\cup}V_T\), root \(r\in V_0\), and arcs only from \(V_{t-1}\) to \(V_t\). Each node \(v\) carries a realization \(\xi_v\), and every arc \((v,w)\) from a nonleaf node carries a conditional transition probability \(q_{vw}\), where \(q_{vw}\ge 0\) and \(\sum_{w:(v,w)\in E}q_{vw}=1\) for every nonleaf \(v\). The unique root-to-node path represents one observed history; distinct nodes never recombine.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A scenario tree is a finite rooted, stagewise tree whose unique paths encode uncertainty histories and whose outgoing arc probabilities at each nonleaf node define their distribution.
assumptions_latex: \(T<\infty\).
Every nonleaf node has finitely many children.
Every nonroot node has exactly one parent.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: Each \(v\in V_t\) represents exactly one length-\(t\) history and has probability equal to the product of transition probabilities on its root path.

notation.meaning: conditional probability of child w given nonleaf node v

children.title: Scenario-Fan Representations

knowledge_statements.title: Scenario-Fan Representations
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Root-only branching representation of sampled complete uncertainty paths.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Given complete trajectories \(\xi^i_{1:T}\) and weights \(w_i>0\) with \(\sum_{i=1}^Nw_i=1\), a scenario-fan representation is the rooted graph formed by one common root and \(N\) distinct branches, branch \(i\) carrying the entire path \(\xi^i_{1:T}\) and probability \(w_i\). Apart from the root, nodes belonging to different branches are distinct even when their realized prefixes coincide. Consequently, a fan represents the empirical distribution \(\widehat P_N=\sum_{i=1}^Nw_i\delta_{\xi^i_{1:T}}\) but does not itself identify equal sampled prefixes or enforce their nonanticipative coupling.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A scenario fan places each sampled full trajectory on a separate root branch; it represents an empirical path distribution but does not merge equal prefixes.
assumptions_latex: \(N,T<\infty\).
Each \(\xi^i_{1:T}\) is a complete sampled path.
The weights are positive and normalized.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The fan has path law \(\widehat P_N\), while common-history decisions require additional prefix coupling.

children.title: Path-Sample Representations
children.top_down_role: Finite samples of complete uncertainty trajectories.

knowledge_statements.title: Path-Sample Representations
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Weighted empirical representation using complete sampled process trajectories.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(\Xi=(\Xi_1,\ldots,\Xi_T)\) have law \(P\), and let \(\xi^1_{1:T},\ldots,\xi^N_{1:T}\) be sampled complete paths with normalized weights \(w_i\). The path-sample representation replaces \(P\) by \(\widehat P_N=\sum_{i=1}^Nw_i\delta_{\xi^i_{1:T}}\). Hence every functional \(F\) that is integrable under \(\widehat P_N\) is represented by \[\mathbb E_{\widehat P_N}[F(\Xi)]=\sum_{i=1}^Nw_iF(\xi^i_{1:T}).\] For multistage decisions, path indexing alone does not enforce nonanticipativity: decisions attached to identical observed prefixes must be equated or generated by a common history-dependent policy.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Complete sampled trajectories and weights define an empirical path law, so expectations become weighted sums; path indexing alone does not enforce the nonanticipativity required of multistage decisions.
assumptions_latex: \(N,T<\infty\).
\(w_i\ge0\) and \(\sum_iw_i=1\).
\(F(\xi^i_{1:T})\) is finite for every positively weighted sample.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: Integration under \(\widehat P_N\) equals the weighted sample average, while policy feasibility additionally requires prefix-based nonanticipativity.

children.title: Shared-Prefix Coupling
children.top_down_role: Nonanticipative links induced by common sampled histories.

knowledge_statements.title: Shared-Prefix Coupling
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Nonanticipativity predicate for decisions indexed by sampled complete paths.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For sampled paths \(\xi^i_{1:T}\), let \(x_t^i\) be the decision on path \(i\) at stage \(t\), selected after observing \(\xi^i_{1:t}\). Shared-prefix coupling is the condition \[\xi^i_{1:t}=\xi^j_{1:t}\ \Longrightarrow\ x_t^i=x_t^j,\qquad i,j\in\{1,\ldots,N\},\quad t\in\{1,\ldots,T\}.\] If decisions precede observation of \(\xi_t\), the antecedent is instead \(\xi^i_{1:t-1}=\xi^j_{1:t-1}\). The equalities make the path-indexed decisions induce a single well-defined policy on every history represented in the sample.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Decisions on two sampled paths must coincide whenever their observable prefixes coincide; the relevant prefix ends before or after current uncertainty according to decision timing.
assumptions_latex: All sampled paths use the same horizon and information timing.
Equality of prefixes means equality of all observations available at the decision time.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The coupled variables define a nonanticipative policy on the set of sampled histories.

notation.meaning: stage-t decision on sampled path i
observed prefix of sampled path i

children.title: Sample-Coverage Boundaries
children.top_down_role: Representation limits caused by incomplete path coverage.

knowledge_statements.title: Sample-Coverage Boundaries
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Limits of finite complete-path samples as representations of adaptive decisions.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(H_t^N=\{\xi^i_{1:t}:i=1,ldots,N\}\) be the sampled histories at stage \(t\). A path-sample formulation constrains and evaluates a policy only on \(\bigcup_tH_t^N\). If a history \(h_t\) has positive probability under the true law but \(h_t\notin H_t^N\), the sampled formulation supplies neither a decision value nor feasibility guarantees at \(h_t\) unless an external policy extension rule is imposed. Moreover, two policies agreeing on every sampled history have identical sampled objectives, although their true expected costs or feasibility may differ outside the sample.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A finite path sample covers only its observed prefixes; it cannot determine policy behavior, feasibility, or true performance on unsampled positive-probability histories.
assumptions_latex: The true process admits a positive-probability history absent from the finite sample.
No policy extension or structural function class fixes decisions outside sampled histories.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: Sample agreement does not imply equality of true feasibility or true expected performance.

notation.meaning: set of stage-t prefixes appearing in the sample

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The failure-boundary claim has no citation, and the displayed definition of the sampled-history set contains the malformed index text `i=1,ldots,N`. An authoritative source and corrected mathematical notation are required before the scope and conclusion can be reviewed reliably.

children.title: Scenario Lattices
children.top_down_role: Recombining uncertainty structures indexed by shared states.

knowledge_statements.title: Scenario Lattices
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Finite recombining graph representation indexed by stage and retained state.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: A scenario lattice is a finite staged directed acyclic graph \(G=(V,E)\), with \(V=V_0\mathbin{\dot\cup}\cdots\mathbin{\dot\cup}V_T\) and arcs from \(V_{t-1}\) to \(V_t\), in which a node may have multiple parents. Each node \(v\) represents a retained state \(s_v\), and each outgoing arc \((v,w)\) has conditional probability \(q_{vw}\), with \(q_{vw}\ge0\) and \(\sum_wq_{vw}=1\). Distinct histories may reach the same node only when the retained state is sufficient to use the same feasible continuation model and conditional future law.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A scenario lattice is a finite staged probability graph that recombines different histories at a common state when their feasible and probabilistic continuations coincide.
assumptions_latex: The graph is finite, staged, and acyclic.
Outgoing transition probabilities are normalized.
Every recombined node carries a continuation-sufficient state.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: Root-to-terminal paths define scenarios, while multiple paths may share later nodes without changing the continuation model.

notation.meaning: transition probability on arc from v to w

children.title: Policy Graphs
children.top_down_role: Graph-based organization of reusable policy states.

knowledge_statements.title: Policy Graphs
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Graph representation coupling policy states, decisions, observations, and transitions.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: A finite-horizon policy graph is a staged directed graph \(G=(V,E)\) whose node \(v\in V_t\) carries a decision rule \(\pi_v:S_v\to A_v\). Given graph state \(v_t\), controlled state \(s_t\), and newly revealed observation \(z_{t+1}\), the action is \(a_t=\pi_{v_t}(s_t)\), and an admissible labeled arc determines \(v_{t+1}\). The representation is nonanticipative when both \(\pi_{v_t}\) and the selected outgoing arc depend only on information available by their selection times. Multiple histories may share a graph node, thereby sharing its continuation decision rule.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A policy graph assigns a decision rule to each staged graph node and uses observed information to select transitions; shared nodes reuse continuation rules across histories.
assumptions_latex: The horizon and graph are finite.
Every reachable node-observation pair has an admissible successor.
Decision and transition rules respect the specified information timing.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The graph induces a nonanticipative policy on every history for which its node transitions are defined.

notation.meaning: controlled state supplied to the node rule
decision rule stored at node v

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: No source is supplied for this particular meaning of policy graph. The observation-labeled successor mechanism is also described only informally, so the domains and rule selecting admissible arcs are not sufficiently defined to establish the claimed induced policy.

children.title: Recombination Criteria
children.top_down_role: Conditions supporting the merger of distinct scenario histories.

knowledge_statements.title: Recombination Criteria
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Exact criterion for safely merging two represented histories.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(h_t\) and \(h'_t\) be stage-\(t\) histories. They are exactly recombinable for a recourse model if there exists a common retained state \(s_t\) such that: their admissible continuation-policy sets coincide when conditioned on \(s_t\); their accumulated past contributions differ at most by a decision-independent constant; and, for every admissible continuation action, the conditional law of the next retained state, constraint data, and incremental cost is identical under \(h_t\) and \(h'_t\). Under these conditions the two histories have the same continuation value function and may be represented by one graph node.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Two histories may recombine exactly when a common state gives identical feasible continuations, conditional transition-and-cost laws, and continuation values, up to irrelevant past constants.
assumptions_latex: Both histories occur at the same decision stage.
Conditional distributions are defined under both histories.
The retained state contains every variable affecting future feasibility and cost.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The continuation value satisfies \(V_t(h_t)=V_t(h'_t)\) after removal of any decision-independent past-cost constant.

notation.meaning: optimal continuation value at stage t

source_refs.locator: 2.3 Markov Processes with Arbitrary State Space p. 101

children.title: Graph-State Aliasing Boundaries
children.top_down_role: Representation failures caused by merging behaviorally distinct histories.

knowledge_statements.title: Graph-State Aliasing Boundaries
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Failure caused by merging histories with different continuation-relevant information.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Suppose a graph map \(\phi_t\) assigns histories to retained states and merges \(h_t\ne h'_t\) because \(\phi_t(h_t)=\phi_t(h'_t)\). If the histories have different feasible action sets, different conditional laws of future data, or different action-dependent continuation costs, then any node policy must use one continuation rule for two distinguishable recourse problems. For example, if a hidden regime \(r\in\{0,1\}\) is observed in the history, the unique feasible next action is \(a=r\), and \(\phi_t\) omits \(r\), no action assigned to the merged node is feasible for both histories.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Merging histories is invalid when omitted information changes future feasibility, distributions, or costs; a hidden observed regime with regime-specific feasible actions gives a concrete failure.
assumptions_latex: The representation forces histories with equal graph state to share a node policy.
At least one omitted history feature affects the continuation problem.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The aliased graph can lose feasibility or optimality relative to the original history-dependent model.

notation.meaning: map from histories to graph states
observed regime omitted by the graph state

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The concrete regime example is coherent, and failure_boundary is the correct content kind, but no source supports the broader claim about aliasing histories with differing conditional laws, feasible sets, or continuation costs.

children.title: Stochastic-Process Models

knowledge_statements.title: Stochastic-Process Models
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Finite-horizon process model for sequentially revealed uncertainty.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: A discrete-time stochastic-process model on horizon \(T\) is a probability space \((\Omega,\mathcal F,\mathbb P)\) together with measurable maps \(\Xi_t:\Omega\to S_t\) for \(t=1,\ldots,T\), where each \((S_t,\mathcal S_t)\) is a measurable state space. The random vector \(\Xi_{1:T}\) induces a probability law \(P=\mathbb P\circ\Xi_{1:T}^{-1}\) on the product path space \((\prod_{t=1}^TS_t,\bigotimes_{t=1}^T\mathcal S_t)\). Sequential decisions use histories \(\Xi_{1:t}\), or a specified information process derived from them.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A stochastic-process model consists of measurable time-indexed random variables on a probability space and the induced probability law on complete paths.
assumptions_latex: \(T<\infty\).
Each \((S_t,\mathcal S_t)\) is a measurable space.
Every \(\Xi_t\) is \(\mathcal F/\mathcal S_t\)-measurable.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\Xi_{1:T}\) defines a probability measure \(P\) on the measurable path space.

notation.meaning: random process state or observation at stage t

children.title: Filtration Models
children.top_down_role: Representations of information growth through observable histories.

knowledge_statements.title: Filtration Models
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Discrete-time information model for a finite-horizon multistage recourse problem.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: On a probability space \((\Omega,\mathcal F,\mathbb P)\), a filtration model over stages \(t=0,\ldots,T\) is a family \((\mathcal F_t)_{t=0}^T\) of sub-\(\sigma\)-algebras satisfying \(\{\varnothing,\Omega\}\subseteq\mathcal F_0\subseteq\cdots\subseteq\mathcal F_T\subseteq\mathcal F\). The algebra \(\mathcal F_t\) represents all events distinguishable when the stage-\(t\) decision is selected. An admissible decision process \((x_t)_{t=0}^T\), with \(x_t:\Omega\to X_t\), is nonanticipative when every \(x_t\) is \(\mathcal F_t\)-measurable.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A filtration is an increasing sequence of event algebras representing available information; admissible stage decisions must be measurable with respect to the current algebra.
assumptions_latex: \(T<\infty\).
\((\Omega,\mathcal F,\mathbb P)\) is a probability space.
Each \(X_t\) is a measurable decision space.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(x_t\text{ is admissible only if }x_t\text{ is }\mathcal F_t\text{-measurable for every }t.\)

children.title: Process–Filtration Compatibility
children.top_down_role: Alignment between uncertainty evolution plus information revelation.

knowledge_statements.title: Process–Filtration Compatibility
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Compatibility between an uncertainty process and the information available to decisions.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \((\Omega,\mathcal F,\mathbb P)\) be a probability space, let \((\mathcal F_t)_{t=0}^T\) be a filtration, and let \(\xi_t:\Omega\to E_t\) for \(t=1,\ldots,T\), where each \(E_t\) is a standard Borel space. The uncertainty process and filtration are compatible under the stage-\(t\) observation convention when \(\xi_t\) is \(\mathcal F_t\)-measurable for every \(t\). Its natural filtration is \(\mathcal F_t^{\xi}=\sigma(\xi_1,\ldots,\xi_t)\); initially available information represented by a sigma-algebra \(\mathcal G_0\) may instead give \(\mathcal F_t=\mathcal G_0\vee\mathcal F_t^{\xi}\). Under the standard-Borel assumptions, the conditional law \(\mathbb P((\xi_{t+1},\ldots,\xi_T)\in\cdot\mid\mathcal F_t)\) exists as a regular conditional distribution.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The process and filtration are compatible when each observation is measurable with respect to the information available at that stage. The natural filtration is generated by observations through the current stage and may be enlarged by initial information.
assumptions_latex: \((\Omega,\mathcal F,\mathbb P)\) is a probability space.
\((\mathcal F_t)_{t=0}^T\) is a filtration.
Each \(\xi_t\) takes values in a standard Borel space \(E_t\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\xi_t\text{ is }\mathcal F_t\text{-measurable for every }t=1,\ldots,T.\)

notation.meaning: natural filtration generated by observations through stage t

children.title: Nonenumerative Representation Boundaries

knowledge_statements.title: Nonenumerative Representation Boundaries
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Limits of finite scenario enumeration for general process–filtration models.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: A finite scenario tree represents a process–filtration pair exactly only when, at every stage \(t\), the information algebra relevant to decisions has finitely many distinguishable atoms of positive probability and the required conditional transitions can be assigned to those atoms. If some \(\mathcal F_t\) is nonatomic, or has infinitely many decision-relevant atoms, no finite tree can preserve all \(\mathcal F_t\)-measurable decisions and conditional laws exactly. Sampling or state aggregation then yields an approximation, not an equivalent enumeration.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Finite scenario trees are exact only for finitely atomic decision-relevant information; continuous or infinitely branching information requires approximation or a nonenumerative model.
assumptions_latex: \((\mathcal F_t)_{t=0}^T\) is the decision-relevant filtration.
A finite scenario tree is required to preserve measurability and conditional laws exactly.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\mathcal F_t\text{ nonatomic or infinitely atomic for some }t\Longrightarrow\text{ no exact finite scenario-tree representation}.\)
review_flags: exact finite-representation boundary requires a directly supporting source

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The failure-boundary kind fits, but the exact finite-atomic characterization and preservation of all conditional laws require a direct source. The statement also needs sourced clarification about equality modulo null events.

knowledge_statements.title: Node-Indexed Decisions
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Scenario-tree representation using one decision variable for each observable history node.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(\mathcal N_t\) be the nodes at stage \(t\) of a finite scenario tree, and let \(n_t(\omega)\in\mathcal N_t\) denote the node reached by scenario \(\omega\). A node-indexed policy consists of variables \(x_n\in X_n\) for \(n\in\bigcup_{t=0}^T\mathcal N_t\), with scenario decision \(x_t(\omega)=x_{n_t(\omega)}\). Consequently, any two scenarios occupying the same stage-\(t\) node use the same decision without additional equality constraints.

Each stage-t node represents one equivalence class of scenarios with the same observed history.

knowledge_statements.title: Path-Indexed Decisions with Explicit Coupling
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Scenario-copy formulation in which nonanticipativity is imposed by explicit equalities.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For a finite scenario set \(\Omega_S\), introduce a stage decision copy \(x_t^{\omega}\in X_t^{\omega}\) for every \(\omega\in\Omega_S\). Define \(\omega\sim_t\omega'\) when the two scenarios have identical observations through the information available before choosing the stage-\(t\) decision. The path-indexed formulation is nonanticipative precisely when it includes \(x_t^{\omega}=x_t^{\omega'}\) for every pair with \(\omega\sim_t\omega'\). Thus feasibility is restricted to scenario copies constant on each history-equivalence class.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A decision copy is assigned to each scenario path, and equalities force copies to agree whenever their observable histories coincide.
assumptions_latex: \(\Omega_S\) is finite.
\(\sim_t\) is the equivalence relation induced by information available at decision time.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\omega\sim_t\omega'\Longrightarrow x_t^{\omega}=x_t^{\omega'}\text{ for every }t.\)

children.title: Nonanticipativity Matrix Encodings

knowledge_statements.title: Nonanticipativity Matrix Encodings
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Linear-algebraic encoding of equality among scenario decision copies.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Stack the stage-\(t\) scenario copies as \(x_t=(x_t^{\omega})_{\omega\in\Omega_S}\). A nonanticipativity matrix \(A_t\) has rows of the form \((e_{\omega}-e_{\omega'})^{\mathsf T}\otimes I\), where each selected pair satisfies \(\omega\sim_t\omega'\). The homogeneous system \(A_t x_t=0\) encodes equality along the selected pairs. It enforces complete nonanticipativity exactly when, within every equivalence class of \(\sim_t\), the selected equality pairs form a connected graph.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A sparse difference matrix enforces equality of scenario copies; connected equality links within every shared-history class are necessary and sufficient.
assumptions_latex: \(\Omega_S\) is finite.
All copies in a stage have the same finite dimension.
\(\sim_t\) partitions scenarios by observable history.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\ker A_t=\{x_t:x_t^{\omega}=x_t^{\omega'}\text{ whenever }\omega\sim_t\omega'\}\) exactly under within-class connectivity.

notation.meaning: coordinate vector associated with scenario omega
identity matrix on one decision copy

review_flags: matrix formulation is standard but supplied locators do not directly support the exact kernel characterization

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The matrix representation and connectivity characterization are mathematically plausible and appropriately classified, but no source supports the exact Kronecker-row and kernel equivalence claim.

children.title: Nonanticipativity Graph Encodings
children.top_down_role: Graph-based organization of shared-history equivalence.

knowledge_statements.title: Nonanticipativity Graph Encodings
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Graph representation of pairwise equalities among scenario decision copies.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: At stage \(t\), form an undirected graph \(G_t=(\Omega_S,E_t)\) whose edges join only scenarios satisfying \(\omega\sim_t\omega'\). Associate the equality \(x_t^{\omega}=x_t^{\omega'}\) with every edge \(\{\omega,\omega'\}\in E_t\). The graph encodes all stage-\(t\) nonanticipativity constraints exactly if and only if the subgraph induced by each equivalence class of \(\sim_t\) is connected; equality then propagates along paths within that class.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Scenarios are vertices and equality constraints are edges; one connected subgraph per shared-history class enforces all required equalities.
assumptions_latex: \(\Omega_S\) is finite.
Edges connect only scenarios in the same stage-t history class.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(G_t[C]\text{ connected for every equivalence class }C\Longleftrightarrow x_t^{\omega}=x_t^{\omega'}\text{ for all }\omega,\omega'\in C.\)

notation.meaning: subgraph induced by history class C

review_flags: graph encoding requires a directly supporting source locator

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The graph representation fits the leaf, but the necessary-and-sufficient induced-connectivity characterization has no cited source.

children.title: Encoding Equivalence
children.top_down_role: Correspondence between algebraic constraints plus graph connectivity.

knowledge_statements.title: Encoding Equivalence
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Equivalence of node variables, coupled scenario copies, matrices, and equality graphs.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Fix a finite scenario tree and a stage \(t\). Suppose its stage-\(t\) nodes coincide with the equivalence classes of observable scenario histories. Then the following feasible policy sets coincide: scenario-expanded node-indexed decisions; path-indexed copies constant on every history class; the kernel of a nonanticipativity matrix whose selected equality rows connect every history class; and graph-encoded copies whose induced graph on every history class is connected. A node value is copied to every scenario passing through that node, and the inverse correspondence assigns to each node the common value of its scenario copies.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Node variables, history-coupled scenario copies, connected difference-matrix constraints, and connected equality graphs represent the same stagewise nonanticipative policies.
assumptions_latex: The scenario tree and scenario set are finite.
Stage-\(t\) nodes coincide with equivalence classes of observable histories.
Matrix rows and graph edges encode the same selected pairwise equalities.
The selected equality graph is connected within every history class.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\mathcal X_t^{\mathrm{node}}=\mathcal X_t^{\mathrm{path}}=\ker A_t=\mathcal X_t^{\mathrm{graph}}.\)

notation.meaning: scenario-expanded policies induced by node variables
path copies constant on history classes

review_flags: four-way encoding equivalence requires a directly supporting source

children.title: Redundancy Structure
children.top_down_role: Duplicated coupling information within nonanticipativity encodings.

knowledge_statements.title: Redundancy Structure
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Rank and redundancy of pairwise nonanticipativity equalities within history classes.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let a stage-\(t\) history class \(C\) contain \(m\) scenarios, each with a decision in \(\mathbb R^d\). All \(\binom{m}{2}\) pairwise equalities have rank \((m-1)d\). Hence any spanning tree on \(C\) supplies \((m-1)d\) independent scalar constraints and has the same feasible set as the complete equality graph. Every additional within-class edge creates a linearly dependent cycle constraint and is redundant for feasibility, although it may affect numerical behavior.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Within a class of m scenarios, a spanning tree gives all necessary equalities; remaining pairwise constraints are linearly redundant.
assumptions_latex: Each scenario copy lies in \(\mathbb R^d\).
Equalities are homogeneous componentwise differences.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\operatorname{rank}(A_C)=(m-1)d\), and any connected edge set on \(C\) defines the same equality subspace.

notation.meaning: number of scenarios in the class

review_flags: exact rank and cycle-redundancy claim requires a direct source

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The property kind fits, and the rank and spanning-tree statements are standard finite-dimensional linear algebra, but the exact rank and cycle-redundancy claims lack a direct source.

children.title: Dependence-State Interface
children.top_down_role: Dependence regimes governing compact representation and recursion.

children.title: Stagewise-Independent Uncertainty
children.top_down_role: Stage-separated conditional structure.

knowledge_statements.title: Stagewise-Independent Uncertainty
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Finite-horizon exogenous uncertainty with independent innovations across stages.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: An uncertainty process \((W_t)_{t=1}^T\) is stagewise independent when the random elements \(W_1,\ldots,W_T\) are mutually independent. Equivalently, for every stage \(t\) and measurable set \(B\), \(\mathbb P(W_{t+1}\in B\mid\sigma(W_1,\ldots,W_t))=\mathbb P(W_{t+1}\in B)\) almost surely. Thus the conditional distribution of the next exogenous observation is independent of the realized observation history; this condition does not by itself make decisions or endogenous states independent across stages.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Stagewise independence means each new exogenous observation has its unconditional distribution even after conditioning on all earlier observations.
assumptions_latex: \(W_t\) is a random element of a standard Borel space for each \(t\).
The process is exogenous to the decisions.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\mathcal L(W_{t+1}\mid W_{1:t})=\mathcal L(W_{t+1})\text{ almost surely for every }t<T.\)

children.title: Markovian Uncertainty
children.top_down_role: Dependence summarized by a current information state.

knowledge_statements.title: Markovian Uncertainty
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Conditional dependence summarized by the current uncertainty state.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \((\Omega,\mathcal F,\mathbb P)\) carry a filtration \((\mathcal F_t)_{t=0}^T\), and let \(S_t:\Omega\to E\) be an \(\mathcal F_t\)-measurable uncertainty-state process on a standard Borel space \(E\). The process is Markovian with respect to this filtration when, for every \(t<T\), there is a transition kernel \(K_t\) on \(E\) such that \(\mathbb P(S_{t+1}\in B\mid\mathcal F_t)=K_t(S_t,B)\) almost surely for every measurable set \(B\subseteq E\). Thus the current state summarizes the observed history relevant to the next-state law.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: An uncertainty-state process is Markovian when its current state determines the conditional distribution of the next state given all currently available information.
assumptions_latex: \((\Omega,\mathcal F,\mathbb P)\) is a probability space with filtration \((\mathcal F_t)_{t=0}^T\).
\(E\) is a standard Borel state space.
Each \(S_t:\Omega\to E\) is \(\mathcal F_t\)-measurable.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\mathcal L(S_{t+1}\mid\mathcal F_t)=K_t(S_t,\cdot)\text{ almost surely for every }t<T.\)

source_refs.locator: 2.5.2 The Markovian structure of a Discrete-Event process p. 121

children.title: History-Dependent Uncertainty
children.top_down_role: Dependence requiring extended histories or states.

knowledge_statements.title: History-Dependent Uncertainty
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Failure of a proposed current state to summarize the uncertainty history.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(H_t=(W_1,\ldots,W_t)\) be the observed uncertainty history, let \(S_t=\phi_t(H_t)\) be a proposed state summary, and let \(Q_t(H_t,\cdot)\) be a regular conditional law of \(W_{t+1}\) given \(H_t\). The uncertainty is history-dependent relative to \(S_t\) when there is no transition kernel \(K_t\) satisfying \(Q_t(H_t,\cdot)=K_t(S_t,\cdot)\) almost surely. In that case, the proposed state does not retain all history relevant to the next-observation law, so additional history must be retained or the state must be augmented.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Uncertainty is history-dependent relative to a proposed state when no transition kernel based only on that state reproduces the conditional next-observation law almost surely.
assumptions_latex: The histories \(H_t\), states \(S_t\), and observations \(W_{t+1}\) take values in standard Borel spaces.
\(S_t=\phi_t(H_t)\) is the proposed information state.
\(Q_t(H_t,\cdot)\) is a regular conditional law of \(W_{t+1}\) given \(H_t\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\nexists K_t\text{ such that }Q_t(H_t,\cdot)=K_t(S_t,\cdot)\text{ almost surely}.\)

notation.meaning: observed uncertainty history through stage t
regular conditional next-observation law given the history
hypothetical transition kernel depending only on the proposed state

children.title: Decision-Dependent Uncertainty
children.top_down_role: Future distributions affected by earlier decisions.

knowledge_statements.title: Decision-Dependent Uncertainty
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Controlled transition-kernel formulation of endogenous future uncertainty.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let stages be indexed by \(t=0,\ldots,T-1\), let \(H_t\) be the observable history, and let \(x_t\in X_t(H_t)\) be the current decision. Uncertainty is decision-dependent if its conditional law admits a kernel \(Q_{t+1}\) satisfying \[\mathbb P(\xi_{t+1}\in B\mid H_t,x_t)=Q_{t+1}(B\mid H_t,x_t)\] for every measurable set \(B\), and there exist an admissible history \(h\), decisions \(x,x'\in X_t(h)\), and a measurable \(B\) such that \(Q_{t+1}(B\mid h,x)\ne Q_{t+1}(B\mid h,x')\). Thus an earlier decision changes at least one future conditional distribution.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Uncertainty is decision-dependent when two admissible decisions at the same observed history induce different conditional laws for a future random quantity.
assumptions_latex: \(Q_{t+1}(\cdot\mid h,x)\) is a probability kernel on the next-stage uncertainty space.
Decisions are selected nonanticipatively from \(X_t(H_t)\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\exists h,x,x',B:\ Q_{t+1}(B\mid h,x)\ne Q_{t+1}(B\mid h,x')\).
