children.title: State Sufficiency Regimes
children.top_down_role: Dependence structures admitting compact state representations.

knowledge_statements.title: State Sufficiency Regimes
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Finite-horizon controlled Markov sufficiency for feasibility, costs, and future uncertainty.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Consider a finite-horizon problem with stages \(t=0,\ldots,T\), observable histories \(H_t\), additive one-stage costs \(c_t\), and terminal cost \(g\). Measurable statistics \(S_t=\sigma_t(H_t)\) form a sufficient-state regime if, for every \(t<T\), histories \(h,h'\) with \(\sigma_t(h)=\sigma_t(h')=s\) satisfy \[X_t(h)=X_t(h')=:X_t(s),\qquad c_t(h,x)=c_t(h',x)=:c_t(s,x)\] for every \(x\in X_t(s)\), and \[\mathbb P(S_{t+1}\in B\mid H_t=h,x)=\mathbb P(S_{t+1}\in B\mid H_t=h',x)=Q_{t+1}(B\mid s,x)\] for every measurable set \(B\). At the terminal stage, histories with the same state must also satisfy \(g(h)=g(h')=:g_T(s)\). Under these conditions, the finite-horizon continuation problem depends on the observed history only through the current state.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A finite-horizon state regime is sufficient when histories with the same state have identical feasible actions, one-stage costs, controlled next-state laws, and terminal costs; the continuation problem then depends only on that state.
assumptions_latex: \(H_t\) contains all information observable when the stage-\(t\) decision is selected.
\(S_t=\sigma_t(H_t)\) is measurable for every \(t=0,\ldots,T\).
The objective is the expected sum of the stated one-stage costs and terminal cost.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\text{The continuation problem conditional on }H_t\text{ depends on }H_t\text{ only through }S_t.\)

notation.meaning: terminal cost expressed as a function of the terminal state

children.title: State Augmentation Boundaries
children.top_down_role: Cases requiring additional history summaries for valid recursion.

knowledge_statements.title: State Augmentation Boundaries
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Boundary between recursively Markovizable histories and irreducible full-history dependence.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: A history-dependent model admits recursive state augmentation when there are measurable spaces \(\mathcal S_t\), maps \(S_0=\sigma_0(H_0)\), and updates \[S_{t+1}=F_t(S_t,x_t,\xi_{t+1})\] such that \(S_t\) satisfies the state-sufficiency conditions for feasibility, cost, and transition law. The augmentation boundary is crossed for a prescribed state class \(\mathfrak S\) if no \(S_t\in\mathfrak S\) and measurable update \(F_t\) satisfy those conditions. Beyond that boundary, restricting policies to feedback on states in \(\mathfrak S\) can discard decision-relevant history.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Recursive augmentation succeeds only if an allowed state can be updated from the previous state, action, and observation while retaining all decision-relevant history.
assumptions_latex: \(\mathfrak S\) specifies the permitted state spaces or finite-dimensional state representations.
All observations used by \(F_t\) are available before the next decision.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: If no sufficient recursive \(S_t\in\mathfrak S\) exists, policies restricted to \(S_t\) need not represent every admissible history policy.

children.title: Dependence-to-State Interfaces
children.top_down_role: Links from uncertainty dependence to recursive state design.

knowledge_statements.title: Dependence-to-State Interfaces
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Factorization converting history dependence into a controlled state transition.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: A dependence-to-state interface consists of measurable maps \(S_t=\sigma_t(H_t)\), an innovation \(W_{t+1}\), and an update \(F_t\) such that \[S_{t+1}=F_t(S_t,x_t,W_{t+1}),\qquad \mathcal L(W_{t+1}\mid H_t,x_t)=R_{t+1}(\cdot\mid S_t,x_t).\] Consequently, for each measurable \(B\), the induced controlled state kernel is \[Q_{t+1}(B\mid s,x)=\int \mathbf 1_B(F_t(s,x,w))\,R_{t+1}(dw\mid s,x).\] The interface is exact when feasibility, one-stage cost, and every continuation-relevant conditional law also factor through \((S_t,x_t)\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The interface represents history-dependent evolution through a state, controlled innovation law, and recursive update, and is exact when all decision-relevant quantities factor likewise.
assumptions_latex: \(S_t\), \(W_{t+1}\), and \(F_t\) are measurable.
The innovation kernel \(R_{t+1}\) is defined for every feasible state-action pair.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The history-indexed dynamics induce the controlled Markov kernel \(Q_{t+1}(\cdot\mid S_t,x_t)\).

children.title: Multistage Policy Representations
children.top_down_role: Exact and restricted representations of adaptive decisions.

children.title: Full-History Policies
children.top_down_role: Policies retaining complete observable histories.

knowledge_statements.title: Full-History Policies
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Deterministic nonanticipative policies on complete observable histories.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For stages \(t=0,\ldots,T\), let \(H_t\) denote the complete information observed before choosing \(x_t\), and let \(X_t(h_t)\) be the feasible action set at history \(h_t\). A deterministic full-history policy is a sequence \(\pi=(\pi_0,\ldots,\pi_T)\) of measurable maps satisfying \[\pi_t:\mathcal H_t\to\mathcal X_t,\qquad \pi_t(h_t)\in X_t(h_t)\quad\text{for every }h_t\in\mathcal H_t.\] The implemented decision is \(x_t=\pi_t(H_t)\); hence it may depend on every observed component of the past but not on future observations.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A full-history policy maps the entire information available at each stage to a feasible action and cannot depend on future observations.
assumptions_latex: Each history space \(\mathcal H_t\) and action space \(\mathcal X_t\) is measurable.
\(X_t(h_t)\) is the feasible-action correspondence.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(x_t=\pi_t(H_t)\in X_t(H_t)\) is nonanticipative at every stage.

notation.meaning: complete observable history at stage t

children.title: State-Feedback Policies
children.top_down_role: Policies indexed by sufficient states.

knowledge_statements.title: State-Feedback Policies
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Policies measurable with respect to a sufficient state.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(S_t=\sigma_t(H_t)\) be a sufficient state and let \(X_t(s)\) be its feasible action set. A deterministic state-feedback policy is a sequence \(\mu=(\mu_0,\ldots,\mu_T)\) of measurable maps satisfying \[\mu_t:\mathcal S_t\to\mathcal X_t,\qquad \mu_t(s)\in X_t(s).\] It implements \(x_t=\mu_t(S_t)\). Equivalently, its induced full-history rule is \(\pi_t=\mu_t\circ\sigma_t\), so any two histories with the same sufficient state receive the same action.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A state-feedback policy chooses a feasible action from the current sufficient state, treating histories mapped to the same state identically.
assumptions_latex: \(S_t\) is sufficient for feasibility, costs, and controlled future evolution.
The state and action spaces are measurable.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\sigma_t(h)=\sigma_t(h')\Rightarrow \pi_t(h)=\pi_t(h')\).

children.title: Linear Decision-Rule Family
children.top_down_role: Linear restrictions on adaptive policies.

children.title: Affine Decision Rules
children.top_down_role: Adaptive policies with intercept terms plus linear signal dependence.

knowledge_statements.title: Affine Decision Rules
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Finite-dimensional affine policies in observable-history features.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Fix a measurable feature map \(\phi_t:\mathcal H_t\to\mathbb R^{k_t}\) constructed only from information observed by stage \(t\). An affine decision rule has the form \[x_t(h_t)=b_t+K_t\phi_t(h_t),\] where \(b_t\in\mathbb R^{m_t}\) and \(K_t\in\mathbb R^{m_t\times k_t}\) are parameters chosen before implementation. The rule is admissible for a history set \(\mathcal H_t^{\mathrm{adm}}\) only if \(b_t+K_t\phi_t(h_t)\in X_t(h_t)\) for every \(h_t\in\mathcal H_t^{\mathrm{adm}}\), or almost surely under the specified uncertainty law.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: An affine decision rule is an intercept plus a linear transformation of features observable at the decision stage, subject to feasibility on relevant histories.
assumptions_latex: \(x_t\in\mathbb R^{m_t}\) and \(\phi_t(h_t)\in\mathbb R^{k_t}\).
Features use no information unavailable at stage \(t\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(x_t=b_t+K_t\phi_t(H_t)\) is nonanticipative, and admissibility additionally requires \(x_t\in X_t(H_t)\).

children.title: Homogeneous Linear Decision Rules
children.top_down_role: Adaptive policies restricted to linear signal dependence without intercepts.

knowledge_statements.title: Homogeneous Linear Decision Rules
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Intercept-free linear policies in observable features.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Fix a measurable, nonanticipative feature map \(\phi_t:\mathcal H_t\to\mathbb R^{k_t}\). A homogeneous linear decision rule is a policy of the form \[x_t(h_t)=K_t\phi_t(h_t),\] with coefficient matrix \(K_t\in\mathbb R^{m_t\times k_t}\) selected before the uncertainty is observed. It is homogeneous because \(x_t=0\) whenever \(\phi_t(h_t)=0\), and \(K_t(\alpha z)=\alpha K_tz\) for every scalar \(\alpha\). Admissibility requires \(K_t\phi_t(h_t)\in X_t(h_t)\) on every required history, or almost surely when feasibility is probabilistic.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A homogeneous linear rule applies a fixed matrix to observable features without an intercept and must satisfy the model's chosen feasibility convention.
assumptions_latex: \(x_t\in\mathbb R^{m_t}\) and \(\phi_t(h_t)\in\mathbb R^{k_t}\).
The feature map contains only stage-t observable information.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(x_t=K_t\phi_t(H_t)\) is nonanticipative and satisfies \(x_t(0)=0\) in feature coordinates.

children.title: Feature-Space Selection
children.top_down_role: Choice of observed quantities entering finite-dimensional decision rules.

knowledge_statements.title: Feature-Space Selection
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Information-compatible feature design for finite-dimensional decision rules.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \((\Omega,\mathcal F,\mathbb P)\) be the underlying probability space, let \(\mathcal F_t\subseteq\mathcal F\) be the information available before choosing \(x_t\), and consider a rule \(x_t=b_t+K_t\phi_t(H_t)\). Nonanticipativity requires \[\phi_t(H_t)\in L^0(\Omega,\mathcal F_t;\mathbb R^{k_t}).\] Call the feature map lossless for optimal stage-\(t\) action selection if an optimal action can be selected as a function of \(\phi_t(h)\) at every relevant history \(h\). A necessary condition for losslessness is \[X_t^\star(h)\cap X_t^\star(h')=\varnothing\ \Longrightarrow\ \phi_t(h)\ne\phi_t(h'),\] where \(X_t^\star(h)\) is the set of optimal stage-\(t\) actions at history \(h\). Thus feature selection trades parameter dimension against the history distinctions expressible by the policy class.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Features must be observable when the action is chosen. If two histories admit no common optimal action, a feature map that is lossless for optimal action selection must distinguish those histories.
assumptions_latex: \((\Omega,\mathcal F,\mathbb P)\) is the underlying probability space.
\(\mathcal F_t\) is the information available immediately before choosing \(x_t\).
\(X_t^\star(h)\) denotes the set of optimal stage-\(t\) actions at history \(h\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(X_t^\star(h)\cap X_t^\star(h')=\varnothing\Rightarrow\phi_t(h)\ne\phi_t(h')\) is necessary for losslessness.

children.title: Linear-Rule Expressiveness Boundaries
children.top_down_role: Adaptive behavior not representable within linear policy restrictions.

knowledge_statements.title: Linear-Rule Expressiveness Boundaries
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Concrete nonrepresentability boundary for finite affine feature rules.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let the observable scalar history feature range over an interval \(I\subset\mathbb R\) containing at least three distinct points, and suppose the required policy is \(x^star(z)=z^2\). No affine rule \(x(z)=b+kz\) agrees with \(x^star\) on all of \(I\): otherwise the polynomial \(z^2-kz-b\) would vanish at every point of \(I\), although a nonzero quadratic has at most two roots. Hence affine rules in the raw feature \(z\) cannot represent this policy exactly; adding the feature \(z^2\) or using a richer rule family removes this particular boundary.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A quadratic policy on an interval cannot be represented exactly by an affine rule using only the raw scalar observation, demonstrating a basic expressiveness boundary.
assumptions_latex: \(I\) contains at least three distinct real numbers.
The affine rule uses only the feature \(z\), without nonlinear transformations.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\nexists(b,k)\in\mathbb R^2\) such that \(b+kz=z^2\) for every \(z\in I\).

notation.meaning: range of the observed scalar feature

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The elementary nonrepresentability example fits a failure-boundary leaf, but the record has no source, includes proof text, and writes x^star instead of the declared x^\star notation. A sourced, proof-free corrected record is required.

children.title: Finite-Basis Decision-Rule Family
children.top_down_role: Richer finite-dimensional policy restrictions.

children.title: Piecewise Decision Rules
children.top_down_role: Policies using distinct local responses across information regions.

knowledge_statements.title: Piecewise Decision Rules
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Region-indexed policy rules over a measurable history-feature partition.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(\phi_t:\mathcal H_t\to Z_t\) be observable at stage \(t\), and let \(\{R_{tj}\}_{j=1}^{J_t}\) be a measurable partition of \(Z_t\). A piecewise decision rule is \[x_t(h_t)=f_{tj}(\phi_t(h_t))\quad\text{when }\phi_t(h_t)\in R_{tj},\] where each \(f_{tj}:R_{tj}\to\mathbb R^{m_t}\) is measurable. With affine pieces, \(f_{tj}(z)=b_{tj}+K_{tj}z\). Boundary assignments must make the regions disjoint, and admissibility requires \(f_{tj}(\phi_t(h_t))\in X_t(h_t)\) for every relevant history in region \(R_{tj}\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A piecewise decision rule partitions observable feature space and applies a specified measurable, often affine, action rule within each region.
assumptions_latex: The regions \(R_{tj}\) form a measurable disjoint partition of \(Z_t\).
The feature map is measurable with respect to stage-t information.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The region assignment and local maps define a single-valued nonanticipative policy.

knowledge_statements.title: Basis-Expansion Decision Rules

The expansion is admissible only when the resulting action belongs to \(X_t(h_t)\) for all required histories, or almost surely under the declared feasibility convention.

children.title: Region-Partition Design

knowledge_statements.title: Region-Partition Design
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Measurable finite partitions supporting piecewise finite-basis, nonanticipative policies.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Let \(H_t\) be the measurable space of information histories available at stage \(t\). A region-partition design is a finite family \(\mathcal P_t=\{R_{t1},\ldots,R_{tK}\}\) of measurable, pairwise-disjoint sets satisfying \(H_t=\bigcup_{k=1}^K R_{tk}\), together with a fixed convention assigning boundary histories to exactly one region. Given measurable basis functions \(\phi_{kj}:H_t\to\mathbb R\), the associated piecewise decision rule is
\[x_t(h)=\sum_{k=1}^K\mathbf 1_{R_{tk}}(h)\sum_{j=1}^{m_k}\theta_{kj}\phi_{kj}(h),\qquad h\in H_t.\]
Feasibility requires \(x_t(h)\in X_t(h)\) for every modeled history \(h\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A region design measurably partitions available histories and assigns each region a finite-basis decision rule, with unambiguous boundary assignment and historywise feasibility.
assumptions_latex: \(H_t\) is equipped with the information sigma-field available before the stage-\(t\) decision.
Each \(R_{tk}\) and \(\phi_{kj}\) is measurable.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(x_t\) is a measurable, nonanticipative piecewise finite-basis policy whenever its displayed values satisfy \(x_t(h)\in X_t(h)\).

notation.meaning: Feasible action set at history h

children.title: Policy Approximation Boundaries
children.top_down_role: Adaptive responses outside the selected regions or basis span.

knowledge_statements.title: Policy Approximation Boundaries
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Expressiveness boundary for policies determined by finitely many prescribed features.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Fix a feature map \(\Phi_t:H_t\to\mathbb R^m\) and restrict decisions to \(x_t(h)=g(\Phi_t(h))\), including linear finite-basis rules as a special case. If two histories \(h,h'\in H_t\) satisfy \(\Phi_t(h)=\Phi_t(h')\), every policy in this family assigns them the same action. Consequently, if \(X_t(h)=\{a\}\) and \(X_t(h')=\{b\}\) with \(a\ne b\), no policy in the family is feasible at both histories. More generally, if an optimal policy \(x_t^*\) has \(x_t^*(h)\ne x_t^*(h')\), exact representation is impossible; uniform approximation error is at least \(\tfrac12\lVert x_t^*(h)-x_t^*(h')\rVert\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Histories collapsed by the chosen features must receive one action; differing required or optimal actions therefore cause infeasibility or a positive approximation-error floor.
assumptions_latex: The action space is normed for the approximation bound.
Policies factor through the fixed feature map \(\Phi_t\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\Phi_t(h)=\Phi_t(h')\) prevents the policy family from distinguishing \(h\) and \(h'\), producing the stated feasibility or approximation boundary.

notation.meaning: Feasible action set at history h

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Block-separable recourse
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Structural definition for a multistage stochastic linear program.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: A multistage stochastic linear program has block-separable recourse if, for every \(t=1,\ldots,H\) and every \(\omega\), \(x^t(\omega)=(w^t(\omega),y^t(\omega))\), where \(w^t\) and \(y^t\) are aggregate- and detailed-level decisions, respectively; \(c^t x^t(\omega)=r^t w^t(\omega)+q^t y^t(\omega)\); \(W^t=\begin{pmatrix}W^t&0\\0&T^t\end{pmatrix}\); and the random constraint components satisfy \(T^t(\omega)=\begin{pmatrix}R^t(\omega)&0\\S^t(\omega)&0\end{pmatrix}\) and \(h^t(\omega)=\begin{pmatrix}b^t(\omega)\\d^t(\omega)\end{pmatrix}\), with the zero columns corresponding to the detailed-level variables.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Recourse is block separable when, at every stage and realization, decisions split into aggregate and detailed components, the objective separates across that split, the recourse matrix is block diagonal, and the random linking components have the stated block form with zero columns for detailed variables.
assumptions_latex: t\in\{1,\ldots,H\}
\omega\text{ ranges over all realizations}
x^t(\omega)=(w^t(\omega),y^t(\omega))
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: c^t x^t=r^t w^t+q^t y^t,\quad W^t=\begin{pmatrix}W^t&0\\0&T^t\end{pmatrix},\quad T^t(\omega)=\begin{pmatrix}R^t(\omega)&0\\S^t(\omega)&0\end{pmatrix},\quad h^t(\omega)=\begin{pmatrix}b^t(\omega)\\d^t(\omega)\end{pmatrix}.

children.title: Sufficient State Representations
children.top_down_role: State summaries retaining information needed for recursive recourse.

knowledge_statements.title: Sufficient State Representations
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Controlled-Markov sufficiency relative to the observed history.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For a finite-horizon stochastic control model, let \(H_t\) be the observed history before decision \(A_t\). A measurable statistic \(S_t=\sigma_t(H_t)\) is a sufficient state representation if, whenever \(\sigma_t(h)=\sigma_t(h')\), the admissible-action sets coincide and, for every common action \(a\), both the conditional expected stage cost and the conditional law of \(S_{t+1}\) are identical under \(h\) and \(h'\). Equivalently, there exist \(\mathcal A_t\), \(c_t\), and a controlled kernel \(P_t\) such that admissibility, expected current cost, and next-state distribution depend on history only through \((S_t,A_t)\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A state is sufficient when it determines feasible actions, expected current cost, and the controlled distribution of the next state, without additional history.
assumptions_latex: State and action spaces are measurable spaces admitting the stated conditional kernels.
The horizon is finite and relevant costs are integrable.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: Optimization over history-dependent policies can be represented recursively using \(S_t\) and Markov decision rules \(A_t=\pi_t(S_t)\).

children.title: State Augmentation
children.top_down_role: Expansion of state descriptions to recover recursive validity.

knowledge_statements.title: State Augmentation
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Restoring controlled-Markov sufficiency by adjoining retained information.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Let \(Z_t=z_t(H_t)\) be a possibly insufficient state statistic and let \(U_t=u_t(H_t)\) retain additional history information. The augmented state is \(S_t=(Z_t,U_t)\). It is a sufficient augmentation if there are measurable functions or kernels for which the admissible-action set, conditional expected stage cost, and conditional law of \(S_{t+1}\), given \((H_t,A_t)\), depend only on \((S_t,A_t)\). Thus, for every measurable set \(B\),
\[\mathbb P(S_{t+1}\in B\mid H_t,A_t)=P_t(B\mid S_t,A_t)\quad\text{a.s.}\]
Augmentation is valid only when \(U_t\) is available before \(A_t\) is selected.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: State augmentation appends available history information to a deficient statistic until feasibility, current cost, and next-state dynamics depend only on the augmented state and action.
assumptions_latex: \(Z_t\) and \(U_t\) are measurable with respect to the pre-decision information.
Regular conditional distributions exist on the chosen state spaces.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: When the displayed factorization and analogous cost and feasibility factorizations hold, \(S_t=(Z_t,U_t)\) is sufficient for recursive optimization.

children.title: Minimal State Structure
children.top_down_role: Compact state descriptions preserving relevant dependence.

knowledge_statements.title: Minimal State Structure
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Coarsest sufficient statistic, up to measurable recoding.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: A sufficient state statistic \(S_t^*=\sigma_t^*(H_t)\) is minimal if, for every other sufficient statistic \(S_t=\sigma_t(H_t)\), there exists a measurable map \(f_t\) such that \(S_t^*=f_t(S_t)\) almost surely. Hence every sufficient representation distinguishes at least the history classes distinguished by \(S_t^*\). If two minimal sufficient states \(S_t^*\) and \(\widetilde S_t^*\) take values in standard Borel spaces and their factor maps can be restricted to their essential ranges, each is a measurable function of the other; they are therefore equivalent up to an almost-sure measurable one-to-one recoding on those ranges.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A minimal state is the coarsest sufficient statistic: it can be recovered measurably from every other sufficient state and is unique up to measurable recoding.
assumptions_latex: All compared statistics are sufficient for the same feasibility, cost, and transition model.
State spaces are standard Borel for the stated equivalence conclusion.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(S_t^*\) contains no distinction that can be removed while remaining sufficient, modulo null sets and measurable recoding.

children.title: Insufficient-State Boundaries
children.top_down_role: Failures caused by omitting decision-relevant history.

knowledge_statements.title: Insufficient-State Boundaries
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Observable-history distinctions whose removal destroys recursive validity.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Let \(Z_t=z_t(H_t)\) be a proposed state. It is insufficient if there exist histories \(h,h'\) with \(z_t(h)=z_t(h')\) for which at least one controlled-Markov datum differs: the feasible-action sets are unequal, the conditional expected stage costs differ for a common action, or the conditional laws of \(Z_{t+1}\) differ for a common action. In particular, if some common action \(a\) and measurable set \(B\) satisfy
\[\mathbb P(Z_{t+1}\in B\mid H_t=h,A_t=a)\ne\mathbb P(Z_{t+1}\in B\mid H_t=h',A_t=a),\]
then no transition kernel depending only on \((Z_t,A_t)\) represents both histories.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A proposed state fails when histories it merges have different feasible actions, expected costs, or controlled next-state laws; then a state-only Bellman recursion is invalid.
assumptions_latex: The compared histories have positive-probability or otherwise model-relevant conditional laws.
Conditional costs and transition probabilities are well-defined.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: Any such pair \((h,h')\) certifies that \(Z_t\) is not a sufficient state representation.

children.title: Decision-Relative State Representation Pair

children.title: Pre-Decision States
children.top_down_role: State descriptions available immediately before a decision.

knowledge_statements.title: Pre-Decision States
knowledge_statements.scope_note: State measured immediately before the stage decision.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Let \(\mathcal F_t\) denote the information available immediately before the stage-\(t\) action. A pre-decision state \(S_t\) is an \(\mathcal F_t\)-measurable sufficient statistic such that the admissible action set is \(\mathcal A_t(S_t)\), the selected action \(A_t\) is \(\mathcal F_t\)-measurable, and the conditional stage cost and future evolution depend on the past only through \((S_t,A_t)\). Its timing is
\[\mathcal F_t\longrightarrow S_t\longrightarrow A_t\longrightarrow W_{t+1},\]
where \(W_{t+1}\) denotes information revealed only after the action. Thus \(S_t\) may contain all information known at decision time but cannot contain unrevealed \(W_{t+1}\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A pre-decision state summarizes all relevant information available immediately before choosing the current action, excluding information revealed afterward.
assumptions_latex: \((\mathcal F_t)\) is the model's information filtration.
\(S_t\) satisfies the controlled-Markov sufficiency conditions.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: An admissible Markov decision has the form \(A_t=\pi_t(S_t)\) and cannot depend on \(W_{t+1}\) before its revelation.

children.title: Post-Decision States
children.top_down_role: State descriptions after a decision but before subsequent uncertainty.

knowledge_statements.title: Post-Decision States
knowledge_statements.scope_note: State after the action but before the next exogenous information.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Given a pre-decision state \(S_t\) and admissible action \(A_t\), a post-decision state is a sufficient statistic \(S_t^x=M_t(S_t,A_t)\) describing the system immediately after implementing \(A_t\) and before observing the next exogenous information \(W_{t+1}\). The next pre-decision state is generated by
\[S_{t+1}=G_{t+1}(S_t^x,W_{t+1}).\]
Conditional on \(S_t^x\), downstream uncertainty and continuation cost must be independent of earlier history. When the action transition \(M_t\) is deterministic, moving from \(S_t\) to \(S_t^x\) introduces no new exogenous randomness.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A post-decision state records the system after the action and before new information, separating the controlled transition from the subsequent random transition.
assumptions_latex: \(A_t\) is admissible and chosen using pre-decision information.
\(W_{t+1}\) is revealed after \(S_t^x\) is formed.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(S_t^x\) supports a continuation value evaluated before integrating over \(W_{t+1}\), with \(S_{t+1}=G_{t+1}(S_t^x,W_{t+1})\).

children.title: State-Placement Crosswalks
children.top_down_role: Correspondence between state descriptions placed around a decision.

knowledge_statements.title: State-Placement Crosswalks
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Equivalent Bellman placement before and after the controlled transition.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Suppose \(S_t^x=M_t(S_t,A_t)\), \(S_{t+1}=G_{t+1}(S_t^x,W_{t+1})\), and the stage cost is \(c_t(S_t,A_t)\). Define the post-decision continuation value by
\[V_t^x(s^x)=\mathbb E\!\left[V_{t+1}(G_{t+1}(s^x,W_{t+1}))\mid S_t^x=s^x\right].\]
Then the pre-decision Bellman equation is equivalently
\[V_t(s)=\inf_{a\in\mathcal A_t(s)}\left\{c_t(s,a)+V_t^x(M_t(s,a))\right\}.\]
Conversely, substituting the first display into the second recovers the usual expectation-over-next-state recursion. The crosswalk is valid only when both state placements encode the same timing and information filtration.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Pre- and post-decision Bellman forms are equivalent when the controlled transition precedes the random transition and both representations use the same information timing.
assumptions_latex: The displayed conditional expectation exists and costs are integrable.
\(S_t^x\) is sufficient for downstream evolution after the action.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The pre-decision and post-decision value functions represent the same continuation costs through the two displayed equations.

children.title: Information-Revelation Boundaries

knowledge_statements.title: Information-Revelation Boundaries
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Filtration condition separating admissible decisions from future observations.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \((\mathcal F_t)_{t=0}^T\) be the information filtration, and let \(W_{t+1}\) be revealed between the post-decision state at stage \(t\) and the pre-decision state at stage \(t+1\). Admissibility requires \(S_t\) and \(A_t\) to be \(\mathcal F_t\)-measurable. Consequently, if \(S_t^x=M_t(S_t,A_t)\) for a measurable map \(M_t\), then \(S_t^x\) is also \(\mathcal F_t\)-measurable. The update \(S_{t+1}=G_{t+1}(S_t^x,W_{t+1})\) may use \(W_{t+1}\). If \(A_t\) depends on a component of \(W_{t+1}\) that is not \(\mathcal F_t\)-measurable, the policy is anticipative and is not admissible for the stated information structure.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Current actions may use only currently revealed information; the next observation enters the next state after the action, and using it earlier is anticipative.
assumptions_latex: \((\mathcal F_t)\) represents exactly the observations available before each action.
The revelation time of \(W_{t+1}\) is fixed by the model.
\(M_t\) and \(G_{t+1}\) are measurable maps on their stated domains.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The requirement that \(A_t\) be \(\mathcal F_t\)-measurable, with \(W_{t+1}\) entering only through the subsequent state update, defines the decision-stage information boundary.

children.title: Cost-to-Go Representations
children.top_down_role: Continuation-value organization of downstream recourse.

knowledge_statements.title: Cost-to-Go Representations
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Finite-horizon Bellman representation of downstream recourse value.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
For stages \(t=0,\ldots,T\), let \(S_t\) be a sufficient pre-decision state, \(\mathcal A_t(s)\) its nonempty admissible-action set, \(c_t(s,a)\) the expected stage cost, and \(P_t(\cdot\mid s,a)\) the next-state kernel. With terminal cost \(V_{T+1}(s)=g(s)\), define recursively
\[V_t(s)=\inf_{a\in\mathcal A_t(s)}\left\{c_t(s,a)+\int V_{t+1}(s')P_t(ds'\mid s,a)\right\}.\]
Then \(V_t(s)\) is the infimum expected cost from stage \(t\) through termination, conditional on \(S_t=s\). If each infimum has a measurable selector, choosing such selectors stagewise yields an optimal Markov policy.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The cost-to-go equals current cost plus expected optimal downstream cost, minimized over feasible actions; measurable stagewise minimizers form an optimal Markov policy.
assumptions_latex: The finite-horizon costs are measurable and integrable from every admissible state-action pair.
The state is sufficient and the controlled kernels are well-defined.
Measurable minimizers exist for the policy-attainment conclusion.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The displayed Bellman recursion represents the optimal downstream recourse value \(V_t\), with measurable minimizers attaining an optimal Markov policy when they exist.

children.title: Stagewise Feasibility Duality

knowledge_statements.title: Stagewise Feasibility Duality
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Farkas certificates for linear recourse feasibility at each realized stage state.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
At stage \(t\), fix the realized predecessor state and information, and write the linear recourse constraints as \(W_t x_t=r_t\) with \(x_t\ge0\), where \(r_t=h_t-T_t x_{t-1}\). Exactly one of the following holds: there exists \(x_t\ge0\) satisfying \(W_t x_t=r_t\); or there exists a multiplier \(y_t\) satisfying
\[W_t^{\mathsf T}y_t\ge0,\qquad r_t^{\mathsf T}y_t<0.\]
Equivalently, stagewise recourse is feasible if and only if \(r_t^{\mathsf T}y_t\ge0\) for every \(y_t\) with \(W_t^{\mathsf T}y_t\ge0\). Applying this condition at every reachable stage history characterizes sequential feasibility of the linear recourse system.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Each linear recourse stage is feasible exactly when every Farkas multiplier has nonnegative pairing with its residual; a negative pairing certifies infeasibility.
assumptions_latex: \(W_t\) and \(r_t\) are finite-dimensional real data after the stage history is fixed.
Stage feasibility has equality form \(W_t x_t=r_t\) with \(x_t\ge0\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The multiplier \(y_t\) is a stagewise infeasibility certificate precisely when \(W_t^{\mathsf T}y_t\ge0\) and \(r_t^{\mathsf T}y_t<0\).

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Stagewise multiplier characterization of optimal multistage policies
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Necessary and sufficient optimality conditions for feasible policies in convex multistage recourse.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: In the convex multistage model, suppose either that both (D2) and (D3) hold or that (D1) holds. A feasible policy \(\bar{\mathbf x}_t(\xi_{[t]})\) is optimal if and only if there exist mappings \(\bar{\boldsymbol\pi}_t(\xi_{[t]})\), \(t=1,\ldots,T\), such that, for every \(t\) and almost every \(\xi_{[t]}\), \[0\in\partial f_t(\bar{\mathbf x}_t(\xi_{[t]}),\xi_t)-A_t^\top\bar{\boldsymbol\pi}_t(\xi_{[t]})+\mathbb E[\partial Q_{t+1}(\bar{\mathbf x}_t(\xi_{[t]}),\xi_{[t+1]})\mid\xi_{[t]}].\] Moreover, these multiplier mappings satisfy the stationarity inclusion if and only if, for almost every \(\xi_{[t]}\), \[\bar{\boldsymbol\pi}_t(\xi_{[t]})\in\mathfrak D_t(\bar{\mathbf x}_{t-1}(\xi_{[t-1]}),\xi_{[t]}).\]
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Under either D2 together with D3 or the finite-scenario polyhedral condition D1, a feasible multistage policy is optimal exactly when it admits history-dependent stage multipliers satisfying the conditional subgradient stationarity system. Those multipliers satisfy stationarity exactly when they are stagewise dual optimizers almost surely.
assumptions_latex: \text{The policy belongs to the convex multistage model and is feasible.}
\bigl[(D2)\wedge(D3)\bigr]\ \lor\ (D1).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \bar{\mathbf x}\text{ is optimal}\iff\exists(\bar{\boldsymbol\pi}_t)_{t=1}^T\ \forall t\ \text{a.s.}:\ 0\in\partial f_t(\bar{\mathbf x}_t,\xi_t)-A_t^\top\bar{\boldsymbol\pi}_t+\mathbb E[\partial Q_{t+1}(\bar{\mathbf x}_t,\xi_{[t+1]})\mid\xi_{[t]}],\quad \text{and stationarity}\iff\bar{\boldsymbol\pi}_t\in\mathfrak D_t(\bar{\mathbf x}_{t-1},\xi_{[t]}).

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Stagewise strong duality, optimality, and value-function subgradients
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Duality and sensitivity for one equality-constrained stage of the convex nested multistage recursion.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Fix \((x_{t-1},\xi_{[t]})\) in the convex multistage model. Suppose either that (D1) holds and \(Q_t(x_{t-1},\xi_{[t]})\in\mathbb R\), or that (D2) holds. Then \[Q_t(x_{t-1},\xi_{[t]})=\sup_{\pi_t}\{-\psi_t^*(A_t^\top\pi_t,\xi_{[t]})+\pi_t^\top(b_t-B_tx_{t-1})\}.\] Moreover, \(\bar x_t\) is optimal for the stage problem if and only if there exists \(\bar\pi_t\in\mathfrak D_t(x_{t-1},\xi_{[t]})\) such that \(0\in\partial L_t(\bar x_t,\bar\pi_t)\). Finally, \(Q_t(\cdot,\xi_{[t]})\) is subdifferentiable at \(x_{t-1}\), with \[\partial Q_t(x_{t-1},\xi_{[t]})=-B_t^\top\mathfrak D_t(x_{t-1},\xi_{[t]}).\]
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Under either finite-scenario polyhedrality with a finite stage value or local finiteness under right-hand-side perturbations, the stage problem has no duality gap. Its primal solutions are characterized by dual-optimal multipliers and Lagrangian stationarity, and its value-function subdifferential is obtained from the dual-solution set through the coupling matrix.
assumptions_latex: f_t(\cdot,\xi_t)\text{ and the continuation term define the convex stage problem with affine equality coupling.}
\bigl[(D1)\wedge Q_t(x_{t-1},\xi_{[t]})\in\mathbb R\bigr]\ \lor\ (D2).

children.title: Multistage Nonanticipativity Duality
children.top_down_role: Dual treatment of history-consistency constraints.

knowledge_statements.title: Multistage Nonanticipativity Duality
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Fenchel duality for finite-horizon convex models with nonanticipative policies.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Let \(H\) be the Hilbert space of square-integrable scenario-indexed decisions, let \(N\subseteq H\) be the closed subspace of policies adapted to \((\mathcal F_t)_{t=0}^T\), and let \(F:H\to(-\infty,+\infty]\) be proper, closed, and convex. If \(\operatorname{ri}(\operatorname{dom}F)\cap N\neq\varnothing\), then
\[\inf_{x\in N}F(x)=\sup_{y\in N^\perp}-F^*(y).\]
Thus nonanticipativity may be dualized by multipliers in \(N^\perp\). Componentwise, orthogonality to all \(\mathcal F_t\)-measurable decisions is equivalent to \(\mathbb E[y_t\mid\mathcal F_t]=0\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A convex nonanticipative problem equals a dual maximization over multipliers orthogonal to adapted policies, provided a relative-interior qualification holds.
assumptions_latex: \(H\) is a Hilbert space and \(N\subseteq H\) is a closed linear subspace.
\(F\) is proper, closed, and convex.
\(\operatorname{ri}(\operatorname{dom}F)\cap N\neq\varnothing\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\inf_{x\in N}F(x)=\sup_{y\in N^\perp}-F^*(y)\).

notation.meaning: Convex conjugate of the extended-value objective.

children.title: Martingale Dual Structures
children.top_down_role: Dynamic dual representations tied to information flow.

knowledge_statements.title: Martingale Dual Structures
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Martingale-difference representation of dual variables associated with information flow.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: On a finite filtered probability space, let \(d_t\in L^2(\mathcal F_t)\) satisfy \(\mathbb E[d_t\mid\mathcal F_{t-1}]=0\) for \(t=1,\ldots,T\). Then \(M_0=0\) and \(M_t=\sum_{s=1}^t d_s\) define an \((\mathcal F_t)\)-martingale. Conversely, every square-integrable martingale \((M_t)_{t=0}^T\) has increments \(d_t=M_t-M_{t-1}\) with this conditional-zero-mean property. Consequently, dual penalties invisible to decisions based on past information can be parameterized by martingale differences.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Dual penalties orthogonal to past information are conditional-zero-mean increments, equivalently increments of a square-integrable martingale.
assumptions_latex: \((\mathcal F_t)_{t=0}^T\) is a filtration on a finite probability space.
\(d_t\in L^2(\mathcal F_t)\) for every \(t\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\mathbb E[d_t\mid\mathcal F_{t-1}]=0\) if and only if \(M_t=\sum_{s=1}^t d_s\) is a martingale with \(M_0=0\).

notation.meaning: Stage-t martingale difference or dynamic dual increment.

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The martingale-difference equivalence is standard and the representation kind fits the leaf, but no source is supplied for either the equivalence or its interpretation as a multistage dual structure.

children.title: Expectation-Based Dynamic Consistency
children.top_down_role: Consistency structure of risk-neutral recursive models.

knowledge_statements.title: Expectation-Based Dynamic Consistency
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Risk-neutral consistency induced by conditional expectation and Bellman recursion.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
For integrable terminal cost \(Z\) and filtration \((\mathcal F_t)_{t=0}^T\), define \(V_t(Z)=\mathbb E[Z\mid\mathcal F_t]\). For \(0\leq s\leq t\leq T\), the tower property gives
\[V_s(Z)=\mathbb E[V_t(Z)\mid\mathcal F_s].\]
Hence, in a risk-neutral multistage control problem with an additively separable expected cost and feasible continuations determined only by the current information state, an optimal policy tail selected at time \(s\) remains optimal when its reached time-\(t\) subproblem is re-solved.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Conditional expectation composes through time, so Bellman-optimal risk-neutral policy tails remain optimal after later histories are reached.
assumptions_latex: \(Z\in L^1(\mathcal F_T)\).
The objective is an additive expected cost.
Continuation feasibility is determined by the current information state.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(V_s(Z)=\mathbb E[V_t(Z)\mid\mathcal F_s]\), yielding dynamic consistency of Bellman-optimal policy tails.

notation.meaning: Conditional expected-cost evaluation at time t.

children.title: Risk-Functional Consistency Interface
children.top_down_role: Boundary to recursively composed risk models.

knowledge_statements.title: Risk-Functional Consistency Interface
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Recursive condition connecting conditional risk mappings to dynamic consistency.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Let \(\rho_t:L^p(\mathcal F_{t+1})\to L^p(\mathcal F_t)\) be monotone conditional risk mappings. Define the terminal evaluation by \(R_T(Z)=Z\) and recursively define \(R_t(Z)=\rho_t(R_{t+1}(Z))\). The resulting family is strongly time consistent: for any \(s<t\) and terminal costs \(X,Y\),
\[R_t(X)\leq R_t(Y)\quad\Longrightarrow\quad R_s(X)\leq R_s(Y).\]
Thus recursive composition is the interface through which a one-step risk functional yields history-consistent multistage preferences.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Nested monotone conditional risk mappings preserve later cost rankings at every earlier stage, supplying a dynamically consistent risk evaluation.
assumptions_latex: \(1\leq p\leq\infty\) and \((\mathcal F_t)_{t=0}^T\) is a filtration.
Each \(\rho_t\) maps \(L^p(\mathcal F_{t+1})\) into \(L^p(\mathcal F_t)\) and is monotone.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(R_t(X)\leq R_t(Y)\Rightarrow R_s(X)\leq R_s(Y)\) for every \(s<t\).

notation.meaning: Recursively composed risk evaluation from time t.

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: Recursive monotone conditional mappings do imply the stated ranking consistency, and condition is the appropriate knowledge kind, but the nontrivial conditional-risk result has no cited evidence.

children.title: Time-Inconsistent Formulations
children.top_down_role: Models whose planned and reoptimized policies may differ.

knowledge_statements.title: Time-Inconsistent Formulations
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Mean-variance evaluation as a sharp failure of recursive composition.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
For minimization, fix \(\lambda>0\) and define the conditional mean-variance evaluation
\[R_t(X)=\mathbb E[X\mid\mathcal F_t]+\lambda\operatorname{Var}(X\mid\mathcal F_t).\]
Generally, \(R_0(X)\neq R_0(R_1(X))\): the conditional variance decomposition introduces variability of \(\mathbb E[X\mid\mathcal F_1]\), while composition also evaluates the random conditional-variance term. Therefore a policy minimizing the time-zero mean-variance objective need not minimize the corresponding conditional objective after information is revealed. Equality is recovered only in special cases where the omitted intertemporal variance terms vanish.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Mean-variance objectives generally fail recursive composition, so a policy planned initially can cease to be optimal after information arrives.
assumptions_latex: \(X\in L^2(\mathcal F_T)\).
\(\lambda>0\).
\(\mathcal F_0\subsetneq\mathcal F_1\subseteq\mathcal F_T\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: In general, \(R_0(X)\neq R_0(R_1(X))\), allowing planned and reoptimized policies to differ.

notation.meaning: Conditional mean-variance evaluation at time t.

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The mean-variance failure phenomenon fits this leaf and is generally correct, but no source supports the recursive-composition calculation or the policy-level time-inconsistency conclusion.

knowledge_statements.title: Prior-to-Revelation Commitment
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Timing condition for the stochastic-program benchmark.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(\xi\) be revealed only after a decision is selected. A prior-to-revelation commitment requires the decision rule \(x\) to be measurable with respect to the pre-revelation information \(\mathcal F_0\). If \(\mathcal F_0\) is trivial, admissibility reduces to choosing one deterministic \(x\in X\) for every realization of \(\xi\). The committed stochastic problem therefore minimizes \(\mathbb E[f(x,\xi)]\) over such pre-revelation choices, rather than selecting a separate optimizer after observing \(\xi\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The decision is fixed using only pre-revelation information and cannot be revised after the uncertain outcome becomes known.
assumptions_latex: \(f(x,\xi)\) is measurable and integrable for every admissible \(x\).
The decision precedes observation of \(\xi\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: Admissible decisions satisfy \(x\in L^0(\mathcal F_0;X)\).

notation.meaning: Information available before uncertainty is revealed.

children.title: Nonanticipative Policy Restriction

knowledge_statements.title: Nonanticipative Policy Restriction
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Measurability restriction excluding decisions based on unrevealed uncertainty.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
For a filtration \((\mathcal F_t)_{t=0}^T\), a multistage policy \(x=(x_0,\ldots,x_T)\) is nonanticipative exactly when each \(x_t\) is \(\mathcal F_t\)-measurable. On a finite scenario tree, this is equivalent to
\[x_t(\omega)=x_t(\omega')\]
whenever scenarios \(\omega\) and \(\omega'\) have identical histories through stage \(t\). The restriction prevents the policy from using future observations while allowing decisions to respond to all information already revealed.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: At each stage, decisions may depend on the observed history but must agree across scenarios that remain indistinguishable.
assumptions_latex: \((\mathcal F_t)_{t=0}^T\) represents the information flow.
Each decision \(x_t\) takes values in its stagewise feasible space.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(x_t\in L^0(\mathcal F_t)\) for every \(t\), equivalently scenario-tree decisions agree on common histories.

notation.meaning: Information generated by observations through stage t.

knowledge_statements.title: Stochastic Benchmark Value
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Optimal value of the prior-revelation stochastic model.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Let \(X\) be a nonempty feasible set and suppose \(f(x,\xi)\) is integrable for every \(x\in X\). The stochastic benchmark value for a minimization problem with a decision committed before observing \(\xi\) is
\[z_{\mathrm{SP}}=\inf_{x\in X}\mathbb E[f(x,\xi)].\]
If decisions are multistage, \(X\) is replaced by the set of feasible nonanticipative policies. This value is the reference against which expected-value and perfect-information benchmark models are compared.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The stochastic benchmark is the best expected objective attainable by a feasible decision or policy that respects the information structure.
assumptions_latex: \(X\neq\varnothing\).
\(f(x,\xi)\) is measurable and integrable for every \(x\in X\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(z_{\mathrm{SP}}=\inf_{x\in X}\mathbb E[f(x,\xi)]\).

knowledge_statements.title: Perfect-Information Access
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Information relaxation underlying the wait-and-see benchmark.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(\xi\) denote the complete uncertain outcome and let \(\mathcal F_T=\sigma(\xi)\). Perfect-information access allows the decision to be \(\mathcal F_T\)-measurable before its cost is incurred, even when the original model permits only pre-revelation information. Thus an admissible selector may take the form \(x(\xi)\in X(\xi)\), with no equality requirement between decisions associated with distinct realized scenarios. This enlarges the feasible policy class and produces a lower bound for a minimization problem.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The benchmark lets the decision observe the full outcome before acting, relaxing the original nonanticipativity restriction.
assumptions_latex: \(\mathcal F_T=\sigma(\xi)\) contains the complete scenario information.
A measurable feasible selector \(x(\xi)\in X(\xi)\) exists.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: Perfect-information policies belong to \(L^0(\mathcal F_T)\), and their minimization value cannot exceed the nonanticipative value.

notation.meaning: Feasible set under the realized scenario.

knowledge_statements.title: Scenario-Specific Decisions
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Decision selectors permitted by the perfect-information scenario model.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Given scenario space \(\Omega\), scenario-dependent feasible sets \(X(\omega)\), and full information \(\mathcal F_T\), a scenario-specific decision is an \(\mathcal F_T\)-measurable mapping \(x:\Omega\to\mathbb R^n\) satisfying \(x(\omega)\in X(\omega)\) almost surely. Unlike a nonanticipative pre-revelation decision, it may satisfy \(x(\omega)\neq x(\omega')\) for any distinct scenarios, including scenarios sharing the same earlier history. In a finite scenario model, it is simply one feasible decision vector per scenario.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A scenario-specific decision is a measurable feasible selector that may choose a different action for every fully revealed scenario.
assumptions_latex: \((\Omega,\mathcal F_T,\mathbb P)\) is the terminal scenario space.
The multifunction \(X(\omega)\) admits a measurable selector.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(x\in L^0(\mathcal F_T;\mathbb R^n)\) and \(x(\omega)\in X(\omega)\) almost surely.

knowledge_statements.title: Perfect-Information Benchmark Value
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Wait-and-see value for a minimization stochastic program.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Let \(X(\xi)\) be the feasible set after observing \(\xi\), and assume the scenario optimum is measurable and integrable. The perfect-information, or wait-and-see, benchmark is
\[z_{\mathrm{PI}}=\mathbb E\!\left[\inf_{x\in X(\xi)} f(x,\xi)\right].\]
For the prior-revelation stochastic value \(z_{\mathrm{SP}}=\inf_{x\in X}\mathbb E[f(x,\xi)]\), with every fixed feasible decision also scenario-feasible, \(z_{\mathrm{PI}}\leq z_{\mathrm{SP}}\). The difference \(z_{\mathrm{SP}}-z_{\mathrm{PI}}\) is the expected value of perfect information under minimization.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The perfect-information value averages scenario-wise optimal costs and lower-bounds the committed stochastic value in minimization.
assumptions_latex: The random scenario-wise optimal value is measurable and integrable.
Every committed feasible decision is feasible in each relevant scenario.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(z_{\mathrm{PI}}=\mathbb E[\inf_{x\in X(\xi)}f(x,\xi)]\leq z_{\mathrm{SP}}\).

knowledge_statements.title: Expected-Value Model
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Deterministic proxy obtained by replacing random data with their mean.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Let \(\xi\in L^1(\Omega;\mathbb R^m)\), let \(\bar\xi=\mathbb E[\xi]\), and let \(X(\zeta)\) and \(f(x,\zeta)\) denote the feasible set and cost under data \(\zeta\). The expected-value model is the deterministic optimization problem
\[z_{\mathrm{EV}}=\inf_{x\in X(\bar\xi)} f(x,\bar\xi).\]
Any optimizer \(x_{\mathrm{EV}}\) is an expected-value solution. Its stochastic performance must be evaluated separately as \(\mathbb E[f(x_{\mathrm{EV}},\xi)]\), subject to scenario feasibility; replacing data by their mean does not generally commute with optimization.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The expected-value model replaces random parameters by their means; its optimizer must then be evaluated under the original uncertainty.
assumptions_latex: \(\xi\in L^1(\Omega;\mathbb R^m)\).
\(X(\mathbb E[\xi])\neq\varnothing\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(z_{\mathrm{EV}}=\inf_{x\in X(\mathbb E[\xi])}f(x,\mathbb E[\xi])\).

notation.meaning: Optimal value of the deterministic expected-value model.

knowledge_statements.title: Expected Value of Perfect Information
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Minimization convention for a stochastic program with nonanticipative and wait-and-see benchmarks.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(C(u,\xi)\) be an integrable random cost. Define the recourse value \(z_{\mathrm{RP}}=\inf_{u\in\mathcal P_{\mathrm{NA}}}\mathbb E[C(u,\xi)]\) and the wait-and-see value \(z_{\mathrm{WS}}=\mathbb E[\inf_{u\in\mathcal P(\xi)}C(u,\xi)]\), assuming both are finite and the displayed expectation is well defined. The expected value of perfect information is \[\operatorname{EVPI}=z_{\mathrm{RP}}-z_{\mathrm{WS}}.\] Since every nonanticipative policy is admissible after perfect revelation, \(z_{\mathrm{WS}}\le z_{\mathrm{RP}}\), hence \(\operatorname{EVPI}\ge0\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: EVPI is the expected-cost reduction obtained by revealing all uncertainty before decisions: the recourse optimum minus the wait-and-see optimum.
assumptions_latex: \(C(u,\xi)\) is measurable and integrable for every admissible policy.
\(z_{\mathrm{RP}}\) and \(z_{\mathrm{WS}}\) are finite.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\operatorname{EVPI}=z_{\mathrm{RP}}-z_{\mathrm{WS}}\ge0\).

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Wait-and-see value and expected value of perfect information
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Uses the minimization convention; consequently, perfect information is valued as the here-and-now objective minus the wait-and-see objective.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
When the scenario-wise minima and expectations are well defined, the wait-and-see and here-and-now recourse values are
\[WS=\mathbb{E}_{\boldsymbol\xi}\!\left[\min_x z(x,\boldsymbol\xi)\right]=\mathbb{E}_{\boldsymbol\xi}\!\left[z(\bar x(\boldsymbol\xi),\boldsymbol\xi)\right],\qquad RP=\min_x\mathbb{E}_{\boldsymbol\xi}[z(x,\boldsymbol\xi)].\]
For a minimization problem, the expected value of perfect information is
\[EVPI=RP-WS.\]
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The wait-and-see value is the expected scenario-wise optimal objective, while the recourse value minimizes the expected objective using a here-and-now decision. Under the minimization convention, EVPI equals RP minus WS.
assumptions_latex: \bar x(\xi)\in\operatorname*{argmin}_x z(x,\xi)\quad\text{for each relevant }\xi
\mathbb{E}_{\boldsymbol\xi}[\min_x z(x,\boldsymbol\xi)]\text{ and }\min_x\mathbb{E}_{\boldsymbol\xi}[z(x,\boldsymbol\xi)]\text{ are well defined}
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: EVPI=RP-WS

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Pairwise-scenario subproblem
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Defines a two-scenario recourse problem whose scenarios share one first-stage decision.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
For realizations \(\xi^r\) and \(\xi^k\), the pairs subproblem is
\[
\min_{x,y(\xi^r),y(\xi^k)} c^Tx+p^r q^Ty(\xi^r)+(1-p^r)q^Ty(\xi^k)
\]
subject to
\[
Ax=b,\qquad Wy(\xi^r)=\xi^r-Tx,\qquad Wy(\xi^k)=\xi^k-Tx,
\]
\[
x\ge0,\qquad y(\xi^r)\ge0,\qquad y(\xi^k)\ge0.
\]
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The pairs subproblem combines the reference realization and one other scenario using a common first-stage decision and separate recourse decisions, with recourse costs weighted by p^r and 1-p^r.
assumptions_latex: \xi^r,\xi^k,p^r,A,b,W,T,c,q\text{ are defined in the two-stage stochastic-programming model}
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \operatorname{val}(P_{rk})=\min\left\{c^Tx+p^rq^Ty(\xi^r)+(1-p^r)q^Ty(\xi^k):Ax=b,\ Wy(\xi^r)=\xi^r-Tx,\ Wy(\xi^k)=\xi^k-Tx,\ x,y(\xi^r),y(\xi^k)\ge0\right\}

knowledge_statements.title: Value of the Stochastic Solution
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Cost-based VSS for a minimization problem whose expected-value solution is evaluated in the stochastic model.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(\bar\xi=\mathbb E[\xi]\), and let \(\bar u\) solve the deterministic expected-value model obtained by replacing \(\xi\) with \(\bar\xi\). If fixing the relevant first-stage decisions to \(\bar u\) admits feasible recourse, define \(z_{\mathrm{EEV}}=\mathbb E[C(\bar u,\xi)]\), including optimal recourse decisions where applicable. For the stochastic recourse optimum \(z_{\mathrm{RP}}\), the value of the stochastic solution is \[\operatorname{VSS}=z_{\mathrm{EEV}}-z_{\mathrm{RP}}.\] Optimality of the stochastic solution gives \(z_{\mathrm{RP}}\le z_{\mathrm{EEV}}\), so \(\operatorname{VSS}\ge0\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: VSS is the excess expected cost incurred by using an expected-value-model solution instead of optimizing the stochastic recourse model.
assumptions_latex: \(\mathbb E[\xi]\) exists and the expected-value model has a solution \(\bar u\).
Fixing \(\bar u\) yields feasible, integrable recourse costs.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\operatorname{VSS}=z_{\mathrm{EEV}}-z_{\mathrm{RP}}\ge0\).

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Expected Value Problem and Expected Value Solution
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Defines the mean-value benchmark and records the absence of a general proximity guarantee to the recourse solution.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(\bar\xi=\mathbb E[\xi]\). The expected value, or mean value, problem is \(EV=\min_x z(x,\bar\xi)\). An optimizer \(\bar x(\bar\xi)\in\operatorname*{argmin}_x z(x,\bar\xi)\) is called an expected value solution. In general, when the optimizer depends on the realization \(\xi\), no proximity to a solution of the corresponding recourse problem is guaranteed.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The expected value problem replaces the random data by their expectation and minimizes the resulting deterministic objective. Any optimizer is an expected value solution. If optimal decisions depend on the realized data, this benchmark need not be close to a recourse-optimal decision.

\(\operatorname*{argmin}_x z(x,\bar\xi)\neq\varnothing\).

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Generalized reference-scenario VSS
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Defines EVRS and VSS for an arbitrary reference realization and preserves the infeasibility boundary ensuring extended-real nonnegativity.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Let \(\xi^r\) be a reference realization, not necessarily in the possible-scenario set, and let
\[
\bar x^r\in\operatorname*{argmin}_x z(x,\xi^r).
\]
Define
\[
\operatorname{EVRS}:=\mathbb E_{\boldsymbol\xi}\! igl[z(\bar x^r,\boldsymbol\xi)\bigr],
\qquad
\operatorname{VSS}:=\operatorname{EVRS}-\operatorname{RP}.
\]
Then \(\operatorname{VSS}\ge0\). If \(\bar x^r\) is feasible for the recourse problem, \(\operatorname{EVRS}\ge\operatorname{RP}\); otherwise \(\operatorname{EVRS}=+\infty\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: An optimizer for the deterministic reference realization is evaluated under the actual random realization to obtain EVRS, and VSS is EVRS minus the recourse value. VSS is nonnegative; a recourse-infeasible reference decision has infinite EVRS.
assumptions_latex: \xi^r\text{ is a reference realization, possibly outside the possible-scenario set}
\bar x^r\in\operatorname*{argmin}_x z(x,\xi^r)
\operatorname{RP}\text{ is the corresponding recourse-problem value}

children.title: Restricted-Information Value Family
children.top_down_role: Intermediate information comparisons.

children.title: Partial-Information Value
children.top_down_role: Value change attributable to coarsened or incomplete signals.

knowledge_statements.title: Partial-Information Value
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Value of enlarging a baseline policy class using a specified, possibly incomplete signal.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For an integrable cost \(C(u,\xi)\), let \(\mathcal P_0\) be the baseline admissible policy class and let \(\mathcal P_{\mathcal G}\) contain policies additionally measurable with respect to an observed sub-sigma-field \(\mathcal G\subseteq\sigma(\xi)\). Suppose \(\mathcal P_0\subseteq\mathcal P_{\mathcal G}\), and define \(z(\mathcal P)=\inf_{u\in\mathcal P}\mathbb E[C(u,\xi)]\). The partial-information value of \(\mathcal G\) is \[V(\mathcal G)=z(\mathcal P_0)-z(\mathcal P_{\mathcal G}).\] Thus \(V(\mathcal G)\ge0\); it measures improvement relative to the declared baseline, not relative to perfect information.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Partial-information value is the optimal expected-cost reduction from allowing decisions to use a specified incomplete signal.
assumptions_latex: \(\mathcal G\subseteq\sigma(\xi)\) is observed before the decisions it may influence.
\(\mathcal P_0\subseteq\mathcal P_{\mathcal G}\), and both optimal values are finite.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(V(\mathcal G)=z(\mathcal P_0)-z(\mathcal P_{\mathcal G})\ge0\).

notation.meaning: sigma-field generated by the partial signal
policies adapted to the augmented information
optimal expected cost over policy class

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The policy-class construction is plausible, but no source establishes the intended partial-signal timing, augmented measurability convention, or terminology for this taxonomy leaf.

children.title: Delayed-Information Value
children.top_down_role: Value change attributable to later signal availability.

knowledge_statements.title: Delayed-Information Value
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Value of a signal that becomes usable only from a specified decision stage onward.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: In a \(T\)-stage minimization problem, let \(\mathcal P_0\) be the baseline nonanticipative policy class. For a signal sigma-field \(\mathcal G\) and release stage \(\tau\), let \(\mathcal P_{\mathcal G,\tau}\) consist of policies whose decisions before \(\tau\) use only baseline information and whose decisions from \(\tau\) onward may also use \(\mathcal G\). If \(\mathcal P_0\subseteq\mathcal P_{\mathcal G,\tau}\), define \[V_{\tau}(\mathcal G)=\inf_{u\in\mathcal P_0}\mathbb E[C(u,\xi)]-\inf_{u\in\mathcal P_{\mathcal G,\tau}}\mathbb E[C(u,\xi)].\] Then \(V_{\tau}(\mathcal G)\ge0\), and delaying release cannot increase value when the resulting policy classes are nested.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Delayed-information value is the expected-cost reduction when a signal becomes available only at or after a specified stage.
assumptions_latex: \(1\le\tau\le T\), and the signal is unavailable to decisions before stage \(\tau\).
All compared policy classes are nonempty and have finite values.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(V_{\tau}(\mathcal G)\ge0\), and \(\tau_1\le\tau_2\) with nested classes implies \(V_{\tau_1}(\mathcal G)\ge V_{\tau_2}(\mathcal G)\).

notation.meaning: policy class using the signal from stage tau

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The nested-class monotonicity is mathematically plausible, but the precise release-stage and filtration convention requires a source before this definition can be relied upon.

children.title: Combined-Restriction Value
children.top_down_role: Value effect when incomplete signals also arrive late.

knowledge_statements.title: Combined-Restriction Value
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Value under simultaneous restrictions on signal content, release time, or admissible decision dependence.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(\mathcal R\) denote a collection of information restrictions and let \(\mathcal P_{\mathcal R}\) be the resulting admissible policy class. Relative to a baseline class \(\mathcal P_0\), suppose \(\mathcal P_0\subseteq\mathcal P_{\mathcal R}}\subseteq\mathcal P_{\mathrm{PI}}\), where \(\mathcal P_{\mathrm{PI}}\) permits perfect information. With \(z(\mathcal P)=\inf_{u\in\mathcal P}\mathbb E[C(u,\xi)]\), define \[V(\mathcal R)=z(\mathcal P_0)-z(\mathcal P_{\mathcal R}).\] Consequently, \(0\le V(\mathcal R)\le z(\mathcal P_0)-z(\mathcal P_{\mathrm{PI}})\). If restrictions \(\mathcal R_2\) produce a subset of the policies allowed by \(\mathcal R_1\), then \(V(\mathcal R_2)\le V(\mathcal R_1)\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Combined-restriction value measures improvement when signal content, timing, and admissibility restrictions are imposed together; tighter restrictions cannot yield greater value.
assumptions_latex: The compared policy classes are nonempty and have finite expected-cost infima.
\(\mathcal P_0\subseteq\mathcal P_{\mathcal R}\subseteq\mathcal P_{\mathrm{PI}}\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(0\le V(\mathcal R)\le z(\mathcal P_0)-z(\mathcal P_{\mathrm{PI}})\).

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: No source supports the proposed combined-restriction convention, and the expression for the policy-class inclusion contains an unmatched closing brace in \(\mathcal P_{\mathcal R}}\).

children.title: Zero-Improvement Regimes
children.top_down_role: Settings where intermediate information changes do not alter the benchmark value.

knowledge_statements.title: Zero-Improvement Regimes
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Exact condition for a restricted information expansion to leave the optimal value unchanged.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(\mathcal P_0\subseteq\mathcal P_1\) be nonempty policy classes with finite values \(z_i=\inf_{u\in\mathcal P_i}\mathbb E[C(u,\xi)]\). The information expansion has zero improvement exactly when \[z_0=z_1.\] If both infima are attained, this is equivalent to the existence of an optimizer of the enlarged problem lying in the baseline class: \[\operatorname*{argmin}_{u\in\mathcal P_1}\mathbb E[C(u,\xi)]\cap\mathcal P_0\ne\varnothing.\] Hence additional information may enlarge the feasible policy class without value whenever some baseline policy remains optimal after the enlargement.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Additional information has zero improvement exactly when enlarging the policy class leaves the optimal expected cost unchanged.
assumptions_latex: \(\mathcal P_0\subseteq\mathcal P_1\), and both optimal values are finite.
For the optimizer characterization, both infima are attained.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(z_0-z_1=0\iff z_0=z_1\), with the stated optimizer characterization under attainment.

notation.meaning: optimal expected cost over the indexed class

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The value-equality and attainment-based optimizer characterizations are mathematically coherent and the condition kind fits the leaf, but the record supplies no evidence source.

children.title: Information-Value Ordering System

children.title: Benchmark Value Orderings
children.top_down_role: Ordering relationships among information benchmarks.

knowledge_statements.title: Benchmark Value Orderings
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Canonical ordering of wait-and-see, recourse, and expected-value-solution benchmarks for minimization.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Assume the wait-and-see, stochastic recourse, and expected-value-solution benchmarks are feasible and finite. Perfect information enlarges the admissible policy class, while the expected-value solution is a particular admissible first-stage choice in the recourse model. Therefore \[z_{\mathrm{WS}}\le z_{\mathrm{RP}}\le z_{\mathrm{EEV}}.\] Equivalently, \(\operatorname{EVPI}=z_{\mathrm{RP}}-z_{\mathrm{WS}}\ge0\) and \(\operatorname{VSS}=z_{\mathrm{EEV}}-z_{\mathrm{RP}}\ge0\), with \[z_{\mathrm{EEV}}-z_{\mathrm{WS}}=\operatorname{VSS}+\operatorname{EVPI}.\] The inequalities reverse for a consistently formulated maximization convention.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: For minimization, wait-and-see cost is no greater than recourse cost, which is no greater than the cost of using the expected-value solution.
assumptions_latex: All three benchmark values are finite.
The expected-value solution admits feasible recourse in the stochastic model.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(z_{\mathrm{WS}}\le z_{\mathrm{RP}}\le z_{\mathrm{EEV}}\).

notation.meaning: expected result of the expected-value solution

children.title: Zero-Value Regimes
children.top_down_role: Structures in which a diagnostic vanishes.

knowledge_statements.title: Zero-Value Regimes
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Attainment-based characterizations of vanishing EVPI and VSS in a minimization model.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Assume all benchmark optima are attained and finite. Then \(\operatorname{EVPI}=0\) exactly when \(z_{\mathrm{RP}}=z_{\mathrm{WS}}\); equivalently, some nonanticipative recourse optimizer also attains the wait-and-see expected cost. Likewise, \(\operatorname{VSS}=0\) exactly when \(z_{\mathrm{EEV}}=z_{\mathrm{RP}}\); equivalently, an expected-value-model solution, together with its optimal recourse decisions, is optimal for the stochastic recourse problem. These conditions concern objective values and do not require uniqueness of any benchmark optimizer.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: EVPI vanishes when nonanticipativity costs nothing; VSS vanishes when an expected-value solution is already optimal for the stochastic model.
assumptions_latex: The wait-and-see, recourse, and expected-value-solution benchmarks are finite and attained.
The expected-value solution admits feasible recourse.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\operatorname{EVPI}=0\iff z_{\mathrm{RP}}=z_{\mathrm{WS}}\), and \(\operatorname{VSS}=0\iff z_{\mathrm{EEV}}=z_{\mathrm{RP}}\).

children.title: Information-Value Bounds
children.top_down_role: Upper and lower comparison families for information values.

knowledge_statements.title: Information-Value Bounds
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Policy-class bounds comparing restricted information with no information and perfect information.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(\mathcal P_0\subseteq\mathcal P_{\mathcal I}\subseteq\mathcal P_{\mathrm{PI}}\) be baseline, restricted-information, and perfect-information policy classes, with finite values \(z(\mathcal P)=\inf_{u\in\mathcal P}\mathbb E[C(u,\xi)]\). Define \(V(\mathcal I)=z(\mathcal P_0)-z(\mathcal P_{\mathcal I})\). Set inclusion yields \[0\le V(\mathcal I)\le z(\mathcal P_0)-z(\mathcal P_{\mathrm{PI}}).\] When \(\mathcal P_0\) is the ordinary nonanticipative recourse class and \(\mathcal P_{\mathrm{PI}}\) is the wait-and-see class, the upper bound equals \(\operatorname{EVPI}\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The value of any restricted information lies between zero and the value of perfect information, provided the corresponding policy classes are nested.
assumptions_latex: \(\mathcal P_0\subseteq\mathcal P_{\mathcal I}\subseteq\mathcal P_{\mathrm{PI}}\).
All three expected-cost infima are finite.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(0\le V(\mathcal I)\le\operatorname{EVPI}\) under the recourse and wait-and-see endpoint conventions.

knowledge_statements.title: Two-Stage Extensive Forms
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Finite-scenario deterministic equivalent of a two-stage stochastic linear recourse problem.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let scenarios \(s=1,\ldots,S\) have probabilities \(p_s>0\) with \(\sum_{s=1}^S p_s=1\). For first-stage decisions \(x\) and scenario recourse decisions \(y_s\), the finite-support two-stage problem has extensive form \[\min_{x,y_1,\ldots,y_S}\ c^{\mathsf T}x+\sum_{s=1}^S p_s q_s^{\mathsf T}y_s\quad\text{subject to}\quad Ax=b,\ x\in X,\ T_sx+W_sy_s=h_s,\ y_s\in Y_s\ \text{for all }s.\] A single shared variable \(x\) enforces first-stage nonanticipativity; each \(y_s\) may depend on the realized scenario.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The two-stage extensive form uses one shared first-stage decision and a separate weighted recourse block for each finite-support scenario.
assumptions_latex: The uncertainty has finite support \(\{1,\ldots,S\}\) with probabilities \(p_s\).
All displayed feasible sets and objective terms define a well-posed optimization problem.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The displayed deterministic program has the same feasible policies and objective values as the finite-support two-stage recourse model.

children.title: Node-Based Multistage Forms
children.top_down_role: Tree-node deterministic equivalents.

knowledge_statements.title: Node-Based Multistage Forms
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Deterministic equivalent indexed by nodes of a finite scenario tree.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(\mathcal N\) be a finite rooted scenario tree, with node probability \(p_n\), stage cost vector \(c_n\), and parent \(a(n)\) for each nonroot node. A node-based multistage linear form is \[\min_{(x_n)}\ \sum_{n\in\mathcal N}p_n c_n^{\mathsf T}x_n\quad\text{subject to}\quad A_nx_n+B_nx_{a(n)}=b_n,\ x_n\in X_n\ \text{for every nonroot }n,\] together with the root constraints. Because each node represents one observed history and has one variable \(x_n\), decisions are automatically identical for all scenario paths sharing that history.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A node-based extensive form assigns one decision block to each scenario-tree node, so shared histories automatically share decisions.
assumptions_latex: \(\mathcal N\) is a finite rooted scenario tree with consistent node probabilities.
Constraints at a node depend only on its history and parent decision.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: One variable per history node provides a deterministic equivalent with nonanticipativity enforced by construction.

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The node-indexed representation and its nonanticipativity interpretation are standard, but no source is supplied and the root constraints are left model-dependent.

children.title: Path-Based Multistage Forms
children.top_down_role: Scenario-path equivalents with explicit coupling.

knowledge_statements.title: Path-Based Multistage Forms
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Scenario-path deterministic equivalent with explicit nonanticipativity equations.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(\mathcal S\) be finite terminal scenarios with probabilities \(p_s\), and let \(x_t^s\) be the stage-\(t\) decision copied for path \(s\). A path-based form minimizes \[\sum_{s\in\mathcal S}p_s\sum_{t=1}^T c_t^{s\mathsf T}x_t^s\] subject to every scenario's stagewise feasibility constraints and the coupling equations \[x_t^s=x_t^{s'}\quad\text{whenever scenarios }s\text{ and }s'\text{ have identical observed histories through stage }t.\] These equations are precisely the finite-tree nonanticipativity constraints; quotienting path copies by them yields the corresponding node-based formulation.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A path-based form copies decisions along every scenario path and explicitly equates copies belonging to indistinguishable histories.
assumptions_latex: \(\mathcal S\) is a finite set of complete scenario paths with probabilities summing to one.
History equivalence at every stage is specified consistently with the information filtration.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: Explicit history-coupling equations make the path-based form equivalent to the corresponding node-based deterministic equivalent.

notation.meaning: stage-t decision copy on scenario path s

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The path-copy and coupling formulation is plausible, but a source is needed for the precise filtration-based history equivalence and the asserted quotient equivalence to the node form.

children.title: Decomposability Interfaces

children.title: Scenario Decomposability
children.top_down_role: Separation across scenarios with shared decisions retained.

knowledge_statements.title: Scenario Decomposability
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Finite-scenario two-stage separability with the nonanticipative first-stage decision retained as the coupling variable.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Consider the two-stage problem \[\inf_{x\in X}\left\{c(x)+\sum_{s\in S}p_sQ_s(x)\right\},\qquad Q_s(x):=\inf_{y_s\in Y_s(x)}q_s(x,y_s).\] Suppose that, for every fixed \(x\in X\), each set \(Y_s(x)\) is nonempty and each value \(Q_s(x)\) is finite. Then \[\inf_{(y_s)_{s\in S}\in\prod_{s\in S}Y_s(x)}\sum_{s\in S}p_sq_s(x,y_s)=\sum_{s\in S}p_s\inf_{y_s\in Y_s(x)}q_s(x,y_s).\] Thus the recourse subproblems may be solved separately by scenario. The shared decision \(x\), or nonanticipativity constraints imposed on scenario copies of \(x\), retains the coupling in the complete model.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: When every scenario subproblem has a well-defined finite value, fixing the shared first-stage decision separates the recourse optimization by scenario; the complete model remains coupled through that shared decision.
assumptions_latex: The scenario set \(S\) is finite, with \(p_s>0\) and \(\sum_{s\in S}p_s=1\).
The first-stage feasible set \(X\) is common to all scenarios.
For every \(x\in X\) and \(s\in S\), the set \(Y_s(x)\) is nonempty and \(Q_s(x):=\inf_{y_s\in Y_s(x)}q_s(x,y_s)\) is finite.
For fixed \(x\), each recourse set and cost depends only on its own scenario decision.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: For each fixed \(x\in X\), the recourse minimization separates into independent scenario problems.
