knowledge_statements.scope_note: Finite-horizon stage decomposition under a sufficient-state formulation.

source_refs.locator: 3.2 Finite Horizon Problems p. 65

knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Set \(V_{T+1}(s)=0\). For \(t=T,T-1,\ldots,0\), define \[V_t(s):=\inf_{a\in A_t(s)}\left\{g_t(s,a)+\mathbb E\!\left[V_{t+1}(S_{t+1})\mid S_t=s,\,a_t=a\right]\right\}.\] If \(S_t\) is a sufficient state and admissible actions are \(\mathcal F_t\)-measurable, then the optimal value of the multistage problem is \(\mathbb E[V_0(S_0)]\). Each stage communicates with later stages only through the continuation value \(V_{t+1}\) evaluated at the next state.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A sufficient state separates adjacent stages: each stage minimizes current cost plus the conditional continuation value supplied by the next stage.

children.title: Subsystem Decomposability Family
children.top_down_role: Separation inherited from subsystem structure.

children.title: Block Decomposability
children.top_down_role: Separation induced by weakly coupled model blocks.

knowledge_statements.title: Block Decomposability
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Additive subsystem decomposition conditional on a shared interface variable.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(I\) be finite and fix \(z\in Z\). Suppose each \(X_i(z)\) is nonempty and each value \(v_i(z):=\inf_{x_i\in X_i(z)}f_i(x_i,z)\) is finite. If the joint feasible set is exactly \(\prod_{i\in I}X_i(z)\), then \[\inf_{(x_i)_{i\in I}\in\prod_{i\in I}X_i(z)}\sum_{i\in I}f_i(x_i,z)=\sum_{i\in I}\inf_{x_i\in X_i(z)}f_i(x_i,z).\] Hence fixing the interface \(z\) exposes independent optimization blocks, while optimizing or coordinating \(z\) remains a master-level task.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: If the coupling interface is fixed, the subsystem feasible sets form a Cartesian product, and every subsystem has a finite well-defined value, an additive objective separates into independent blocks.
assumptions_latex: The subsystem index set \(I\) is finite.
The interface value \(z\) belongs to a set \(Z\).
For fixed \(z\), every subsystem set \(X_i(z)\) is nonempty and \(\inf_{x_i\in X_i(z)}f_i(x_i,z)\) is finite.
The joint feasible set is \(\prod_{i\in I}X_i(z)\), and the objective is \(\sum_{i\in I}f_i(x_i,z)\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: Fixing \(z\) makes the optimization over subsystem blocks independent.

children.title: Resource Decomposability
children.top_down_role: Separation induced by shared or partitioned resource structure.

knowledge_statements.title: Resource Decomposability
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Lagrangian resource decomposition; equality with the primal value additionally requires strong duality.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For the minimization problem \[v:=\inf\left\{\sum_{i\in I}f_i(x_i):x_i\in X_i,\ \sum_{i\in I}A_ix_i\le b\right\},\] dualizing the resource constraint with \(\lambda\ge0\) gives \[d(\lambda):=-\lambda^{\mathsf T}b+\sum_{i\in I}\inf_{x_i\in X_i}\left(f_i(x_i)+\lambda^{\mathsf T}A_ix_i\right).\] Every evaluation of \(d(\lambda)\) therefore separates by subsystem. Weak duality gives \(d(\lambda)\le v\). If a convex strong-duality qualification applicable to this problem holds, then \[v=\sup_{\lambda\ge0}d(\lambda).\]
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Pricing the shared resource constraint separates the subsystem minimizations; when an applicable convex strong-duality condition holds, optimizing over all nonnegative resource prices recovers the primal value.
assumptions_latex: The subsystem index set \(I\) is finite.
Subsystem \(i\) has local feasible set \(X_i\), cost \(f_i\), and resource consumption \(A_ix_i\).
The only cross-subsystem restriction is \(\sum_{i\in I}A_ix_i\le b\).
The displayed primal and Lagrangian infima are well defined; primal-dual equality is asserted only when an applicable convex strong-duality qualification holds.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: For each \(\lambda\ge0\), the Lagrangian minimization separates by subsystem; under strong duality, \(v=\sup_{\lambda\ge0}d(\lambda)\).

notation.meaning: resource consumption map for subsystem i

children.title: Linking-Constraint Structure
children.top_down_role: Residual constraints connecting otherwise separable subsystems.

knowledge_statements.title: Linking-Constraint Structure
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Algebraic identification of constraints that prevent subsystem separation.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(I\) be finite, let \(x_i\in X_i\), and let the objective be \(\sum_{i\in I}f_i(x_i)\). A block-structured feasible set has linking-constraint form \[F:=\left\{(x_i)_{i\in I}:x_i\in X_i,\ \sum_{i\in I}B_ix_i=d,\ \sum_{i\in I}C_ix_i\le e\right\}.\] A displayed equality or inequality is linking when at least two of its block maps are nonzero. Deleting all linking constraints leaves \(\prod_{i\in I}X_i\). Alternatively, multipliers \(\pi\) and \(\lambda\ge0\) yield the blockwise terms \[f_i(x_i)+\pi^{\mathsf T}B_ix_i+\lambda^{\mathsf T}C_ix_i,\] so the Lagrangian minimization separates by block for fixed multipliers.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Linking constraints are cross-block equations or inequalities. Removing them exposes the Cartesian product of local feasible sets, while dualizing them makes an additive Lagrangian separable for fixed multipliers.
assumptions_latex: The block index set \(I\) is finite.
Each block decision satisfies \(x_i\in X_i\), and the objective is \(\sum_{i\in I}f_i(x_i)\).
All cross-block restrictions are collected as \(\sum_{i\in I}B_ix_i=d\) and \(\sum_{i\in I}C_ix_i\le e\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: Removing the linking constraints leaves a Cartesian product; dualizing them makes the additive Lagrangian separable for fixed multipliers.

notation.meaning: local feasible set of block i
equality linking map of block i
inequality linking map of block i

children.title: Subsystem Coupling Boundaries
children.top_down_role: Coupling regimes that prevent effective subsystem separation.

knowledge_statements.title: Subsystem Coupling Boundaries
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Incidence-based boundary between local subsystem data and cross-subsystem couplings.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(I\) be a finite subsystem set. For each variable or constraint \(j\), define its subsystem incidence set by \[N(j):=\{i\in I:j\text{ is incident to subsystem }i\},\] and define the coupling boundary by \[\partial I:=\{j:|N(j)|\ge2\}.\] Objects with \(|N(j)|=1\) are local. Direct primal separation occurs when no unfixed shared variable and no active cross-block constraint remains. Fixing the values of all shared variables and thereby reducing each remaining constraint to a local constraint yields a Cartesian product of conditional local feasible sets. Replacing a shared variable by local copies merely isolates the coupling in explicit consistency constraints; separation then requires those consistency constraints to be fixed, removed, or dualized.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The coupling boundary contains variables and constraints incident to multiple subsystems. Fixing shared values can expose conditional local feasible sets, while local copies remain coupled until their consistency constraints are handled.
assumptions_latex: The subsystem index set \(I\) is finite.
Each model variable and constraint has a specified incidence set \(N(j)\subseteq I\).
Local objectives and constraints depend on one subsystem, whereas boundary objects have incidence in at least two subsystems.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: Subsystems separate directly only after no unfixed shared variable or active cross-block constraint remains; local copying alone retains coupling through consistency constraints.

notation.meaning: set of subsystems incident to variable or constraint j

children.title: Finite-Support Approximation
children.top_down_role: Discrete approximation of two-stage distributions.

knowledge_statements.title: Finite-Support Approximation
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Discrete-law approximation of a two-stage expected-recourse objective.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(X\) be the first-stage feasible set, let \(c:X\to\mathbb R\) be the first-stage cost, and let \(Q(x,\xi)\) be the recourse value. For support points \(\xi^1,\ldots,\xi^N\) and weights \(p_n>0\) satisfying \(\sum_{n=1}^{N}p_n=1\), define \[P_N:=\sum_{n=1}^{N}p_n\delta_{\xi^n},\] where \(\delta_{\xi^n}\) is the Dirac probability measure at \(\xi^n\). The finite-support approximation of \(F(x):=c(x)+\mathbb E_P[Q(x,\xi)]\) is \[F_N(x):=c(x)+\mathbb E_{P_N}[Q(x,\xi)]=c(x)+\sum_{n=1}^{N}p_nQ(x,\xi^n).\] The associated approximating problem is \(\inf_{x\in X}F_N(x)\). Convergence of values or minimizers requires additional regularity and convergence hypotheses.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A finite-support approximation replaces the uncertainty law by weighted Dirac atoms, turning expected recourse into a finite scenario sum; convergence requires additional assumptions.
assumptions_latex: The uncertainty \(\xi\) has probability law \(P\) on a measurable space.
The first-stage feasible set is \(X\), the first-stage cost is \(c:X\to\mathbb R\), and the recourse value is \(Q(x,\xi)\).
The support points \(\xi^1,\ldots,\xi^N\) have weights \(p_n>0\) with \(\sum_{n=1}^{N}p_n=1\).
The expectations defining \(F(x)\) and \(F_N(x)\) are finite for the decisions under consideration.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: Replacing \(P\) by \(P_N\) replaces the expected recourse term by \(\sum_{n=1}^{N}p_nQ(x,\xi^n)\).

notation.meaning: Dirac probability measure at support point n

knowledge_statements.statement_latex: A finite scenario-process approximation is a rooted tree with stage sets \(\mathcal N_0,\ldots,\mathcal N_T\), node values \(\hat\xi_n\), and transition probabilities \(p_{m\mid n}\) for every child \(m\) of \(n\), where \(\sum_{m\in\operatorname{ch}(n)}p_{m\mid n}=1\). Each root-to-leaf path \(\omega=(n_0,\ldots,n_T)\) represents the trajectory \((\hat\xi_{n_1},\ldots,\hat\xi_{n_T})\) with probability \[p_\omega:=\prod_{t=0}^{T-1}p_{n_{t+1}\mid n_t}.\] These paths define a finite-support approximation to the joint process law.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A scenario tree approximates a stochastic process by finitely many history-sharing paths, with path probabilities equal to products of conditional branch probabilities.

children.title: Filtration-Preserving Approximation
children.top_down_role: Approximation respecting conditional information structure.

assumptions_latex: The original process is adapted to \(\mathcal F_t:=\sigma(\xi_1,\ldots,\xi_t)\).
The approximation is adapted to a finite filtration \((\widehat{\mathcal F}_t)_{t=0}^{T}\).
Approximate histories that share a node at stage \(t\) are observationally indistinguishable before decisions at that node.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The approximation preserves information structure when every stagewise approximation and admissible decision is measurable with respect to the corresponding approximate history.
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Adapted finite-tree approximation preserving decision information and nonanticipativity.

source_refs.locator: 5.6 The Exogenous Information Process p. 189

knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(q_t\) map each original history \((\xi_1,\ldots,\xi_t)\) to an approximate tree node, and set \[\widehat{\mathcal F}_t:=\sigma\!\left(q_t(\xi_1,\ldots,\xi_t)\right).\] The approximation is filtration-preserving for the decision model if \(\widehat{\mathcal F}_t\subseteq\mathcal F_t\), the parent of \(q_{t+1}(\xi_1,\ldots,\xi_{t+1})\) equals \(q_t(\xi_1,\ldots,\xi_t)\), and every approximate stage-\(t\) decision is \(\widehat{\mathcal F}_t\)-measurable. Equivalently, histories mapped to the same stage-\(t\) node must receive the same stage-\(t\) decision.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A process approximation preserves filtration when nodes refine consistently over time and decisions depend only on the approximate history observed by their stage.

children.title: Uncertainty-Support Growth
children.top_down_role: Complexity induced by expanding outcome support.

assumptions_latex: At stage \(t\), the exogenous uncertainty has finite support of size \(m_t\ge1\).
Every support outcome can follow every partial history.
Distinct outcome sequences define distinct scenario-tree nodes.

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Combinatorial growth for a fully branching process with stagewise finite supports.

source_refs.locator: 2.1.1 Finite state space p. 58

knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For a full scenario tree, each stage-\(t-1\) node has exactly \(m_t\) children. Therefore \[N_0=1,\qquad N_t=\prod_{k=1}^{t}m_k,\qquad L=N_T=\prod_{k=1}^{T}m_k,\] where \(L\) is the leaf-scenario count. The total node count is \[N_{\mathrm{tot}}=1+\sum_{t=1}^{T}\prod_{k=1}^{t}m_k.\] If \(m_t=m\ge2\), then \(L=m^T\) and \(N_{\mathrm{tot}}=(m^{T+1}-1)/(m-1)\), exhibiting exponential growth in the horizon.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Full branching multiplies support sizes across stages, producing exponentially many leaf scenarios when each stage has at least two outcomes.

children.title: Scenario-Count Growth
children.top_down_role: Complexity induced by increasing represented scenarios.

assumptions_latex: A scenario tree has finite node sets \(\mathcal N_t\) and branching degrees \(b(n)\).
Each nonroot node has exactly one parent.

knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: Scenario count equals the number of leaves and is bounded by the product of the largest stagewise branching degrees.

source_refs.locator: 2.1.1 Finite state space p. 58

knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(B_t:=\max_{n\in\mathcal N_{t-1}}b(n)\). Since every stage-\(t\) node has one parent, \[|\mathcal N_t|=\sum_{n\in\mathcal N_{t-1}}b(n)\le B_t|\mathcal N_{t-1}|.\] Consequently the number \(L\) of complete scenarios satisfies \[L=|\mathcal N_T|\le\prod_{t=1}^{T}B_t.\] Equality holds when every node at stage \(t-1\) has exactly \(B_t\) children. Pruning, recombination, or history aggregation can make the inequality strict, although recombination changes the representation from a tree to a directed acyclic graph.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Scenario count is the leaf count; it is at most the product of maximum stagewise branching degrees, with equality under uniform full branching.

children.title: Support Discretization Effects
children.top_down_role: Representation-size consequences of replacing continuous support with finite points.

knowledge_statements.title: Support Discretization Effects
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Wasserstein stability bound for Lipschitz expected recourse under support discretization.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \((\Xi,d)\) be a metric space, and let \(P\) and \(P_N\) be probability laws with finite first moments. Define \[F_P(x):=c(x)+\mathbb E_P[Q(x,\xi)],\qquad F_{P_N}(x):=c(x)+\mathbb E_{P_N}[Q(x,\xi)].\] If, uniformly over \(x\in X\), the mapping \(\xi\mapsto Q(x,\xi)\) is \(L\)-Lipschitz, then for every \(x\in X\), \[|F_P(x)-F_{P_N}(x)|\le L W_1(P,P_N).\] Consequently, \[\sup_{x\in X}|F_P(x)-F_{P_N}(x)|\le L W_1(P,P_N).\] If both optimal values are finite, then \[\left|\inf_{x\in X}F_P(x)-\inf_{x\in X}F_{P_N}(x)\right|\le L W_1(P,P_N).\] Thus a discretization that reduces \(W_1(P,P_N)\) controls objective and optimal-value error under the stated uniform regularity.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Uniform Lipschitz continuity of recourse makes the first Wasserstein distance between the original and discretized laws bound both objective perturbation and, when finite, optimal-value perturbation.
assumptions_latex: The uncertainty laws \(P\) and \(P_N\) have finite first moments on the metric space \((\Xi,d)\).
For every \(x\in X\), the mapping \(\xi\mapsto Q(x,\xi)\) is real-valued and \(L\)-Lipschitz with one constant \(L<\infty\) independent of \(x\).
The first-stage cost \(c(x)\) and feasible set \(X\) are unchanged by discretization.
The expectations are finite for every \(x\in X\); the optimal-value bound additionally assumes both displayed infima are finite.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The uniform objective perturbation is at most \(L W_1(P,P_N)\), and finite optimal values differ by at most the same quantity.

notation.meaning: first Wasserstein distance induced by d
uniform Lipschitz constant of recourse in uncertainty

children.title: Scenario Explosion Boundaries
children.top_down_role: Model sizes where scenario enumeration becomes impractical.

knowledge_statements.title: Scenario Explosion Boundaries
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Explicit scenario enumeration with stagewise finite supports and no recombination.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let a horizon contain \(T\) uncertainty revelations, with \(m_t\ge 1\) possible outcomes at stage \(t\). Full-support enumeration produces \(S_T=\prod_{t=1}^{T}m_t\) terminal scenarios. Hence any deterministic equivalent storing at least one constraint, variable block, or coefficient block per terminal scenario has representation size \(\Omega(S_T)\). If \(m_t\ge m>1\) for every \(t\), then \(S_T\ge m^T\), so explicit enumeration is exponential in the horizon. This boundary concerns the extensive-form representation; aggregation, sampling, decomposition, or sufficient-state recombination may avoid constructing all scenarios.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Without aggregation or recombination, terminal scenarios multiply across stages; any formulation storing data per scenario therefore grows exponentially when branching remains above one.
assumptions_latex: \(T\in\mathbb{N}\) and \(m_t\in\mathbb{N}_{+}\) for \(t=1,\ldots,T\).
All outcome sequences are retained as distinct terminal scenarios.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(S_T=\prod_{t=1}^{T}m_t\), and \(m_t\ge m>1\) implies representation size \(\Omega(m^T)\).

notation.meaning: number of outcomes at stage t

knowledge_statements.title: Scenario-Tree Growth
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Node-count growth in an unrecombined finite scenario tree.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Consider a rooted scenario tree of depth \(T\). If every node at depth \(t-1\) has exactly \(b_t\) children, then the number of nodes at depth \(t\) is \(N_t=\prod_{k=1}^{t}b_k\), and the total number of nodes is \(N=1+\sum_{t=1}^{T}\prod_{k=1}^{t}b_k\). For constant branching \(b_t=b>1\), this becomes \(N=(b^{T+1}-1)/(b-1)\). Thus both leaf count and total tree size are exponential in \(T\) when histories do not recombine.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: An unrecombined tree multiplies its node count by each stage’s branching factor; constant branching above one yields exponential growth in the horizon.
assumptions_latex: \(T\in\mathbb{N}\) and \(b_t\in\mathbb{N}_{+}\).
Nodes belonging to different histories are not merged.

notation.meaning: number of tree nodes at depth t

children.title: Distinct-History Growth
children.top_down_role: Growth in decision-relevant information histories.

knowledge_statements.title: Distinct-History Growth
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Counting observational histories before sufficient-state aggregation.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let the observation at stage \(t\) take values in a finite set \(\Xi_t\) of cardinality \(m_t\). A depth-\(t\) history is \(h_t=(\xi_1,\ldots,\xi_t)\in\Xi_1\times\cdots\times\Xi_t\). If every such sequence has positive probability, the number of distinct histories is \(H_t=\prod_{k=1}^{t}m_k\). A history-dependent policy may therefore require one decision specification for each of \(H_t\) information sets at stage \(t\), unless histories can be identified through a sufficient state or another exact equivalence relation.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: With full Cartesian support, distinct observation histories multiply across stages, and a general nonanticipative policy may need a separate decision for each history.
assumptions_latex: \(|\Xi_t|=m_t<\infty\) for each stage \(t\).
Every element of \(\Xi_1\times\cdots\times\Xi_t\) has positive probability.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(H_t=\left|\Xi_1\times\cdots\times\Xi_t\right|=\prod_{k=1}^{t}m_k\).

children.title: Horizon-Length Effects
children.top_down_role: Representation growth induced by additional decision stages.

knowledge_statements.title: Horizon-Length Effects
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Finite-horizon growth under uniformly bounded branching.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let an unrecombined scenario tree have horizon \(T\) and stagewise branching factors satisfying \(1\le b_t\le B\). Its terminal-node count obeys \(L_T=\prod_{t=1}^{T}b_t\le B^T\), and its total-node count obeys \(N_T=1+\sum_{t=1}^{T}\prod_{k=1}^{t}b_k\le (B^{T+1}-1)/(B-1)\) when \(B>1\). If additionally \(b_t\ge b>1\), then \(L_T\ge b^T\). Thus increasing the horizon alone creates exponential explicit-representation growth whenever nontrivial branching persists.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: For persistent branching, each extra stage multiplies the number of leaves, making explicit finite-horizon representations exponential in horizon length.
assumptions_latex: \(T\in\mathbb{N}\) and \(1\le b_t\le B\).
The scenario tree has no recombination.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(L_T\le B^T\), while \(b_t\ge b>1\) implies \(L_T\ge b^T\).

children.title: Recombination Limits
children.top_down_role: Limits on compressing histories through shared states.

knowledge_statements.title: Recombination Limits
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Exact merging of histories in a sequential recourse model.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Two stage-\(t\) histories \(h_t\) and \(h'_t\) may be recombined exactly only if they induce the same continuation problem: their feasible action sets agree, \(A_t(h_t)=A_t(h'_t)\); their conditional laws of all future exogenous information agree; and, for every common feasible continuation policy, their conditional distributions of future costs agree. Equivalently, an exact sufficient-state map \(s_t\) permits recombination only when \(s_t(h_t)=s_t(h'_t)\) implies equality of these continuation data. Otherwise merging can change feasibility or the optimal value.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Histories can be merged exactly only when they have identical feasible continuations, future uncertainty laws, and continuation costs; otherwise recombination changes the problem.
assumptions_latex: \(h_t\) and \(h'_t\) are histories at the same decision stage.
Continuation policies are nonanticipative.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: Exact recombination requires equality of the continuation problem for \(h_t\) and \(h'_t\).

notation.meaning: feasible action set after history h

children.title: State-Space Dimension
children.top_down_role: Dimensional burden associated with recursive state descriptions.

knowledge_statements.title: State-Space Dimension
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Dimension of a finite-dimensional sufficient state in sequential recourse.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For a stage-\(t\) sequential model, an exact finite-dimensional state representation is a measurable map \(s_t:H_t\to S_t\subseteq\mathbb{R}^{d_t^S}\) such that conditional feasibility, one-stage cost, state transition, and the conditional law of future exogenous information depend on a history \(h_t\in H_t\) only through \(s_t(h_t)\). The ambient coordinate dimension of the representation is \(d_t^S\). If \(S_t\) lies in a lower-dimensional affine set, its effective affine dimension is \(\dim(\operatorname{aff}S_t)\). An intrinsic state dimension may be defined by minimizing a specified dimension measure over an explicitly fixed admissible class of exact state representations; it is therefore representation-class dependent and need not equal the dimension of the raw history vector.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: State-space dimension may mean the ambient coordinate count or the effective affine dimension of an exact sufficient state. Any intrinsic minimum must be defined relative to a specified admissible class of state representations.
assumptions_latex: \(H_t\) is the measurable set of histories available at stage \(t\).
Admissible exact state maps take values in finite-dimensional Euclidean spaces.
The admissible representation class and the dimension measure used for minimization are explicitly specified.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The chosen representation has ambient dimension \(d_t^S\) and effective affine dimension \(\dim(\operatorname{aff}S_t)\); an intrinsic dimension is a minimum over the specified admissible class.

notation.meaning: image space of the chosen state representation

knowledge_statements.title: Action-Space Dimension
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Dimension or cardinality of feasible recourse actions at a state.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: At stage \(t\) and state \(s\), let the feasible action set be \(A_t(s)\). For a finite action set, the corresponding discrete size parameter is \(|A_t(s)|\), not a Euclidean dimension. A model-wide parameter may be defined by taking the maximum over all reachable states and stages.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Action-space size is measured by Euclidean or affine dimension for continuous actions and by cardinality for finite actions, maximized over relevant states if needed.
assumptions_latex: \(A_t(s)\) is the feasible action set at reachable state \(s\).

children.top_down_role: Dimensional burden associated with uncertain innovations.

knowledge_statements.title: Outcome-Space Dimension
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Dimension or support size of stagewise exogenous outcomes.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let the stage-\(t\) exogenous outcome be \(W_t\) with support \(\mathcal{W}_t\). If \(\mathcal{W}_t\subseteq\mathbb{R}^{d_t^W}\), its ambient outcome-space dimension is \(d_t^W\); its effective geometric dimension may instead be \(\dim(\operatorname{aff}\mathcal{W}_t)\). If \(\mathcal{W}_t\) is finite, the enumeration parameter is \(m_t=|\mathcal{W}_t|\). Dimension and support cardinality are distinct: a one-dimensional continuous outcome can have infinite support, while a high-dimensional distribution can have finite support.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Outcome-space complexity uses geometric dimension for continuous supports and support cardinality for finite outcomes; these two quantities measure different features.
assumptions_latex: \(W_t\) is the exogenous information revealed at stage \(t\).
\(\mathcal{W}_t\) denotes its support.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: Geometric size is \(d_t^W\) or \(\dim(\operatorname{aff}\mathcal{W}_t)\), whereas finite enumeration size is \(m_t=|\mathcal{W}_t|\).

source_refs.locator: 2.1.1 Finite state space p. 58

children.title: Cross-Dimensional Scaling
children.top_down_role: Complexity arising from simultaneous growth across multiple spaces.

knowledge_statements.title: Cross-Dimensional Scaling
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Tabular Bellman backup with finite state, action, and outcome sets.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: At stage \(t\), suppose a tabular Bellman backup evaluates every state-action-outcome triple \((s,a,w)\in S_t\times A_t(s)\times\mathcal{W}_{t+1}\), and each transition, cost, and table lookup takes constant time. With \(|S_t|=n_t\), \(\max_s|A_t(s)|=a_t\), and \(|\mathcal{W}_{t+1}|=m_{t+1}\), one complete backup requires at most \(O(n_ta_tm_{t+1})\) elementary evaluations and \(O(n_t)\) value-table storage. Over horizon \(T\), the work is \(O(\sum_{t=0}^{T-1}n_ta_tm_{t+1})\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A direct tabular Bellman backup scales multiplicatively with state count, available actions, and outcome count, then adds these costs across stages.
assumptions_latex: All sets \(S_t\), \(A_t(s)\), and \(\mathcal{W}_{t+1}\) are finite.
Each triple evaluation and value-table access has constant cost.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: Work is \(O(n_ta_tm_{t+1})\) per stage and \(O(\sum_{t=0}^{T-1}n_ta_tm_{t+1})\) over the horizon.

notation.meaning: maximum number of feasible actions per state

children.title: Nonconvexity-Integrality Barrier Family
children.top_down_role: Hardness associated with discrete or nonconvex recourse.

children.title: Integrality Barriers
children.top_down_role: Computational burdens caused by integer or categorical recourse choices.

knowledge_statements.title: Integrality Barriers
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Loss of convex recourse structure when continuation decisions are integral.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For a parameterized recourse problem \(Q(x)=\inf\{q^{\mathsf T}y:Wy\ge h-Tx,\ y\in\mathbb{Z}^{p}\times\mathbb{R}^{r}\}\), integrality destroys the general guarantee that \(Q\) is convex or polyhedral-convex in \(x\). Consequently, supporting-hyperplane cuts obtained from the continuous relaxation need not represent the integer value function exactly, and finite-valuedness of the relaxation does not imply integer feasibility. Convex recourse methods apply without modification only under additional structure ensuring integral optimal solutions, such as an appropriate integral polyhedron for every relevant right-hand side.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Integer recourse can make the value function nonconvex and can invalidate exact continuous-relaxation cuts or feasibility conclusions unless special integrality structure is present.
assumptions_latex: \(x\) is a first-stage parameter and \(y\) contains at least one integer component.
The recourse constraints depend affinely on \(x\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: Without an integrality-preserving structure, convexity of \(Q\) and exactness of continuous-relaxation cuts are not guaranteed.

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The failure-boundary role is appropriate and the claims are plausible, but the record supplies no citation for the nonconvex integer-recourse value function, relaxation-cut limitations, or integer-feasibility distinction.

children.title: Continuous Nonconvexity Barriers
children.top_down_role: Computational burdens caused by nonconvex continuous recourse geometry.

knowledge_statements.title: Continuous Nonconvexity Barriers
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Failure of convex recourse properties with continuous nonconvex feasible sets or costs.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(Q(x)=\inf_{y\in Y(x)}f(x,y)\), where \(y\) is continuous. If the joint feasible graph \(\{(x,y):y\in Y(x)\}\) is nonconvex or \(f\) is not jointly convex, the partial minimization defining \(Q\) is not guaranteed to be convex. Local minimizers of the recourse subproblem may then fail to be global, and local dual or first-order information need not yield globally valid supporting cuts for \(Q\). These failures persist despite continuity of variables; global guarantees require additional convexity or a valid global-optimization mechanism.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Continuous variables do not ensure tractability: nonconvex feasible sets or costs can produce nonconvex value functions, nonglobal local solutions, and invalid local cuts.
assumptions_latex: \(x\) parameterizes a continuous recourse problem.
At least one joint convexity condition on the objective or feasible graph is absent.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: Convexity of \(Q\), global optimality of local solutions, and validity of local supporting cuts are not guaranteed.

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The qualified non-guarantee claims fit a continuous-nonconvexity failure boundary, but no source supports the partial-minimization, local-optimality, and cut-validity assertions.

children.title: Mixed-Structure Barriers
children.top_down_role: Hardness produced by discrete choices within nonconvex recourse.

knowledge_statements.title: Mixed-Structure Barriers
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Combined discrete and continuous-nonconvex recourse structure.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Consider \(Q(x)=\inf\{f(x,y,z):(y,z)\in F(x),\ y\in\mathbb{Z}^{p},\ z\in\mathbb{R}^{r}\}\), where either \(F(x)\) is nonconvex or \(f\) is nonconvex. This mixed structure combines discrete feasibility with continuous global optimization: relaxing integrality may admit infeasible fractional solutions, while convexifying the continuous part may underestimate nonconvex costs or constraints. Therefore neither the integer relaxation nor a local continuous solution alone certifies the original recourse value. Exact solution requires a method that globally accounts for both sources of nonconvexity or additional structure making both relaxations exact.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Mixed integer and continuous-nonconvex recourse defeats certificates based solely on either an integrality relaxation or local continuous optimization.
assumptions_latex: \(p\ge1\) and \(r\ge1\).
The model contains integrality and at least one continuous nonconvexity.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: A fractional relaxation value or local continuous optimum need not equal \(Q(x)\).

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The content kind and local scope are appropriate, but the combined claims about integrality relaxation, continuous convexification, and exact certification require an authoritative mixed-integer nonconvex optimization source.

children.title: Relaxation-Gap Regimes
children.top_down_role: Settings where tractable relaxations poorly represent the original recourse structure.

knowledge_statements.title: Relaxation-Gap Regimes
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Additive minimization gap for scenario-wise recourse relaxations; multiplicative gaps require separate positivity conventions.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For each \(\xi\in\Xi_0\), let \(F(\xi)\subseteq R(\xi)\) be the original and relaxed feasible sets of a minimization recourse problem. Define \(v_F(\xi)=\inf_{z\in F(\xi)}f(z,\xi)\) and \(v_R(\xi)=\inf_{z\in R(\xi)}f(z,\xi)\). Assume \(v_R(\xi)\in\mathbb R\) and \(v_F(\xi)\in\mathbb R\cup\{+\infty\}\), and define \(g(\xi)=v_F(\xi)-v_R(\xi)\). Then \(g(\xi)\in[0,+\infty]\). The relaxation is exact on \(\Xi_0\) if \(g(\xi)=0\) for every \(\xi\in\Xi_0\), bounded-gap if \(\sup_{\xi\in\Xi_0}g(\xi)<+\infty\), and unbounded-gap if this supremum is \(+\infty\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: When the relaxed value is finite and the original value is finite or positive infinity, the additive relaxation gap is nonnegative. It is exact when uniformly zero, bounded-gap when uniformly finite, and unbounded-gap when its supremum is infinite.
assumptions_latex: For every \(\xi\in\Xi_0\), the minimization feasible sets satisfy \(F(\xi)\subseteq R(\xi)\).
For every \(\xi\in\Xi_0\), \(v_R(\xi)\in\mathbb R\) and \(v_F(\xi)\in\mathbb R\cup\{+\infty\}\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(g(\xi)=v_F(\xi)-v_R(\xi)\in[0,+\infty]\), with exact, bounded-gap, and unbounded-gap regimes determined by \(g\) on \(\Xi_0\).

notation.meaning: Optimal value over the original feasible set.
Optimal value over the relaxed feasible set.

children.title: Recourse Modeling Failure Taxonomy
children.top_down_role: Structural failures affecting recourse validity, representation, and decomposition.

children.title: Information-Structure Failures
children.top_down_role: Invalid modeling of observability and adaptation.

children.title: Anticipativity Leakage
children.top_down_role: Use of information unavailable at decision time.

assumptions_latex: At decision time \(t\), admissible controls must be measurable with respect to the available-information sigma-field \(\mathcal F_t\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: Anticipativity leakage occurs exactly when some implemented decision \(U_t\) is not \(\mathcal F_t\)-measurable, equivalently when it depends nontrivially on information revealed strictly after time \(t\).

notation.meaning: Information available when the stage-t decision is selected.
Sigma-field generated by the full uncertainty trajectory.

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Nonanticipativity boundary for multistage stochastic decisions.

source_refs.locator: 1.1.1 Recourse problems p. 5

knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \((\mathcal F_t)_{t=0}^T\) be the filtration representing information available over time, and let \(U_t\) be the decision selected at time \(t\). The model is nonanticipative at that time precisely when \(U_t\) is \(\mathcal F_t\)-measurable. Anticipativity leakage occurs when the modeled or implemented \(U_t\) is only measurable with respect to a strictly richer sigma-field, such as \(\mathcal F_T\), and its value varies with future information conditional on \(\mathcal F_t\). Such a policy is infeasible for the intended information structure.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Anticipativity leakage occurs when a decision uses uncertainty information that is unavailable at the time the decision must be made.
knowledge_statements.title: Anticipativity Leakage

source_witnesses.locator: 1.1.1 Recourse problems p. 5

children.title: Temporal Specification Failures
children.top_down_role: Incorrect chronology of decisions and observations.

children.title: Stage-Assignment Misspecification
children.top_down_role: Incorrect placement of decisions, observations, or transitions across stages.

knowledge_statements.title: Stage-Assignment Misspecification
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Failure caused by assigning a physical decision to a stage whose information structure changes its admissible policy class.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \((\Omega,\mathcal F,\mathbb P)\) be a probability space, let \(U\) take values in a measurable action space \(\mathcal U\), and let \(\tau(U)\) and \(s(U)\) denote its physical selection time and modeled stage. Write \(\mathcal D(\mathcal G,\mathcal U)\) for the equivalence classes of \(\mathcal G\)-measurable \(\mathcal U\)-valued decisions, modulo almost-sure equality. Stage-assignment misspecification occurs when \(\mathcal D(\mathcal F_{s(U)},\mathcal U)\neq\mathcal D(\mathcal F_{\tau(U)},\mathcal U)\). A strict enlargement can grant unavailable decision dependence, while a strict restriction can suppress physically usable dependence.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A decision is stage-misspecified when its modeled stage changes the class of decisions measurable with the information physically available at selection time.
assumptions_latex: \((\Omega,\mathcal F,\mathbb P)\) is a probability space with information sigma-fields \(\mathcal F_t\).
The decision \(U\) takes values in a measurable action space \(\mathcal U\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The stage assignment is faithful exactly when \(\mathcal D(\mathcal F_{s(U)},\mathcal U)=\mathcal D(\mathcal F_{\tau(U)},\mathcal U)\); otherwise it changes the admissible-decision class.

notation.meaning: Physical time at which the decision must be selected.
Stage assigned to the decision in the model.
Almost-sure equivalence classes of measurable decisions based on information \(\mathcal G\).

source_refs.locator: 1.1.1 Recourse problems p. 5

source_witnesses.locator: 1.1.1 Recourse problems p. 5

children.title: Event-Order Misspecification
children.top_down_role: Incorrect sequencing of events within a stage.

assumptions_latex: Physical events carry a precedence relation \(\prec\).
Each modeled event is assigned an ordered stage index \(s(e)\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The modeled order is valid only if \(e\prec e'\) implies \(s(e)\leq s(e')\), with strict inequality whenever information from \(e\) must be available before the action at \(e'\).

notation.meaning: Modeled stage index of event e.

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Order-preservation boundary between physical events and modeled stages.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(E\) be the relevant physical events, with \(e\prec e'\) meaning that \(e\) occurs before \(e'\), and let \(s:E\to\{0,\ldots,T\}\) be the modeled stage map. Event-order misspecification occurs if the stage map reverses a required precedence, so that \(e\prec e'\) but \(s(e)>s(e')\), or merges events into one information epoch when \(e'\) must react to information revealed by \(e\). The resulting filtration and admissible decisions represent a different causal system from the physical process.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Event-order misspecification occurs when modeled stages reverse or improperly merge physical events whose order determines what decisions can observe.
knowledge_statements.title: Event-Order Misspecification

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The failure-boundary role and order-preservation formulation are plausible, but no inspectable source supports the specific precedence and within-stage information assertions.

children.title: Implicit Foresight Leakage
children.top_down_role: Unintended future-information access caused by chronology errors.

assumptions_latex: The intended decision \(U_t\) must be \(\mathcal F_t\)-measurable.
Auxiliary variables and constraints are included in the implemented formulation.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: Implicit foresight leakage is present when \(U_t\) becomes a nonconstant function of future uncertainty conditional on \(\mathcal F_t\), even though no explicit future argument appears in its declaration.
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Indirect violation of nonanticipativity through formulation dependencies.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Suppose \(U_t\) is declared as a stage-\(t\) decision and is intended to be \(\mathcal F_t\)-measurable. Implicit foresight leakage occurs when auxiliary variables, scenario-indexed constraints, preprocessing, or shared parameters induce a representation \(U_t=\phi(H_t,\xi_{t+1:T})\) that is nonconstant in \(\xi_{t+1:T}\) for some fixed observed history \(H_t\). Equivalently, two scenarios indistinguishable under \(\mathcal F_t\) receive different stage-\(t\) decisions. This violates nonanticipativity despite the absence of an explicit future-information argument in the decision declaration.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Implicit foresight leakage arises when hidden formulation dependencies make a nominally current decision vary across scenarios that are indistinguishable at decision time.
knowledge_statements.title: Implicit Foresight Leakage

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The scenario-indistinguishability criterion is mathematically plausible and fits the leaf, but the specific hidden-dependency failure claim has no cited source.

children.title: Recourse-Timing Distortion
children.top_down_role: Misrepresentation of feasible adaptation caused by faulty temporal placement.

knowledge_statements.title: Recourse-Timing Distortion
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Mismatch between modeled and physical availability of corrective action that changes the admissible recourse class.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \((\Omega,\mathcal F,\mathbb P)\) be a probability space, let the corrective decision \(Y_t\) take values in a measurable action space \(\mathcal Y_t\), and let \(\mathcal G_t\) and \(\mathcal F_{\tau_t}\) be the modeled and physically available information sigma-fields. Write \(\mathcal D(\mathcal G,\mathcal Y_t)\) for the almost-sure equivalence classes of \(\mathcal G\)-measurable \(\mathcal Y_t\)-valued decisions. Recourse-timing distortion occurs when \(\mathcal D(\mathcal G_t,\mathcal Y_t)\neq\mathcal D(\mathcal F_{\tau_t},\mathcal Y_t)\). An enlargement can permit premature adaptation, whereas a restriction can delay or suppress feasible adaptation.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Recourse timing is distorted when modeled information changes the class of corrective decisions available at the physical correction time.
assumptions_latex: \((\Omega,\mathcal F,\mathbb P)\) is a probability space.
The corrective decision \(Y_t\) takes values in a measurable action space \(\mathcal Y_t\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: Recourse timing is faithful exactly when \(\mathcal D(\mathcal G_t,\mathcal Y_t)=\mathcal D(\mathcal F_{\tau_t},\mathcal Y_t)\); otherwise modeled recourse feasibility or value may differ from that of the physical system.

notation.meaning: Information assigned to the modeled recourse epoch.
Information physically available when correction is possible.
Almost-sure equivalence classes of corrective decisions measurable with respect to \(\mathcal G\).

source_refs.locator: 1.1.1 Recourse problems p. 5

source_witnesses.locator: 1.1.1 Recourse problems p. 5

children.title: History-Sufficiency Failure Boundary
children.top_down_role: Merging histories requiring different future decisions.

children.title: State Aliasing
children.top_down_role: Decision-relevant distinctions lost when multiple histories share one state representation.

assumptions_latex: Histories at time \(t\) form a set \(\mathcal H_t\).
A state representation is a map \(S_t:\mathcal H_t\to\mathcal S_t\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: State aliasing occurs when distinct histories \(h,h'\) satisfy \(S_t(h)=S_t(h')\); it is harmful when their feasible continuations, transition laws, or continuation values differ under some common action.

notation.meaning: Set of histories observable through time t.
Continuation value from history h under action a.

knowledge_statements.scope_note: History aggregation that may erase decision-relevant distinctions.

source_refs.locator: 3 Introduction to Markov Decision Processes p. 57
2.5.2 The Markovian structure of a Discrete-Event process p. 121

knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Given a state map \(S_t:\mathcal H_t\to\mathcal S_t\), state aliasing occurs when two distinct histories \(h,h'\in\mathcal H_t\) satisfy \(S_t(h)=S_t(h')\). The aliasing is decision-relevant if there exists an action \(a\) admissible after both histories for which the conditional transition law, immediate cost, feasible continuation set, or continuation value differs; in particular, \(Q_t(h,a)\neq Q_t(h',a)\) suffices. A state-based policy then cannot condition differently on these histories.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: State aliasing maps distinct histories to one state; it is harmful when those histories require different feasible or optimal continuations.
knowledge_statements.title: State Aliasing

source_witnesses.locator: 3 Introduction to Markov Decision Processes p. 57
2.5.2 The Markovian structure of a Discrete-Event process p. 121

children.title: Insufficient History Representations
children.top_down_role: History summaries that omit information needed for future decisions.

assumptions_latex: The full observed history at time \(t\) is \(H_t\).
The model retains only \(S_t=\phi_t(H_t)\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The representation is insufficient when some admissible action has a conditional cost, feasibility condition, or next-state distribution that is not determined by \((S_t,a)\).

notation.meaning: Compressed state retained by the model.

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Failure of a compressed history to support valid state-based optimization.

source_refs.locator: 3 Introduction to Markov Decision Processes p. 57
4.7 Low-Dimensional Representations of Value Functions p. 144

knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(S_t=\phi_t(H_t)\) compress the complete observed history \(H_t\). The representation is sufficient for state-based control only if, for every admissible action \(a\), the current feasible-action predicate, conditional one-step cost, and conditional law of \(S_{t+1}\) depend on \(H_t\) only through \(S_t\). It is an insufficient history representation if any one of these quantities differs for two histories having the same state. Then a recursion or policy based only on \(S_t\) generally solves an aggregated, not equivalent, control problem.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A history representation is insufficient when retained state does not determine action feasibility, conditional costs, or controlled state transitions.
knowledge_statements.title: Insufficient History Representations

source_witnesses.locator: 3 Introduction to Markov Decision Processes p. 57
4.7 Low-Dimensional Representations of Value Functions p. 144

children.title: Decision-Relevant History Collisions
children.top_down_role: Merged histories whose appropriate future decisions differ.

knowledge_statements.title: Decision-Relevant History Collisions
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Predicate for an aggregation collision that affects feasible or valued continuations.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(\mathcal H_t\) be the time-\(t\) history space, let \(\phi_t:\mathcal H_t\to\mathcal S_t\) be a state representation, let \(A_t(h)\) be the feasible-action set after history \(h\), and let \(Q_t(h,a)\) be the continuation value whenever \(a\in A_t(h)\). Distinct histories \(h,h'\in\mathcal H_t\) form a decision-relevant history collision when \(\phi_t(h)=\phi_t(h')\) and either \(A_t(h)\neq A_t(h')\) or there exists \(a\in A_t(h)\cap A_t(h')\) such that \(Q_t(h,a)\neq Q_t(h',a)\). A collision lacking both differences is not decision-relevant under these criteria.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Merged histories form a decision-relevant collision when they have different feasible actions or give a common action different continuation values.
assumptions_latex: \(\mathcal H_t\) is the time-\(t\) history space and \(\phi_t:\mathcal H_t\to\mathcal S_t\) is a state representation.
For each \(h\in\mathcal H_t\), \(A_t(h)\) is its feasible-action set and \(Q_t(h,a)\) is defined for \(a\in A_t(h)\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: A decision-relevant collision exists when distinct \(h,h'\in\mathcal H_t\) satisfy \(\phi_t(h)=\phi_t(h')\) and differ in feasible actions or in the continuation value of some common feasible action.

notation.meaning: Continuation value for a feasible history-action pair.

source_refs.locator: 4.7 Low-Dimensional Representations of Value Functions p. 144

source_witnesses.locator: 4.7 Low-Dimensional Representations of Value Functions p. 144

children.title: State-Sufficiency Boundaries
children.top_down_role: Regimes separating adequate state compression from information loss.

knowledge_statements.title: State-Sufficiency Boundaries
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Factorization criterion separating state representations adequate for state-based control from lossy representations.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(H_t\) be the complete observed history and let \(S_t=\phi_t(H_t)\) be a measurable state representation. For each admissible action \(a\), suppose the model specifies history-dependent action feasibility, conditional expected one-step cost, and the conditional law of \(S_{t+1}\). The representation is state-sufficient for these objects when there exist state-based functions \(A_t\), \(c_t\), and a transition kernel \(K_t\) such that feasibility is equivalent to \(a\in A_t(S_t)\), the conditional expected cost is \(c_t(S_t,a)\), and \(\mathbb P(S_{t+1}\in B\mid H_t,a)=K_t(B\mid S_t,a)\) for every measurable \(B\). The sufficiency boundary is crossed when any required factorization fails.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A state is sufficient when action feasibility, conditional expected one-step costs, and controlled next-state laws all depend on history only through that state; failure of any required factorization crosses into insufficiency.
assumptions_latex: \(S_t=\phi_t(H_t)\) is a measurable function of the complete observed history \(H_t\).
Action feasibility, conditional expected one-step cost, and the controlled conditional law of \(S_{t+1}\) are specified for every admissible history-action pair.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The representation is state-sufficient exactly when all required feasibility, cost, and transition objects factor through \((S_t,a)\); failure of any factorization crosses the stated sufficiency boundary.

notation.meaning: Controlled transition kernel of the next state.

source_refs.locator: 2.5.2 The Markovian structure of a Discrete-Event process p. 121
3 Introduction to Markov Decision Processes p. 57

children.title: Recourse Feasibility-Value Failure Family
children.top_down_role: Failures of corrective feasibility or finite value.

children.title: Scenario-Dependent Recourse Infeasibility
children.top_down_role: Relevant realizations without corrective actions.

assumptions_latex: For first-stage decision \(x\) and realization \(\xi\), the recourse feasible set is \(Y(x,\xi)\).
A relevant scenario set \(\Xi_0\) is fixed.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: Scenario-dependent recourse infeasibility occurs when \(Y(x,\xi)=\varnothing\) for at least one \(\xi\in\Xi_0\); relatively complete recourse requires \(Y(x,\xi)\neq\varnothing\) for every relevant \(\xi\) and admissible \(x\).

notation.meaning: Second-stage feasible set after x and scenario xi.

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Scenario-wise failure of second-stage feasibility and its relatively-complete-recourse boundary.

source_refs.locator: 1.1.1 Recourse problems p. 5

knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(X\) be the admissible first-stage set and let \(Y(x,\xi)\) be the feasible set of corrective decisions after realization \(\xi\in\Xi_0\). For a fixed \(x\in X\), scenario-dependent recourse infeasibility occurs if there exists \(\xi\in\Xi_0\) with \(Y(x,\xi)=\varnothing\). The model has relatively complete recourse on \(X\times\Xi_0\) precisely when \(Y(x,\xi)\neq\varnothing\) for every \((x,\xi)\in X\times\Xi_0\). Thus failure in even one relevant realization excludes that first-stage decision from the relatively-complete-recourse domain.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Recourse is scenario-infeasible when some relevant realization admits no corrective action; relatively complete recourse excludes this for every admissible first-stage decision.
knowledge_statements.title: Scenario-Dependent Recourse Infeasibility

source_witnesses.locator: 1.1.1 Recourse problems p. 5

children.title: Unbounded Recourse
children.top_down_role: Second-stage models without finite values.

assumptions_latex: For fixed \((x,\xi)\), recourse minimizes \(q(x,\xi,y)\) over \(y\in Y(x,\xi)\).
The feasible set \(Y(x,\xi)\) is nonempty.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: Recourse is unbounded below exactly when \(Q(x,\xi)=-\infty\), equivalently when feasible recourse decisions attain arbitrarily small objective values.
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Minimization convention; the maximization analogue reverses the infinite-value sign.

source_refs.locator: 1.1.1 Recourse problems p. 5

knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For a minimization recourse problem, define \(Q(x,\xi)=\inf_{y\in Y(x,\xi)}q(x,\xi,y)\) with \(Y(x,\xi)\neq\varnothing\). Recourse is unbounded at \((x,\xi)\) when \(Q(x,\xi)=-\infty\); equivalently, for every \(M\in\mathbb R\) there exists \(y_M\in Y(x,\xi)\) such that \(q(x,\xi,y_M)<M\). This is distinct from recourse infeasibility, which has an empty feasible set, and from a finite but unattained recourse infimum.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A nonempty minimization recourse problem is unbounded when feasible corrective actions can drive its objective below every finite bound.
knowledge_statements.title: Unbounded Recourse

source_witnesses.locator: 1.1.1 Recourse problems p. 5

children.title: Tail-Integrability Failure Regimes
children.top_down_role: Undefined or unstable expected recourse.

children.title: Heavy-Tail Recourse Costs
children.top_down_role: Recourse-cost distributions with extreme-tail behavior relevant to model value.

knowledge_statements.title: Heavy-Tail Recourse Costs
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Moment threshold for finite expected second-stage cost.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(\xi\ge 1\) satisfy \(\mathbb P(\xi>t)=t^{-\alpha}\) for \(t\ge1\), with \(\alpha>0\), and let the recourse value be \(Q(x,\xi)=c(x)\xi^r\), where \(c(x)>0\) and \(r>0\). Then \(\mathbb E[Q(x,\xi)]<\infty\) exactly when \(r<\alpha\). At and beyond the boundary \(r\ge\alpha\), recourse is finite scenario-wise but its expected value is infinite, so an expectation-based two-stage objective is not real-valued at \(x\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Pareto-tailed recourse growing with power r has finite expectation precisely when r is below the tail index; otherwise scenario-wise finite costs have infinite mean.
assumptions_latex: \(\mathbb P(\xi>t)=t^{-\alpha}\) for every \(t\ge1\).
\(Q(x,\xi)=c(x)\xi^r\) with \(c(x)>0\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\mathbb E[Q(x,\xi)]<\infty\iff r<\alpha\), while \(\mathbb E[Q(x,\xi)]=+\infty\) for \(r\ge\alpha\).

notation.meaning: optimal second-stage recourse cost at first-stage decision x and realization xi

review_flags: standard_field_rationale: Pareto moment criterion applied directly to a power-growth recourse value

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The Pareto moment boundary and failure-boundary kind are mathematically correct, but no inspectable source with a specific locator is supplied.

children.title: Integrability Loss
children.top_down_role: Recourse regimes lacking the integrability needed for expected-value modeling.

knowledge_statements.title: Integrability Loss
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Loss of first-moment integrability under changing decisions or models.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For a sequence of decisions \(x_n\) and recourse values \(Q_n=Q(x_n,\xi)\), integrability is lost when each \(Q_n\in L^1\) but the candidate limit \(Q\) is not in \(L^1\), or when \(\sup_n\mathbb E|Q_n|=\infty\). In either case, pointwise or almost-sure convergence \(Q_n\to Q\) alone does not justify convergence of expected recourse values. Uniform integrability of \(\{Q_n:n\ge1\}\), together with convergence in probability, excludes this failure and yields \(L^1\) convergence.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Scenario-wise convergence does not preserve expected recourse when first moments escape. Uniform integrability is the relevant boundary preventing this loss.
assumptions_latex: \(Q_n=Q(x_n,\xi)\) are measurable real-valued random variables.
\(Q_n\to Q\) in probability when the stability conclusion is invoked.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: Uniform integrability implies \(\mathbb E|Q_n-Q|\to0\); without it, convergence of \(\mathbb E Q_n\) need not follow.

notation.meaning: recourse value along the nth decision or model

review_flags: standard_field_rationale: uniform-integrability criterion for convergence in the first moment

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The uniform-integrability conclusion is standard under convergence in probability, but the record also labels unbounded first moments as integrability loss. An authoritative locator is needed to support and delimit that terminology.

children.title: Undefined Expected Recourse Values
children.top_down_role: Expected recourse objectives that cease to yield well-defined finite values.

knowledge_statements.title: Undefined Expected Recourse Values
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Failure of the signed Lebesgue expectation.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For an extended-real recourse value \(Q\), write \(Q^+=\max\{Q,0\}\) and \(Q^-=\max\{-Q,0\}\). The signed expectation \(\mathbb E Q\) is undefined when \(\mathbb E Q^+=\mathbb E Q^-=+\infty\); it is not the indeterminate arithmetic expression \(+\infty-\infty\). Concretely, if \(\mathbb P(Q=n)=\mathbb P(Q=-n)=c n^{-2}\) for \(n\ge1\), where \(c^{-1}=2\sum_{n\ge1}n^{-2}\), then \(Q\) is finite almost surely but both one-sided expectations are infinite.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A signed recourse expectation is undefined when its positive and negative parts both have infinite mean, even if every scenario cost is finite.
assumptions_latex: \(Q\) is an extended-real measurable random variable.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\mathbb E Q\) is undefined whenever \(\mathbb E Q^+=\mathbb E Q^-=+\infty\).

notation.meaning: positive and negative parts of the recourse value
normalizing constant in the discrete example

review_flags: standard_field_rationale: definition of the signed Lebesgue expectation through positive and negative parts

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The characterization of an undefined signed Lebesgue expectation and the discrete example are correct, but no inspectable source locator is supplied.

children.title: Tail-Sensitive Stability Boundaries
children.top_down_role: Transitions where tail behavior undermines stable recourse valuation.

knowledge_statements.title: Tail-Sensitive Stability Boundaries
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Wasserstein order required by recourse growth.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(p\ge1\), \(q>p\), and \(\varepsilon=(q-p)/2\). Define \(\mu_n=(1-n^{-(p+\varepsilon)})\delta_0+n^{-(p+\varepsilon)}\delta_n\). Then \(W_p(\mu_n,\delta_0)^p=n^{-\varepsilon}\to0\), but for the recourse function \(Q(z)=|z|^q\), \(\int Q\,d\mu_n=n^{q-p-\varepsilon}=n^{(q-p)/2}\to\infty\). Thus convergence in \(W_p\) does not stabilize expectations of recourse growing faster than order \(p\); stronger moments or uniform integrability of the recourse family are required.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Wasserstein-p convergence controls recourse expectations only within compatible tail growth; faster-than-p costs can diverge despite distributional convergence.
assumptions_latex: \(p\ge1\) and \(q>p\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(W_p(\mu_n,\delta_0)\to0\) while \(\int Q\,d\mu_n\to+\infty\).
review_flags: standard_field_rationale: explicit two-point measures establish the moment-growth boundary

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The two-point construction and Wasserstein calculation are correct and fit the failure-boundary leaf, but the claimed general stability boundary requires an authoritative source locator.

children.title: Measurable Selection Failure Regimes
children.top_down_role: Failure of admissible scenario-dependent selection.

children.title: Measurability Failures
children.top_down_role: Scenario-dependent recourse objects that lack the required measurable structure.

knowledge_statements.title: Measurability Failures
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Failure of measurable recourse values or policies.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \((\Omega,\mathcal F,\mathbb P)\) be a probability space, \(Y\) a measurable action space, \(F:\Omega\rightrightarrows Y\) a feasible correspondence, and \(g:\Omega\times Y\to\overline{\mathbb R}\) a second-stage cost. A measurability failure occurs if the value \(Q(\omega)=\inf_{y\in F(\omega)}g(\omega,y)\) is not \(\mathcal F\)-measurable or if no \(\mathcal F\)-measurable feasible selector exists. Then \(\mathbb E Q\) is not an ordinary Lebesgue expectation or the recourse policy is inadmissible, respectively.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Recourse fails measurably when its value is not a random variable or its pointwise feasible actions admit no measurable policy.
assumptions_latex: \((\Omega,\mathcal F,\mathbb P)\) is a probability space.
\(F(\omega)\subseteq Y\) is nonempty for every scenario.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: Nonmeasurability of \(Q\), or absence of a measurable selector of \(F\), invalidates the corresponding expected-value recourse formulation.
review_flags: standard_field_rationale: measurable-value and measurable-selector requirements for stochastic recourse

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The record correctly separates nonmeasurable values from absence of measurable feasible selectors, but measurable-value and selection claims require an authoritative, inspectable source.

children.title: Admissible Selection Failures
children.top_down_role: Cases where available scenario-wise choices do not support an admissible selector.

knowledge_statements.title: Admissible Selection Failures
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Pointwise feasibility without an admissible measurable selector.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Given a probability space \((\Omega,\mathcal F,\mathbb P)\), a measurable action space \((Y,\mathcal Y)\), and a nonempty-valued feasible correspondence \(F:\Omega\rightrightarrows Y\), define \(\mathcal A(F)=\{y:\Omega\to Y:y\text{ is }(\mathcal F,\mathcal Y)\text{-measurable and }y(\omega)\in F(\omega)\text{ a.s.}\}\). An admissible selection failure is the condition \(F(\omega)\ne\varnothing\) almost surely but \(\mathcal A(F)=\varnothing\). Hence almost-sure pointwise feasibility does not by itself produce an implementable random recourse decision.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Every scenario may have a feasible action while no measurable policy selects feasible actions almost surely; pointwise recourse then is not implementable.
assumptions_latex: \((\Omega,\mathcal F,\mathbb P)\) is a probability space.
\((Y,\mathcal Y)\) is a measurable action space.
\(F:\Omega\rightrightarrows Y\) has nonempty values almost surely.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(F(\omega)\ne\varnothing\) a.s. does not imply \(\mathcal A(F)\ne\varnothing\).

notation.meaning: set of measurable almost-sure selectors of F
sigma-algebra on the action space Y

review_flags: standard_field_rationale: admissibility requires measurable almost-sure selection, which is stronger than pointwise nonemptiness

children.title: Nonmeasurable Optimizer Correspondences
children.top_down_role: Optimizer mappings whose scenario dependence obstructs measurable policy construction.

knowledge_statements.title: Nonmeasurable Optimizer Correspondences
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Argmin mappings lacking measurable optimal selections.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \((\Omega,\mathcal F)\) be a measurable space, choose \(A\in2^\Omega\setminus\mathcal F\), let \(Y=\{0,1\}\) carry its discrete sigma-algebra, and define \(g:\Omega\times Y\to\mathbb R\) by \(g(\omega,y)=(y-\mathbf 1_A(\omega))^2\). Then \(S(\omega)=\operatorname*{argmin}_{y\in Y}g(\omega,y)=\{\mathbf 1_A(\omega)\}\). Its unique selector is not \(\mathcal F\)-measurable because the inverse image of \(\{1\}\) is \(A\). Thus a unique optimizer can exist at every scenario while the optimizer correspondence has no measurable selector.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A pointwise optimizer can exist uniquely everywhere yet depend on a nonmeasurable event, preventing any measurable optimal policy.
assumptions_latex: \((\Omega,\mathcal F)\) is a measurable space.
\(A\notin\mathcal F\).
\(Y=\{0,1\}\) carries its discrete sigma-algebra.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(S(\omega)=\{\mathbf 1_A(\omega)\}\) has no \(\mathcal F\)-measurable selector.

notation.meaning: indicator of the nonmeasurable set A

review_flags: standard_field_rationale: explicit nonmeasurable singleton-valued argmin construction

children.title: Scenario-Dependent Policy Breakdown
children.top_down_role: Loss of implementable recourse policies across uncertainty realizations.

knowledge_statements.title: Scenario-Dependent Policy Breakdown
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Scenario-indexed decisions that violate policy measurability.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \((\Omega,\mathcal F,\mathbb P)\) be a probability space, let \((Y,\mathcal Y)\) be a measurable action space, let \(F:\Omega\rightrightarrows Y\) be a feasible correspondence, and let \(g:\Omega\times Y\to\overline{\mathbb R}\) be a second-stage cost. Define \(Q(\omega)=\inf_{y\in F(\omega)}g(\omega,y)\), and let \(\mathcal G\subseteq\mathcal F\) be the decision-time information sigma-algebra. Scenario-dependent policy breakdown occurs when every pointwise argmin is nonempty but the argmin correspondence has no \(\mathcal G\)-measurable selector. In that case no policy in \(\mathcal Y_{\mathcal G}=\{y:\Omega\to Y:y\text{ is }(\mathcal G,\mathcal Y)\text{-measurable and }y(\omega)\in F(\omega)\text{ a.s.}\}\) attains \(Q(\omega)\) scenario-wise.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Solving each scenario independently may produce optimizers that cannot be assembled into a policy measurable with respect to the available information.
assumptions_latex: \((\Omega,\mathcal F,\mathbb P)\) is a probability space.
\((Y,\mathcal Y)\) is a measurable action space.
\(\operatorname*{argmin}_{y\in F(\omega)}g(\omega,y)\ne\varnothing\) for every \(\omega\).
\(\mathcal G\subseteq\mathcal F\) is the information available when recourse is chosen.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: If the argmin correspondence has no \(\mathcal G\)-measurable selector, no policy in \(\mathcal Y_{\mathcal G}\) attains \(Q\) scenario-wise.

notation.meaning: feasible policies measurable with respect to available information

review_flags: standard_field_rationale: admissible nonanticipative policies must be measurable with respect to decision-time information

children.title: Process-Representation Failure Family
children.top_down_role: Distortion caused by inadequate uncertainty or policy representations.

children.title: Interstage Dependence Misspecification
children.top_down_role: Invalid simplification of conditional dependence.

knowledge_statements.title: Interstage Dependence Misspecification
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Equal marginals do not preserve adaptive value.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(\xi_1,\xi_2\) be Bernoulli random variables with parameter \(1/2\), and choose a \(\sigma(\xi_1)\)-measurable prediction \(y\) minimizing \(\mathbb E[(y-\xi_2)^2]\). If \(\xi_1\) and \(\xi_2\) are independent, the optimizer is \(y=1/2\) and the value is \(1/4\). If \(\xi_2=\xi_1\) almost surely, the optimizer is \(y=\xi_1\) and the value is \(0\). Both models have identical one-stage marginals, so replacing conditional dependence by marginal information can change the recourse value.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Two processes with identical stagewise marginals yield different adaptive values when one is independent and the other perfectly dependent.
assumptions_latex: \(\xi_1\) and \(\xi_2\) each have the Bernoulli distribution with parameter \(1/2\).
\(y\) is measurable with respect to \(\sigma(\xi_1)\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The independent model has value \(1/4\), whereas the model \(\xi_2=\xi_1\) a.s. has value \(0\).

notation.meaning: information generated by the first-stage observation

children.title: Scenario-Tree Misspecification
children.top_down_role: Distorted marginal, conditional, or pathwise behavior.

knowledge_statements.title: Scenario-Tree Misspecification
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Mismatch between a tree law and the target process law.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(P\) be the target law of \(\xi_{1:T}\), and let \(\widehat P\) be the path law induced by a scenario tree on the same measurable path space. The tree is correctly specified for the modeled process exactly when \(\widehat P=P\). When regular conditional distributions exist, equality of the initial law together with equality, up to the relevant almost-sure versions, of \(\widehat P(\xi_{t+1}\in B\mid\xi_{1:t})\) and \(P(\xi_{t+1}\in B\mid\xi_{1:t})\) for every \(t<T\) and measurable \(B\) is sufficient to reproduce the joint law. A mismatch in the initial law or in a conditional law on a history set of positive probability constitutes scenario-tree misspecification and may distort marginal, conditional, or path-dependent objectives.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A scenario tree is correctly specified when its path law equals the target process law; a mismatch in the initial distribution or a conditional transition on relevant histories is misspecification.
assumptions_latex: \(P\) and \(\widehat P\) are probability laws on the same measurable path space.
Regular conditional distributions exist when the kernel characterization is used.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: Correct specification requires \(\widehat P=P\); disagreement of the initial law or a relevant conditional law implies misspecification.

notation.meaning: path law represented by the scenario tree

children.title: Filtration Distortion
children.top_down_role: Approximation that changes available information.

knowledge_statements.title: Filtration Distortion
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Optimization value changes when represented information changes.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For sigma-algebras \(\mathcal G\subseteq\mathcal H\), define \(V(\mathcal K)=\inf\{\mathbb E[\ell(y,\xi)]:y\text{ is }\mathcal K\text{-measurable}\}\). Since every \(\mathcal G\)-measurable policy is \(\mathcal H\)-measurable, \(V(\mathcal H)\le V(\mathcal G)\). The inequality can be strict: if \(\xi\) is Bernoulli with parameter \(1/2\), \(\ell(y,\xi)=(y-\xi)^2\), \(\mathcal G=\{\varnothing,\Omega\}\), and \(\mathcal H=\sigma(\xi)\), then \(V(\mathcal G)=1/4\) and \(V(\mathcal H)=0\). Thus changing the represented information can bias the computed optimal value.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Refining the represented information enlarges the admissible policy set and can strictly lower a minimization value; deleting information can therefore worsen the computed value.
assumptions_latex: \(\mathcal G\subseteq\mathcal H\) are decision-time sigma-algebras.
\(\xi\) is a random variable on the underlying probability space.
The displayed expectations and infima are well defined.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(V(\mathcal H)\le V(\mathcal G)\), with strict inequality possible.

notation.meaning: optimal value under policies measurable with respect to information sigma-algebra K

children.title: Decision-Rule Restriction Bias
children.top_down_role: Loss of adaptive value from a restricted policy class.

knowledge_statements.title: Decision-Rule Restriction Bias
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Optimality gap induced by a restricted policy class.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(\Pi_r\subseteq\Pi\) be a restricted class of admissible decision rules, and suppose the finite values \(V_r=\inf_{\pi\in\Pi_r}J(\pi)\) and \(V^*=\inf_{\pi\in\Pi}J(\pi)\) are well defined. For minimization, the restriction bias is \(B_r=V_r-V^*\ge0\). It can be strict: if \(\xi\) is nondegenerate with finite variance, \(J(y)=\mathbb E[(y(\xi)-\xi)^2]\), \(\Pi\) contains all measurable rules, and \(\Pi_r\) contains only constant rules, then \(V^*=0\) while \(V_r=\operatorname{Var}(\xi)>0\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Restricting admissible policies cannot improve a minimization optimum and can create a strict gap by removing useful adaptation.
assumptions_latex: \(\Pi_r\subseteq\Pi\).
\(J(\pi)\) is well defined for every \(\pi\in\Pi\).
\(V_r\) and \(V^*\) are finite.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(B_r=V_r-V^*\ge0\); moreover, \(B_r=0\) exactly when \(\inf_{\pi\in\Pi_r}J(\pi)=\inf_{\pi\in\Pi}J(\pi)\).

children.title: Nonconvex Certificate Failure Boundary
