children.title: Nonconvex Recourse Geometry
children.top_down_role: Geometric features of recourse models that obstruct convex support structures.

assumptions_latex: \(x\in\mathbb R\).
The second-stage value is \(Q(x)=\min\{(x-1)^2,(x+1)^2\}\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(Q\) is nonconvex, and no affine global lower bound can coincide with \(Q\) at \(x=0\).
review_flags: standard_field_rationale: the two-well value function is a direct finite-dimensional counterexample to convex recourse geometry
source_gap: supplied recourse locator does not specifically document this nonconvex example
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Concrete scalar failure of convex recourse geometry and affine support.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(Q:\mathbb R\to\mathbb R\) be the recourse value function \[Q(x)=\min\{(x-1)^2,(x+1)^2\}.\] Then \(Q(-1)=Q(1)=0\) while \(Q(0)=1\), so the convexity inequality at the midpoint fails. Moreover, if an affine function \(a(x)=\alpha x+\beta\) satisfies \(a(x)\le Q(x)\) for every \(x\), then \(a(-1)\le0\) and \(a(1)\le0\), which imply \(a(0)=\beta\le0<Q(0)\). Thus nonconvex recourse can lack a globally supporting affine certificate at a feasible first-stage point.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A two-well recourse value is nonconvex and admits no globally valid affine lower support touching it at the midpoint.
knowledge_statements.title: Nonconvex Recourse Geometry

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The counterexample is mathematically correct and fits the leaf, but it has no cited source and the statement includes proof-like derivation. Supply a specific source locator before review.

children.title: Supporting-Certificate Failure
children.top_down_role: Loss of globally valid supporting certificates for recourse value representation.

assumptions_latex: \(Q:X\to\mathbb R\cup\{+\infty\}\) is a recourse value function.
\(\bar x\in\operatorname{dom}Q\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: A supporting affine certificate fails at \(\bar x\) exactly when \(\partial Q(\bar x)=\varnothing\).

notation.meaning: global convex subdifferential of Q at the reference point

review_flags: standard_field_rationale: global affine support is equivalent by definition to membership in the convex subdifferential
source_gap: supplied source inventory lacks a locator for nonconvex supporting certificates
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Global affine lower certificates for a possibly nonconvex recourse value.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For \(g\in X^*\), define \(a_g(x)=Q(\bar x)+\langle g,x-\bar x\rangle\). A supporting affine certificate at \(\bar x\) is a vector \(g\) satisfying \[Q(x)\ge Q(\bar x)+\langle g,x-\bar x\rangle\quad\text{for every }x\in X.\] Hence such a certificate exists exactly when the global convex subdifferential \(\partial Q(\bar x)\) is nonempty. A local gradient, multiplier, or stationary-point condition does not provide this certificate unless it also establishes the displayed inequality globally.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A supporting certificate exists precisely when a global affine lower bound touches the recourse value at the reference point.
knowledge_statements.title: Supporting-Certificate Failure

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The global-support characterization fits this failure-boundary leaf, but no source is cited and the structure of X needed to define X* and the dual pairing is unspecified.

children.title: Local Versus Global Certificates
children.top_down_role: Separation between locally informative certificates and globally valid support.

assumptions_latex: \(Q:X\to\mathbb R\cup\{+\infty\}\) and \(\bar x\in\operatorname{dom}Q\).
\(U\subseteq X\) is a neighborhood of \(\bar x\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: Every global certificate is local, but a local certificate is globally valid only if its inequality extends from \(U\) to all of \(X\).
review_flags: standard_field_rationale: local and global support are distinguished by the quantifier domain in their defining inequalities
source_gap: no supplied locator directly treats local versus global recourse certificates
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Quantifier boundary separating local from globally valid supporting cuts.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: A vector \(g\in X^*\) is a local certificate for \(Q\) at \(\bar x\) on \(U\) when \[Q(x)\ge Q(\bar x)+\langle g,x-\bar x\rangle\quad\text{for every }x\in U.\] It is a global certificate when the same inequality holds for every \(x\in X\). Global validity implies local validity for every neighborhood, but the converse fails without an additional global property, such as convexity of \(Q\) together with \(g\in\partial Q(\bar x)\). Therefore a locally valid optimality condition cannot alone justify a decomposition cut imposed over the entire master domain.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Local support controls only a neighborhood; a decomposition cut requires the same lower-bound inequality over the full master domain.
knowledge_statements.title: Local Versus Global Certificates

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The local/global distinction fits the leaf, but it lacks a source. The correction should also state directly that for convex Q, a touching affine minorant valid on a neighborhood extends globally; requiring prior membership in the global subdifferential is circular.

children.title: Decomposition Validity Boundaries
children.top_down_role: Nonconvex regimes where certificate-based decomposition loses global validity.

knowledge_statements.title: Decomposition Validity Boundaries
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Certificate boundary for globally valid cutting-plane decomposition.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(X\) be the master feasible set, let \(c:X\to\mathbb R\), and let \(Q:X\to\mathbb R\cup\{+\infty\}\). For affine functions \(\ell_k:X\to\mathbb R\), define \(\widehat Q(x)=\sup_k\ell_k(x)\). Suppose \(\ell_k(x)\le Q(x)\) for every \(k\) and every \(x\in X\), and let \(x^*\in\operatorname*{arg\,min}_{x\in X}\{c(x)+\widehat Q(x)\}\). If \(\widehat Q(x^*)=Q(x^*)\), then \(x^*\in\operatorname*{arg\,min}_{x\in X}\{c(x)+Q(x)\}\). This global certificate is not established if global cut validity or exactness at \(x^*\) is unavailable.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A master minimizer is certified globally optimal when every cut is a global lower bound for recourse and the cut model is exact at that minimizer; without either condition, this certificate is unavailable.
assumptions_latex: \(X\) is the master feasible set, \(c:X\to\mathbb R\), and \(Q:X\to\mathbb R\cup\{+\infty\}\).
Each \(\ell_k:X\to\mathbb R\) is affine and satisfies \(\ell_k(x)\le Q(x)\) for every \(x\in X\).
\(x^*\in\operatorname*{arg\,min}_{x\in X}\{c(x)+\sup_k\ell_k(x)\}\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: If \(\sup_k\ell_k(x^*)=Q(x^*)\), then \(x^*\in\operatorname*{arg\,min}_{x\in X}\{c(x)+Q(x)\}\).

notation.meaning: master minimizer at which exactness is tested

children.title: Dependence-Induced Nonseparability
children.top_down_role: Unresolved dependence preventing stage separation.

knowledge_statements.title: Dependence-Induced Nonseparability
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Additive-separability test for a recourse value formed under a joint uncertainty law.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(X_1\) and \(X_2\) be nonempty sets and let \(Q:X_1\times X_2\to\mathbb R\). For \(a,a'\in X_1\) and \(b,b'\in X_2\), define \(\Delta Q(a,a';b,b')=Q(a,b)+Q(a',b')-Q(a,b')-Q(a',b)\). If \(\Delta Q(a,a';b,b')\ne0\) for some quadruple, then no functions \(q_1:X_1\to\mathbb R\) and \(q_2:X_2\to\mathbb R\) satisfy \(Q(x_1,x_2)=q_1(x_1)+q_2(x_2)\) for every \((x_1,x_2)\in X_1\times X_2\). When \(Q\) is induced by a dependent joint law, this condition detects resulting nonseparability but does not by itself identify dependence as its cause.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A nonzero rectangular mixed difference rules out additive stage separation. For a value formed under dependent uncertainty, it detects nonseparability but does not alone prove what caused it.
assumptions_latex: \(X_1\) and \(X_2\) are nonempty sets.
\((\xi_1,\xi_2)\) has a specified joint law.
For every \((x_1,x_2)\in X_1\times X_2\), the random variable \(V(x_1,x_2,\xi_1,\xi_2)\) is integrable and \(Q(x_1,x_2)=\mathbb E[V(x_1,x_2,\xi_1,\xi_2)]\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: If \(\Delta Q(a,a';b,b')\ne0\) for some \(a,a'\in X_1\) and \(b,b'\in X_2\), then \(Q\) is not additively separable across \(X_1\) and \(X_2\).

children.title: Nonrecombining History Explosion
children.top_down_role: Failure of compact representation under path dependence.

knowledge_statements.title: Nonrecombining History Explosion
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Exact node-count growth for a regular nonrecombining scenario tree.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(b\ge2\) be a fixed integer and let \(T\in\mathbb N_0\). A rooted regular scenario tree in which every node before stage \(T\) has exactly \(b\) successors and no distinct histories recombine has \(b^t\) nodes at stage \(t\) and \[N_T=\sum_{t=0}^{T}b^t=\frac{b^{T+1}-1}{b-1}.\] Consequently, \(N_T=\Theta(b^T)\) as \(T\to\infty\). Under unit-cost storage and processing per node, explicit enumeration requires \(\Theta(b^T)\) memory and time.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: For a fixed branching factor, a regular nonrecombining scenario tree has exponentially many nodes in the horizon, so explicit enumeration has exponential memory and time requirements.
assumptions_latex: \(b\ge2\) is a fixed integer and \(T\in\mathbb N_0\).
Every node before stage \(T\) has exactly \(b\) successors.
Distinct histories cannot be merged without changing feasibility, transition laws, costs, or continuation values.
Storage and processing cost per explicit node is \(\Theta(1)\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The tree contains \(N_T=(b^{T+1}-1)/(b-1)=\Theta(b^T)\) nodes as \(T\to\infty\), with the same asymptotic explicit-enumeration time and memory bounds.

notation.meaning: total number of nodes through stage T

knowledge_statements.title: Recursive Formulation Failure
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Boundary for representing a finite-horizon multistage preference by Bellman recursion on a proposed state.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Consider stages \(t=0,\ldots,T\), reachable histories \(h_t\), and a proposed state map \(S_t=S_t(h_t)\). A Bellman representation on this state requires value functions \(V_t\) and one-step conditional operators \(\mathcal R_t\) satisfying \[V_t(s)=\inf_{a\in A(s)}\mathcal R_t\bigl(c_t(s,a),V_{t+1}(S_{t+1})\mid S_t=s,a\bigr)\] at every reachable state. Such a representation fails on the proposed state if two histories with the same state induce different feasible actions, conditional transition or cost laws, or continuation rankings. It also fails if the continuation evaluations cannot be represented by nesting the one-step operators \(\mathcal R_t\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Bellman recursion on a proposed state fails when histories merged into that state differ in decision-relevant data or when continuation preferences cannot be nested through one-step operators.
assumptions_latex: The horizon is finite, with stages \(t=0,\ldots,T\).
Each reachable history \(h_t\) is mapped to a proposed state \(S_t(h_t)\).
\(A(s)\) is the feasible action set at state \(s\), and \(J_t(\cdot\mid h_t)\) is the continuation evaluation at history \(h_t\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: No Bellman recursion on the proposed state represents the conditional problems if state-equivalent histories differ in decision-relevant data or continuation rankings, or if the evaluations \(J_t\) admit no compatible one-step nesting.

notation.meaning: feasible action set at state s

Assume \(\pi^*

knowledge_statements.title: Sequential Compatibility Boundaries
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Strong universal conditional-optimality condition for multistage policy compatibility.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(\Pi\) be the feasible policy set and let \(\Pi_0^*=\operatorname*{arg\,min}_{\pi\in\Pi}J_0(\pi)\). For each stage \(t\) and reachable history \(h_t\), let \(\Gamma(h_t)\) be the set of feasible continuations and let \(J_t(\cdot\mid h_t)\) evaluate those continuations. Strong sequential compatibility holds when, for every \(\pi^*\in\Pi_0^*\), every stage \(t\), and every history \(h_t\) reachable under \(\pi^*\), \[\pi^*_{t:}\in\operatorname*{arg\,min}_{\gamma\in\Gamma(h_t)}J_t(\gamma\mid h_t).\] Its failure boundary is the existence of one such triple \((\pi^*,t,h_t)\) for which this inclusion fails.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Strong sequential compatibility requires the continuation of every initially optimal policy to remain conditionally optimal after every history reachable under that policy.
assumptions_latex: \(\Pi\) is the feasible policy set, and every \(\pi\in\Pi\) has a well-defined initial evaluation \(J_0(\pi)\).
For each stage \(t\) and reachable history \(h_t\), \(\Gamma(h_t)\) is the set of feasible continuations and \(J_t(\cdot\mid h_t)\) is defined on \(\Gamma(h_t)\).
Continuation feasibility and evaluation are conditioned on the same observed history \(h_t\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: Strong sequential compatibility holds exactly when every \(\pi^*\in\Pi_0^*\) satisfies \(\pi^*_{t:}\in\operatorname*{arg\,min}_{\gamma\in\Gamma(h_t)}J_t(\gamma\mid h_t)\) at every history \(h_t\) reachable under \(\pi^*\).

notation.meaning: continuation of an initially optimal policy after history h_t
